state:
CSI Teardown Path does not contain `volume_id`

Teardown path does not contain `volume_id` or `driver_name`

* During mount, the CSI Mounter (i.e. `NewMounter(...)`), sets `volumeID` and `driverName` to `pvSource.VolumeHandle` and `pvSource.Driver` (see [link]
* `volumeID` and `driverName` are then used to generate the target mount path: e.g. `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/e6a8b147-d74d-11e7-a08f-42010a800002/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/com.google.csi~gcepd/mypd` (see [link]
* On unmount, the CSI unmounter leaves `volumeID` and `driverName` empty (see [link] because it does not have the volume spec on unmount (Kubernetes wants to maintain the ability to unmount even if a spec is not available).
* Therefore when the path to unmount is generated, it is missing the `volumeID` and `driverName` and the unmount function will either be unable to establish a connection to the CSI client (because `volumeID` and `driverName` is missing) or the CSI `NodeUnpublishVolumeRequest` receives an incomplete path (because : e.g. `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/e6a8b147-d74d-11e7-a08f-42010a800002/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi`.
On unmount function should be able to call CSI `NodeUnpublishVolumeRequest` without issue.
See above.
Possible solutions:

1. Attempt to parse the target path to recover these fields
* Cons:
* If multiple CSI volumes exist for 1 pod, this may get tricky.
* If csi volume_id is very long or contains invalid characters recovery via path may not be possible.
2. Store required information (`volumeID` and `driverName`) in a file along with mount.
* Cons: managing a file can get tricky for backwards compatibility.

state:
Mismatch between crio.sock location in crio and kubelet

BUG REPORT

While configuring the kubelet with:
`--container-runtime-endpoint="unix:///var/run/crio.sock"`
And having the sock file on that location (default location from cri), the following error occurs:

`Dec 10 18:30:52 kubeworker01 kubelet[15060]: W1210 18:30:52.739721 15060 manager.go:291] Registration of the crio container factory failed: Get [link] dial unix /var/run/crio/crio.sock: connect: no such file or directory`

Later line:
`Dec 10 18:30:50 kubeworker01 kubelet[15060]: I1210 18:30:50.712558 15060 remote_runtime.go:43] Connecting to runtime service unix:///var/run/crio.sock`

Uses the correct socket.

Result:
Disruptive in understanding other failures.
Containers still start.

state:
Mismatch between crio.sock location in crio and kubelet

BUG REPORT

While configuring the kubelet with:
`--container-runtime-endpoint="unix:///var/run/crio.sock"`
And having the sock file on that location (default location from cri), the following error occurs:

`Dec 10 18:30:52 kubeworker01 kubelet[15060]: W1210 18:30:52.739721 15060 manager.go:291] Registration of the crio container factory failed: Get [link] dial unix /var/run/crio/crio.sock: connect: no such file or directory`

Later line:
`Dec 10 18:30:50 kubeworker01 kubelet[15060]: I1210 18:30:50.712558 15060 remote_runtime.go:43] Connecting to runtime service unix:///var/run/crio.sock`

Uses the correct socket.

Result:
Disruptive in understanding other failures.
Containers still start.

state:
Kubelet often fails on AWS spot instances

In a kops created cluster running Kubernetes 1.8.4 nodes sometimes start but fail to connect to the masters. I have tracked the issue down to this difference:

Failed:
I1216 07:28:57.369519 1900 aws.go:847] Building AWS cloudprovider
I1216 07:28:57.369555 1900 aws.go:810] Zone not specified in configuration file; querying AWS metadata service
E1216 07:28:57.586712 1900 tags.go:94] Tag "KubernetesCluster" nor "kubernetes.io/cluster/..." not found; Kubernetes may behave unexpectedly.
W1216 07:28:57.586744 1900 tags.go:78] AWS cloud - no clusterID filtering applied for shared resources; do not run multiple clusters in this AZ.
I1216 07:28:57.586807 1900 server.go:301] Successfully initialized cloud provider: "aws" from the config file: ""

Successful:
I1218 08:32:38.492573 28476 aws.go:847] Building AWS cloudprovider
I1218 08:32:38.492596 28476 aws.go:810] Zone not specified in configuration file; querying AWS metadata service
I1218 08:32:38.669713 28476 tags.go:76] AWS cloud filtering on ClusterID: kube.test.int
I1218 08:32:38.669788 28476 server.go:301] Successfully initialized cloud provider: "aws" from the config file: ""

So in the failing case the AWS metadata either doesn't respond or the response is missing critical information (I'm not sure how to find out which). This query isn't retried during kubelets general "retry connecting to the api" loop, so the kubelet will keep running but it will never retrieve the information it needs to install and configure calico and join the network.

I1218 08:32:38.669788 28476 server.go:301] Successfully initialized cloud provider: "aws" from the config file: ""

So in the failing case the AWS metadata either doesn't respond or the response is missing critical information (I'm not sure how to find out which). This query isn't retried during kubelets general "retry connecting to the api" loop, so the kubelet will keep running but it will never retrieve the information it needs to install and configure calico and join the network.

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.

Automated Debian Base Images

Our core/base images should be built and housed on Kubernetes Community Infra.

- `debian-base`
- `debian-iptables`
From @user:

Currently, the Debian base images used to create the hyperkube and other images use a Base Debian docker image that is generated and pushed to gcr.io. It would be awesome to automate the debian base images to automatically be built so they contain patched binaries with security updates.

By enabling this functionality, builds would always use a modern base image with patched binaries.

We currently depend an extremely small set of Googlers to push these images.
There's minimal public documentation or visibility into this process and it creates a bottleneck when trying to do updates. This is especially detrimental from a security standpoint.

state:
at large scale, kube-apiserver CPU-starves to death at 8qps of "Endpoints PATCH"

In a 5k-node cluster, the `kube-apiserver` running on a 64-core master, is unable to handle 8qps of `Endpoints` PATCH requests. Its CPU usage exceeds 60 cores for extended amounts of time, at which point kubelet's liveness checks fail, and apiserver is killed.

![repro]([link]

In the above graph, the blue line is `kube-apiserver`'s CPU usage in cores, and the red line is the request rate of `PATCH /api/v1/namespaces/default/endpoints/endpoints-test`.

The PATCH requests above are simply fliping a single `Endpoints` object back and forth between two states: one in which it has 400 fake child addresses, and another in which it has 401 of them. There are no associated `Service`s, `Deployment`s or `Pod`s. Just mutating the `Endpoints` object is enough.

I plan to run this again to collect a profile, but I suspect it will be very similar to the one in [link] - i.e. CPU is burned in memory management due to the expensive `Endpoints` deep-copying when serving the 5000 watches from kube-proxy.
For one thing, propagating `Endpoints` objects should scale better. Some ideas on improvements in this area are in [link] and two comments which follow it, and generally revolve around caching the serialized representation of `Endpoints` objects.

I think there should also be a more generic load shedding mechanism in the API server that would protect against meltdown is these kinds of problems.
1. create a 5000 node cluster
2. log into the master and write the following files:

3. optional: start the following command to collect CPU usage of the API server to graph it later:

4. bash stress.sh > 400.csv
5. optional: `kill %1` to stop CPU usage gathering
The above may at first seem like a use case which nobody would ever exercise.

state:
at large scale, kube-apiserver CPU-starves to death at 8qps of "Endpoints PATCH"

In a 5k-node cluster, the `kube-apiserver` running on a 64-core master, is unable to handle 8qps of `Endpoints` PATCH requests. Its CPU usage exceeds 60 cores for extended amounts of time, at which point kubelet's liveness checks fail, and apiserver is killed.

![repro]([link]

In the above graph, the blue line is `kube-apiserver`'s CPU usage in cores, and the red line is the request rate of `PATCH /api/v1/namespaces/default/endpoints/endpoints-test`.

The PATCH requests above are simply fliping a single `Endpoints` object back and forth between two states: one in which it has 400 fake child addresses, and another in which it has 401 of them. There are no associated `Service`s, `Deployment`s or `Pod`s. Just mutating the `Endpoints` object is enough.

I plan to run this again to collect a profile, but I suspect it will be very similar to the one in [link] - i.e. CPU is burned in memory management due to the expensive `Endpoints` deep-copying when serving the 5000 watches from kube-proxy.
For one thing, propagating `Endpoints` objects should scale better. Some ideas on improvements in this area are in [link] and two comments which follow it, and generally revolve around caching the serialized representation of `Endpoints` objects.

I think there should also be a more generic load shedding mechanism in the API server that would protect against meltdown is these kinds of problems.
1. create a 5000 node cluster
2. log into the master and write the following files:

3. optional: start the following command to collect CPU usage of the API server to graph it later:

4. bash stress.sh > 400.csv
5. optional: `kill %1` to stop CPU usage gathering
The above may at first seem like a use case which nobody would ever exercise.

Routing determination: network. Bug assessment: a bug.

state:
Request to add namespace name and namespace UUID to metadata of on-disk log file

We assert that a log file on-disk (via CRI-O, or docker's json-file logging driver) should have metadata associated with that log file to describe the UUIDs _and_ names of the container, pod, **and** namespace associated with the log output to avoid k8s API calls later. Today it does not _appear_ to include the namespace UUID or name (see [link]

Ideally (and arguably), a log collection system *should not be required* to query the Kube APIs about the log data in order to find the UUIDs of the k8s resource hierarchy associated with a container. Only _optional_ metadata that decorates or enriches the log data would necessitate API calls to fetch that metadata; e.g., if one wanted to decorate logs with one or more labels or annotations from a pod or namespace. A log collection system should be able to properly disambiguate and group logs accurately without additional API calls which might cause undo burden on the API server. Since any metadata needed to be fetched via API calls is optional, it can be dropped when inconvenient or added later as a post-processing step.

The "location" of a container in a single k8s cluster is fully described by four pieces of information:

* hostname
* container UUID (and name)
* pod UUID (and name)
* namespace UUID (and name)

With the above information, understanding the origin of one or more log entries in an aggregation of logs can be accomplished unambiguously with respect to k8s in one cluster. Today, it appears that k8s provides 3 of the 4 pieces of data, hostname (implicitly), container, and pod, when constructing the symlink for the log file path.

Can we consider adding namespace UUID and namespace name as well?

We assert that a log file on-disk (via CRI-O, or docker's json-file logging driver) should have metadata associated with that log file to describe the UUIDs _and_ names of the container, pod, **and** namespace associated with the log output to avoid k8s API calls later. Today it does not _appear_ to include the namespace UUID or name (see [link]

Ideally (and arguably), a log collection system *should not be required* to query the Kube APIs about the log data in order to find the UUIDs of the k8s resource hierarchy associated with a container. Only _optional_ metadata that decorates or enriches the log data would necessitate API calls to fetch that metadata; e.g., if one wanted to decorate logs with one or more labels or annotations from a pod or namespace. A log collection system should be able to properly disambiguate and group logs accurately without additional API calls which might cause undo burden on the API server. Since any metadata needed to be fetched via API calls is optional, it can be dropped when inconvenient or added later as a post-processing step.

The "location" of a container in a single k8s cluster is fully described by four pieces of information:

* hostname
* container UUID (and name)
* pod UUID (and name)
* namespace UUID (and name)

With the above information, understanding the origin of one or more log entries in an aggregation of logs can be accomplished unambiguously with respect to k8s in one cluster. Today, it appears that k8s provides 3 of the 4 pieces of data, hostname (implicitly), container, and pod, when constructing the symlink for the log file path.

Can we consider adding namespace UUID and namespace name as well?

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: not a bug.

state:
CRI: Implement container log rotation

TL;DR: We want to allow kubelet to rotate the container stdout/stderr logs, and add a CRI call to ask the runtime to reopen the log file.

kubelet decides the log directory structure and passes to the runtime the path where container log should be stored. Given the level of knowledge and control kubelet has, it is currently the best candidate to rotate the logs (vs. runtime or a separate daemon). The detailed evaluation is in the [proposal doc]([link]

IMO, the initial version should target a simple policy of size limit per file. We can iterate and add more advanced features based on disk management in the future. The stretch goal for this release will be supporting reading logs (`kubectl logs`) from rotated log files.

As for the docker integration (i.e., `--container-runtime=docker`) that does not fully implement CRI logging, kubelet should skip log rotation.

state:
NodePort only responding on node where pod is running

Running a 3-node cluster, NodePort service with one pod only responds on one node, the node where the pod is running. Attempts to access the service on the NodePort via other nodes times out with no response.
Service should respond on the service port from any node.
Base OS Ubuntu 16.04. Install with Calico as the network provider, with the pod CIDR set to a non-default value (in my case, 10.5.0.0/16).

I created my cluster with the following kubeadm init statement:

`kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.5.0.0/16 --apiserver-cert-extra-sans ['kubemaster.wittlesouth.com','192.168.5.10']`

I deployed Calico 3.0.1 with a one-line change to the deployment YAML file to set the environment variable CALICO_IPV4POOL_CIDR to the value 10.5.0.0/16 to match the CIDR set for Kubernetes.
If you run "iptables -P FORWARD ACCEPT" on all of the nodes, the service works as expected, and responds from each node in the cluster.

Service should respond on the service port from any node.
Base OS Ubuntu 16.04. Install with Calico as the network provider, with the pod CIDR set to a non-default value (in my case, 10.5.0.0/16).

I created my cluster with the following kubeadm init statement:

`kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.5.0.0/16 --apiserver-cert-extra-sans ['kubemaster.wittlesouth.com','192.168.5.10']`

I deployed Calico 3.0.1 with a one-line change to the deployment YAML file to set the environment variable CALICO_IPV4POOL_CIDR to the value 10.5.0.0/16 to match the CIDR set for Kubernetes.
If you run "iptables -P FORWARD ACCEPT" on all of the nodes, the service works as expected, and responds from each node in the cluster.

Routing determination: network.

state:
RFC: Some thoughts about node e2e tests

Back in 1.5, sig-node defined a set of node conformance tests (i.e., tagged `[Conformance]`). However, there lacks follow-up efforts to maintain the set of conformance tests. IMO, except for a specific set of features which depend on the OS distribution, container runtime, and/or are still under development, most features/tests should be included in the set of node conformance tests. To maintain the set of the tests and to actually utilize the fact that we have "conformance" tests, I think we can start from the following items.

* Run only the conformance tests in presubmit (`pull-kubernetes-node-e2e` suite) should focus only on the conformance tests.
* The regular post submit node e2e suite should focus only on the conformance tests.
* Any new node e2e test added should either be tagged as `[Conformance]` or `[Feature: XXX]`.
* We should add a dedicated CI test job for features.

If a new test does not have any such tag, it will not be run anywhere in CI. This gives the feature owner some incentive to categorize and promote tests for their features.

*Prerequisite for doing this:*
- Scan and promote/demote tests from the conformance suite.
- Ensure each test is assigned a tag.

*Some potential improvements (details TBD):*
- It should be able to optionally trigger feature-specific test jobs for a given PR.
- Define a set of common tags such as `[Feature: Performance]`.

Thoughts? [team] @user @user

Kubernetes's scheduler defines a default limit of 39 volumes for EBS disks per node (`DefaultMaxEBSVolumes`) but this limit is far lower for NVMe disks (something like 25-28). We need to find out why and if we should document this.

Routing determination: storage. Bug assessment: not a bug.

state:
apiserver allows duplicate service port

I was able to add a conflicting service port to an existing service. Attempting to remove the port by modifying the yml and applying fails with `The Service "atest" is invalid: spec.ports: Required value`

Note: Kubernetes 1.8 will not accept a service.yml with conflicting ports if creating for the first time
The server should reject the request and (in this case) `kubectl` should error.
- Created service.yml with a single port definition and successfully applied it

- Updated service.yml with an additional identical port definition and successfully applied it

- Updated service.yml by removing the additional port but applying it failed
On adding the additional port, the service definition (on the server) still only has the original port but `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration` is now in an inconsistent state making `kubectl` attempt to remove the port when it calculates its diff for the patch request.

state:
Incorrect start times can cause heapster to not have CPU stats

When HPA is supposed to upscale it is intermittently unable to calculate the number of desired replicas because of missing metrics
`$ kubectl describe hpa <hpa-name>`
` 3d 29s 80 horizontal-pod-autoscaler Warning FailedGetResourceMetric unable to get metrics for resource cpu: no metrics returned from heapster`
` 3d 29s 80 horizontal-pod-autoscaler Warning FailedComputeMetricsReplicas failed to get cpu utilization: unable to get metrics for resource cpu: no metrics returned from heapster`

The kubelet was returning an invalid Start time for pods, containers, and the node:
`"podRef": {`
` "uid": "7efbdb50-0830-11e8-9e01-42010af0001e"`
`},`
`"startTime": "2018-02-07T09:53:05Z",`
`"containers": [`
`{`
` "startTime": "2018-02-07T09:53:05Z",`
` "cpu": {`
` "time": "2018-02-07T09:53:03Z",`
` },`
` "memory": {`
` "time": "2018-02-07T09:53:03Z",`
` },`
` "rootfs": {`
`"time": "2018-02-07T09:53:03Z",`
`},`
`"logs": {`
` "time": "2018-02-07T09:53:03Z",`
`},`
`},`

Here is the Heapster code that computes cpu usage rate (this is the metric for HPA): [link] which requires that the current and previous batch have the same start time. A start time which changes often results in very few cpu metrics for heapster.

When cadvisor calculates the start time, it looks at the last time `cgroup.clone_children` was modified. [link]
This is an estimate, at best. We recently changed cAdvisor to use docker's container creation time: [link]
But we still need to get a real Pod, Node and system container Start time.

state:
Device Plugin failure handling in kubelet is racy

As of now Kubelet removes a resource owned by device plugins as soon as it notices that a plugin has failed (plugin socket is removed, or ListWatch fails). This behavior is undesirable because trivial plugin restarts would result in Node Capacity changes which is most likely going to be monitored in production clusters resulting in alerts.

As discussed in [link] we should have kubelet reduce the capacity and allocatable to `0` if a device plugin has failed and then after a timeout remove the resource completely from the Node object.
This timeout ensures that random restarts do not raise alerts for production cluster admins, while continue failure does raise an alert. It also let's us track scenarios where all devices fail while the device plugin stays healthy.
Similarly, during startup, kubelet should wait to known plugins to re-register prior to declaring a plugin to be unavailable.
I'd ideally expect this bug to be fixed as part of beta.

state:
Deletion of AWS EBS is not idempotent

AWS EBS volume may not be deleted when controller-manager is restarted at wrong time.

1. Have dynamically provisioned PVC.
2. Delete the PVC.
3. Controller deletes underlying EBS.
4. Restart controller before it deletes associated PV.
5. Controller finds PV that needs to be deleted and calls cloud provider to do so.

-> AWS cloud provider returns error that the volume has been already deleted
-> The PV is not deleted and stays Failed forever.

AWS cloud provider should be idempotent and treat "not found" error as success.

AWS EBS volume may not be deleted when controller-manager is restarted at wrong time.

1. Have dynamically provisioned PVC.
2. Delete the PVC.
3. Controller deletes underlying EBS.
4. Restart controller before it deletes associated PV.
5. Controller finds PV that needs to be deleted and calls cloud provider to do so.

-> AWS cloud provider returns error that the volume has been already deleted
-> The PV is not deleted and stays Failed forever.

AWS cloud provider should be idempotent and treat "not found" error as success.

Routing determination: storage.

state:
CVE-2017-1002101 - subpath volume mount handling allows arbitrary file access in host filesystem

[CVSS:3.0/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H]([link]

This vulnerability allows containers using [subpath volume mounts]([link] with any volume type (including non-privileged pods, subject to file permissions) to access files/directories outside of the volume, including the host’s filesystem.

Thanks to Maxim Ivanov for reporting this problem.

**Vulnerable versions:**
* Kubernetes 1.3.x-1.6.x
* Kubernetes 1.7.0-1.7.13
* Kubernetes 1.8.0-1.8.8
* Kubernetes 1.9.0-1.9.3

**Vulnerable configurations:**
* Clusters that allow untrusted users to control pod spec content, and prevent host filesystem access via hostPath volumes (or other volume types) using PodSecurityPolicy (or custom admission plugins)
* Clusters that make use of [subpath volume mounts]([link] with untrusted containers or containers that can be compromised

**Vulnerability impact:**
A specially crafted pod spec combined with malicious container behavior can allow read/write access to arbitrary files outside volumes specified in the pod, including the host’s filesystem. This can be accomplished with any volume type, including emptyDir, and can be accomplished with a non-privileged pod (subject to file permissions).

**Mitigations prior to upgrading:**
Prevent untrusted users from creating pods (and pod-creating objects like deployments, replicasets, etc), or [disable all volume types]([link] with PodSecurityPolicy (note that this prevents use of service account tokens in pods, and requires use of [`automountServiceAccountToken: false`]([link]

**Fixed versions:**
* Fixed in v1.7.14 by #61047
* Fixed in v1.8.9 by #61046
* Fixed in v1.9.4 by #61045
* Fixed in master by #61044 (included in v1.10.0-beta.3, will be in v1.10.0)

CVE-2017-1002102 - atomic writer volume handling allows arbitrary file deletion in host filesystem

[CVSS:3.0/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:H]([link]

This vulnerability allows containers using a secret, configMap, projected or downwardAPI volume to trigger deletion of arbitrary files and directories on the nodes where they are running.

Thanks to Joel Smith of Red Hat for reporting this problem.

**Vulnerable versions:**
* Kubernetes 1.3.x-1.6.x
* Kubernetes 1.7.0-1.7.13
* Kubernetes 1.8.0-1.8.8
* Kubernetes 1.9.0-1.9.3

**Vulnerable configurations:**
* Clusters that run untrusted containers with secret, configMap, downwardAPI or projected volumes mounted (including auto-added service account token mounts).

**Vulnerability impact:**
A malicious container running in a pod with a secret, configMap, downwardAPI or projected volume mounted (including auto-added service account token mounts) can cause the Kubelet to remove any file or directory on the host filesystem.

**Mitigations prior to upgrading:**
Do not allow containers to be run with secret, configMap, downwardAPI and projected volumes (note that this prevents use of service account tokens in pods, and requires use of [`automountServiceAccountToken: false`]([link]

**Fixed versions:**
* Fixed in v1.7.14 by #60516
* Fixed in v1.8.9 by #60515
* Fixed in v1.9.4 by #60258
* Fixed in master by #58720 (included in v1.10.0-beta.1 and up, will be in v1.10.0)

**Fix impact:**
Secret, configMap, downwardAPI and projected volumes will be mounted as read-only volumes. Applications that attempt to write to these volumes will receive read-only filesystem errors. Previously, applications were allowed to make changes to these volumes, but those changes were reverted at an arbitrary interval by the system. Applications should be re-configured to write derived files to another location.

CVE-2017-1002102 - atomic writer volume handling allows arbitrary file deletion in host filesystem

[CVSS:3.0/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:H]([link]

This vulnerability allows containers using a secret, configMap, projected or downwardAPI volume to trigger deletion of arbitrary files and directories on the nodes where they are running.

Thanks to Joel Smith of Red Hat for reporting this problem.

**Vulnerable versions:**
* Kubernetes 1.3.x-1.6.x
* Kubernetes 1.7.0-1.7.13
* Kubernetes 1.8.0-1.8.8
* Kubernetes 1.9.0-1.9.3

**Vulnerable configurations:**
* Clusters that run untrusted containers with secret, configMap, downwardAPI or projected volumes mounted (including auto-added service account token mounts).

**Vulnerability impact:**
A malicious container running in a pod with a secret, configMap, downwardAPI or projected volume mounted (including auto-added service account token mounts) can cause the Kubelet to remove any file or directory on the host filesystem.

**Mitigations prior to upgrading:**
Do not allow containers to be run with secret, configMap, downwardAPI and projected volumes (note that this prevents use of service account tokens in pods, and requires use of [`automountServiceAccountToken: false`]([link]

**Fixed versions:**
* Fixed in v1.7.14 by #60516
* Fixed in v1.8.9 by #60515
* Fixed in v1.9.4 by #60258
* Fixed in master by #58720 (included in v1.10.0-beta.1 and up, will be in v1.10.0)

**Fix impact:**
Secret, configMap, downwardAPI and projected volumes will be mounted as read-only volumes. Applications that attempt to write to these volumes will receive read-only filesystem errors. Previously, applications were allowed to make changes to these volumes, but those changes were reverted at an arbitrary interval by the system. Applications should be re-configured to write derived files to another location.

state:
PodSecurityPolicy allowedHostPaths does not effectively restrict to a subpath

the allowedHostPaths feature limits what paths can be specified in a hostPath volume, but does not restrict symlink creation and traversal within that subpath

To prevent this, either of the following are required:
* limit hostPath use to read only volumes (in progress in [link]
* limit hostPath use to exact path matches

Until those changes are made, PodSecurityPolicy objects designed to limit container permissions must completely disable hostPath volumes

Subpaths of volumes with fsGroup may be mounted into a container without SGID bit on themselves:

The mode of `subpath` should be `drwxrwsrwx` instead of `drwxrwxrwx`.

Reason for this is `fchmod` at [link]

1. it should not filter out sgid/suid/sticky flags with `&os.ModePerm`

state:
kubelet cpu-cfs-quota flag does not work properly

The kubelet flag `--cpu-cfs-quota` does not work when pod cgroups are enabled.
The container cgroup is left unbounded but the pod cgroup is bounded.
No cpu quota enforcement should happen at any level of the cgroup tree.
Set --cpu-cfs-quota=false and run `kubectl run nginx --image=nginx --limits=cpu=1,memory=512Mi`, observe the cgroup tree and see the pod cgroup is bounded.
nope, fix is in flight

state:
subPath volume mount umbrella issue

This issue is tracking the status of the fixes for functional regressions related to the design change required to address [CVE-2017-1002101]([link]

- [x] #61076: subPath volume mounts cannot be used with secret, configmap, projected, or downwardAPI volumes. *Fixed in 1.10.0, 1.9.5, 1.8.10, and 1.7.15*.
- [x] #61178: cleanup of subPath volume mounts, and setup of subPath volume mounts when restarting a container does not work properly. *Fixed in 1.10.0, 1.9.5, 1.8.10, and 1.7.15*.
- [x] #61283: subpath mounts in pods using fsGroup do not have set-GID bits set properly. *Fixed in 1.10.0, 1.9.7, 1.8.11, 1.7.16*.
- [x] #61372: volume reconstruction does not work with persistent volumes mounted via subPath. *Fixed in 1.10.0, 1.9.7, 1.8.11, 1.7.16*.
- [x] #61377: special types of files, such as unix sockets, cannot be mounted via subPath. *Fixed in 1.10.1, 1.9.7, 1.8.11.*
- [x] #62752: CreateContainerConfigError : failed to prepare subPath for volumeMount (possibly only for readOnly volumes). *Fixed in Kubernetes v1.8.14+, v1.9.9+, v1.10.4+*.
- [ ] #61446: volume reconstruction does not work with host path volumes mounted via subPath. *No immediate plans to address.*
- [ ] #61545: subpath mounts nested within atomic writer volumes (configmap, secret, downwardAPI, projected) do not work. *No immediate plans to address.*

state:
DNS servers and search domains are not set for Windows Pods

Kubelet is depending on docker container's ResolvConfPath (e.g. `/var/lib/docker/containers/439efe31d70fc17485fb6810730679404bb5a6d721b10035c3784157966c7e17/resolv.conf`) to setup dns servers and search domains. While this is ok for Linux containers, ResolvConfPath is always an empty string for windows containers. So that the DNS setting for windows containers are always not set.

For kubernetes clusters deployed by acs-engine, the Pod's DNS is always set to kube-dns service's clusterIP. This is done via the network plugin (e.g. l2bridge or azure-cni). It makes windows containers only work with ClusterFirst dns policy.

To follow kubernetes dns policies, Kubelet should pass the expected DNS settings directly to windows containers (instead of set it in CNI plugins).

state:
Determine whether we should continue to require UID in node config source reference

#### Reposted from [link]

This has been a requirement of dynamic Kubelet config since the original proposal, to require users to be completely explicit (time and space) about which ConfigMap to use. If the UID in the config source doesn't match the UID of the ConfigMap, the Kubelet currently rejects it.

IIRC there were concerns along the lines of ConfigMaps being deleted and recreated with the same name but different content... though this is less of an issue today now that we have the --append-hash option in kubectl (obviously the potential for in-place ConfigMap mutation still exists, but if users are using --append-hash I wouldn't expect them to mutate the ConfigMap after creation).

The Kubelet also checkpoints by UID, so it was convenient to already have this specified in the object ref, though I guess if we relaxed this requirement it could just resolve the UID and stick it in the local copy of the config source when it first downloads the ConfigMap.

I can't remember other reasons to require UID, if any.

---

A massive downside of requiring the UID is that you cannot fully-statically-specify the configuration of a cluster; the UID is assigned by the API server at creation time.

This *must* be resolved before dynamic Kubelet config ([link] goes beta.

IIRC there were concerns along the lines of ConfigMaps being deleted and recreated with the same name but different content... though this is less of an issue today now that we have the --append-hash option in kubectl (obviously the potential for in-place ConfigMap mutation still exists, but if users are using --append-hash I wouldn't expect them to mutate the ConfigMap after creation).

The Kubelet also checkpoints by UID, so it was convenient to already have this specified in the object ref, though I guess if we relaxed this requirement it could just resolve the UID and stick it in the local copy of the config source when it first downloads the ConfigMap.

I can't remember other reasons to require UID, if any.

---

A massive downside of requiring the UID is that you cannot fully-statically-specify the configuration of a cluster; the UID is assigned by the API server at creation time.

This *must* be resolved before dynamic Kubelet config ([link] goes beta.

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: not a bug.

state:
Provide a solution for instance-specific Kubelet configuration

Certain flags, like `--hostname-override` are instance-specific, and thus won't play nice with shared configmaps under dynamic Kubelet config.

We should still have a solution to expose these parameters via a versioned Kubelet config API, rather than command-line flags.

A simple solution could be:
- Add a `KubeletInstanceConfiguration` object to `kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1`.
- Like `KubeletConfiguration`/`--config`, serialize to a file and provide via `--instance-config`.
- This object is not configurable via dynamic Kubelet config, as it contains parameters that should be deployed with the node.

It strikes me that `KubeletInstanceConfiguration` could also be a natural place for any fields that describe local topology maintained by the Kubelet, e.g. `--dynamic-config-dir` and `--root-dir`. Importantly, these are places the Kubelet should *manage* stuff on the node, *not* places the Kubelet should *get* stuff; the latter should be dynamically configurable so that the *stuff the Kubelet gets* (e.g. `kc.StaticPodPath`) is also deploy-able via dynamic config in the future, if we so desire.

state:
Provide a solution for os-specific component config

The Kubelet currently has a single os-specific flag: `--windows-service`.

We anticipate that the Kubelet, and other components, will require more os-specific flags in the future.

We should standardize how os-specific configuration is structured and managed across componentconfig API groups.

Some options:
- Separate `--windows-config`, `--linux-config`, etc. flags, with corresponding `KubeletWindowsConfiguration`, `KubeletLinuxConfiguration`, etc. objects.
- Separate objects, as above, but paths to the files are provided via `KubeletConfiguration`, allowing deployment via dynamic config.
- Simply add fields to `KubeletConfiguration`, with os-specific prefixes, e.g. `WindowsField`, `LinuxField`, `DarwinField`, etc. (this is perhaps the simplest approach).
- Substructures in `KubeletConfiguration` for each os. I'm personally against this one, as I suspect it will be uglier than a flat namespace.

Note: I'm ignoring cadvisor's linux-specific flags, since most are deprecated in the Kubelet and it's questionable how long we'll have cadvisor as a dependency.

We should standardize how os-specific configuration is structured and managed across componentconfig API groups.

Some options:
- Separate `--windows-config`, `--linux-config`, etc. flags, with corresponding `KubeletWindowsConfiguration`, `KubeletLinuxConfiguration`, etc. objects.
- Separate objects, as above, but paths to the files are provided via `KubeletConfiguration`, allowing deployment via dynamic config.
- Simply add fields to `KubeletConfiguration`, with os-specific prefixes, e.g. `WindowsField`, `LinuxField`, `DarwinField`, etc. (this is perhaps the simplest approach).
- Substructures in `KubeletConfiguration` for each os. I'm personally against this one, as I suspect it will be uglier than a flat namespace.

Note: I'm ignoring cadvisor's linux-specific flags, since most are deprecated in the Kubelet and it's questionable how long we'll have cadvisor as a dependency.

state:
Untagging an image can wedge the Kubelet sync loop

I had a pod running on a node using tag `a/b:latest` (kube 1.9.1 / docker 1.13). I untagged the image (tag removed, image still accessible via local ID) and then delete the pod. However, the pod never terminates (staying in terminating state) and I see the following events:

It looks like the sync loop is failing because it can't inspect the image (this could be a bug in docker 1.13). Failure to inspect the image should *not* block pod shutdown.

An accidental admin script could wedge the node.

[team]

- systemContainers.kubelet

- systemContainers.runtime
- node.fs
- node.network
- pods.cpu
- pods.memory
- pods.network
- pods.volume
- pods.ephemeral-storage

state:
Kubelet config: Validate new config against future feature gates

Today, Kubelet config validation is performed against the currently set feature gates. This ignores the fact that configs can modify feature gates. We should, instead, validate against the future combination of currently set feature gates and feature gates from the config.

WRT dynamic config, this is somewhat complicated by the flag precedence rules we enforce, because until the `--feature-gates` flag is removed from the Kubelet, validation also needs to take the flag layer into account. This may mean validation has to be lifted out of the dynamic config controller (because the controller exists below the flag precedence enforcement), which complicates the config loading workflow, status reporting, etc. (alternatively, we could inject the feature gate overrides into the controller...)

This must be fixed before dynamic Kubelet config can go beta.

state:
kubelet's calculation of whether a container has changed can cause cluster-wide outages

Updated 2020-11-09 by @user:

In 1.16+, the kubelet hashes the serialized container spec:

1. API server sends data
* Defaults for added fields will modify this data
* If an alpha field that is not defaulted graduates to adding a default in beta, an API server upgrade from alpha->beta will modify this data
* [link]
2. Kubelet decodes that data into its v1.Container struct
* If the kubelet is older than the API server, this means it will drop fields added in newer API server versions
3. Kubelet encodes that v1.Container struct to JSON and hashes that data
* [link]

This mechanism is used by the kubelet in `containerChanged` and `getStableKey`, which means an API server upgrade that starts defaulting a container field graduating from alpha will instantly modify the computed hash and trigger a container restart. This results in simultaneous restart of all containers across all pods of a replicaset and can cause outages.

The kubelet should limit the fields it considers in the container hash to the ones it expects to be able to change in ways that would affect the running container (currently just `image`, I think). The pod uid is already included in `getStableKey` so a delete/recreate of the entire pod would already compute a different key.

Changing this mechanism on a minor version boundary (to improve the interactions with the API server changes in 1) is acceptable, because pods are expected to be drained as part of that upgrade (xref [link]

-----------

Kubelet hashes the container spec and store it with the container so that it can detect whether the container meets the current spec. If the hashes do not match, kubelet would kill the container and create a new one.

state:
Following container logs can leave processes running and open inotify watches

If a container log is followed using kubectl or other API client, when the client disconnects, the process watching for changes in the logs does not die.

The process only dies when a new log line is received from the container (which may not happen) and the log process tries to send it to the client and then fails. Furthermore, a inotify watch is also left open, which can potentially cause the OS to run out of watches and eventually results in `failed to create fsnotify watcher: too many open files` when the next container log is followed.
When the client disconnects, the process watching the logs should die within a short time, and the inotify watch should be closed.
This is simplest to reproduce using a single node instance of K8S e.g. minikube
Steps:

1. Create a pod that does not constantly produce log output e.g.

2. With `kubectl` watch the pod logs (for the pod just created) and leave running:

3. On the node that has the pod check the number of inotify watches from kubelet

4. Press ctrl-c to kill the `kubectl` watch started in (2)
5. Check the number of inotify watchers again by repeating (3). The number has not decreased, and will never decrease until either the kubelet is restarted, a log line is received from the pod or the pod terminates.
I believe the problem lies in how the `ReadLogs` function works here:
[link]
Unfortunately this has no way of knowing if the client has disconnected until it tries to send a new log line via the `writer`, which will then fail, close the inotify watcher (via the `defer`) and exit.

A container producing no log output will therefore leave the process running.

state:
Following container logs can leave processes running and open inotify watches

If a container log is followed using kubectl or other API client, when the client disconnects, the process watching for changes in the logs does not die.

The process only dies when a new log line is received from the container (which may not happen) and the log process tries to send it to the client and then fails. Furthermore, a inotify watch is also left open, which can potentially cause the OS to run out of watches and eventually results in `failed to create fsnotify watcher: too many open files` when the next container log is followed.
When the client disconnects, the process watching the logs should die within a short time, and the inotify watch should be closed.
This is simplest to reproduce using a single node instance of K8S e.g. minikube
Steps:

1. Create a pod that does not constantly produce log output e.g.

2. With `kubectl` watch the pod logs (for the pod just created) and leave running:

3. On the node that has the pod check the number of inotify watches from kubelet

4. Press ctrl-c to kill the `kubectl` watch started in (2)
5. Check the number of inotify watchers again by repeating (3). The number has not decreased, and will never decrease until either the kubelet is restarted, a log line is received from the pod or the pod terminates.
I believe the problem lies in how the `ReadLogs` function works here:
[link]
Unfortunately this has no way of knowing if the client has disconnected until it tries to send a new log line via the `writer`, which will then fail, close the inotify watcher (via the `defer`) and exit.

A container producing no log output will therefore leave the process running.

Routing determination: node.

state:
ConfigMap/Secret Volume can become orphaned at termination if a required configmap/secret never exists

Reported by @user

When you deploy a pod with a non-existent ConfigMap or Secret, and then terminate it before it ever starts up, it will leave an unclean configmap/secret volume path on host fileystem. This will result in "orphaned pod" errors for said pod until kubelet is restarted or configmap/secret directories are cleaned manually.

Example:

Reproducable: Always

Error is same for ConfigMaps and Secrets because they have similar SetUpAt functions.

@user believes the error is from:
[link]

And he suggests:
mountpath is created before getting ConfigMap/Secret. If kubelet fails to get ConfigMap, it errors without cleaning up what it started. Easiest fix is to move volume prep to after retrieval of ConfigMap (which should be done anyway), but should also clean up after failure.

state:
CSI Block Implementation sets path to dir not file

Reported by @user

The current CSI in-tree plugin sets the `TargetPath` to a directory, e.g. `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/f01d8107-69cd-11e8-85a4-0cc47ac6c23c/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/pv-block/mount` when calling `NodeStageVolume` or `NodePublishVolume`.
Block devices are files, so the target path should be a file, not a directory. The plugin could create a symlink inside the specified directory, but then Kubernetes won't have a handle to the block device. So Kublet should specify a file path for block devices.

Next question is if the file should exist before calling CSI, my suggestion is that it should not exist. The plugin will create a symlink, and kubelet can verify it after calling `NodeStageVolume` or `NodePublishVolume`.

Block devices are files, so the target path should be a file, not a directory. The plugin could create a symlink inside the specified directory, but then Kubernetes won't have a handle to the block device. So Kublet should specify a file path for block devices.

Next question is if the file should exist before calling CSI, my suggestion is that it should not exist. The plugin will create a symlink, and kubelet can verify it after calling `NodeStageVolume` or `NodePublishVolume`.

state:
Setup docker container's dns directly instead of rewriting resolv.conf

Since #29378, kubelet rewrites container's resolv.conf for setting DNS servers and search domains. This is because Docker 1.12 contains feature "The option --dns and --net=host should not be mutually exclusive", while Docker 1.11 doesn't allow this operation.

But it works since docker v1.12 via docker APIs, e.g.

We should consider replacing the rewriting logic with docker API after deprecated docker v1.11 (Kubernetes v1.10 still supports Docker v1.11).

Note: this is only for Linux containers. Windows containers require Docker EE >= 17.10.0 for propagating sandbox's DNS to containers (with #63905).

state:
CSI volume source fstype incompatible with CSI spec

CSI spec allows for an empty fstype string. This is intended for non-block plugins like nfs and gluster where filesystems are not separately created on the volume.

The Kubernetes CSI volume source API defaults fstype to "ext4" and doesn't allow an empty string:

This makes it impossible for Kubernetes to pass in an empty fs_type to the plugin.
Since we currently leave fs creation and formatting up to the plugin, the plugin should be the one to decide the default.

routing.instructions: Which Kubernetes special interest group (SIG) should own this issue?

state:
If kubelet is unavailable, AttachDetachController fails to force detach on pod deletion

When a pod using an attached volume is deleted (gracefully) but kubelet in the corresponding node is down, the AttachDetachController should assume the node is unrecoverable after a timeout (currently 6min) and forcefully detach the volume.
The volume is never detached.
* Create a pod with a volume using any of the attachable plugins (I used GCE PD to test).
* Stop kubelet inside the node where the pod is scheduled.
* Delete the pod.
* Wait for 6min+
* Check to see if the volume is still attached.
This doesn't happen if the pod is force-deleted.

It's likely due to the last condition checked in [this line]([link] Once kubelet is down, the container status is no longer reported correctly. Inside the Attach Detach Controller, This function is called by the pod update informer handler, which sets whether the volume should be attached in the desired state of the world. On pod force deletion, the pod object is deleted immediately, and this triggers the pod delete informer handler, which doesn't call this function.

routing.instructions: Which Kubernetes special interest group (SIG) should own this issue?

state:
If kubelet is unavailable, AttachDetachController fails to force detach on pod deletion

When a pod using an attached volume is deleted (gracefully) but kubelet in the corresponding node is down, the AttachDetachController should assume the node is unrecoverable after a timeout (currently 6min) and forcefully detach the volume.
The volume is never detached.
* Create a pod with a volume using any of the attachable plugins (I used GCE PD to test).
* Stop kubelet inside the node where the pod is scheduled.
* Delete the pod.
* Wait for 6min+
* Check to see if the volume is still attached.
This doesn't happen if the pod is force-deleted.

It's likely due to the last condition checked in [this line]([link] Once kubelet is down, the container status is no longer reported correctly. Inside the Attach Detach Controller, This function is called by the pod update informer handler, which sets whether the volume should be attached in the desired state of the world. On pod force deletion, the pod object is deleted immediately, and this triggers the pod delete informer handler, which doesn't call this function.

state:
gce-scale-performance suite is failing

I'm opening this issue as an umbrella for sharing thoughts about recent failures coming from it.

In particular:
- run 169: [link]

This seems to be a flake cause by rescheduler. Rescheduler is implemented in a pretty inefficient way listing all pods to decide for rescheduling.
In this particular run, it send ~4k "List all pods" requests (usually it's 2-3 orders of magnitude lower).

Given that we're going to deprecate rescheduler in favor of priority-preemption in 1.12, I don't think we should spend much time on it.

- run 170: [link]

That seems like a more serious issue (we will see if that was flake or a real issue).
A couple of observations about it:
- there is huge amount of extremely long LIST requests for *all* endpoint and service - coming mostly from DNS instances (and a couple originating from kube-proxy)
- I've seen in a log requests that took 6m+
- Looking into traces, it clearly seems that "sending response" is the step that it takes time:

Even though this steps involves serializing the response, I'm fairly convinced that that's not our limiting factor - I spent some time looking into logs, and all other requests around those long requests very served pretty quickly (which suggests there wasn't any resource starvation there).
My hypothesis is network issues (or components themselves weren't able to read the data maybe due to resource starvation on their side?)

But that's not the only problem. There were also problems with individual nodes.
As an example, on node `gce-scale-cluster-minion-group-2-6k9s` Kubelet became unhealthy:

That was a reason for some pods starting for a really long time.

There were also issues at the end of the test where we weren't able to delete the namespace (I guess it's because some Kubelet was down, but didn't have time to confirm that - it should be verified).

But all those issues need to be better understand.

But that's not the only problem. There were also problems with individual nodes.
As an example, on node `gce-scale-cluster-minion-group-2-6k9s` Kubelet became unhealthy:

That was a reason for some pods starting for a really long time.

There were also issues at the end of the test where we weren't able to delete the namespace (I guess it's because some Kubelet was down, but didn't have time to confirm that - it should be verified).

But all those issues need to be better understand.

state:
Masters should not be excluded from service load balancers

I'm running a single node cluster on AWS EC2, ie. scheduling work on the master as well. Now that I tried to add an ELB for my service, the EC2 instance is not associated with the ELB. The ELB gets created but there are 0 EC2 instances associated with it. I'm using ELB for SSL termination, if you wonder why I'd like to load balance a single node cluster.

The service controller logs this message:

The EC2 instance is associated with the ELB.
- Boot an EC2 instance with correct IAM permissions
- Install a single node cluster using `kubeadm` and `cloud-provider=aws`
- Untaint the node
- Schedule eg. nginx
- Create an external load balancer for nginx
- View the ELB in AWS console and note the `Status: 0 of 0 instances in service`
The reason for this seems to be the `node-role.kubernetes.io/master` label. [This]([link] blocks associating a load balancer with the node. On the other hand [this]([link] changed what is included, because `includeNodeFromNodeList` did not check if a node is a master. I'm not sure what would be correct fix. I could try submit a PR, if you guide me how this should behave. Is my scenario even a supported one?

I think this bug should be reproducible on other clouds as well.

Image garbage collection is always disabled in kubelet in 1.11

In the `StartGarbageCollection` function, there is a `defer close(stopChan)` that always runs and closes the channel when returning. This means that instead of running periodically, the image garbage collection will be terminated immediately when the function returns.

[link]

The bug was introduced by #51423 in 1.11

state:
TokenReview audience support for nodes

Once [link] merges, we should add support for audiences to the Kubelet's token review.

This is important as part of the node isolation efforts, as the node could otherwise use tokens sent with requests to the nodes endpoints (e.g. stats requests) to send requests to other nodes.

I think the node should accept 3 types of audiences:

- legacy (no audience) - required for backwards compatibility
- `system:nodes` - token used for all nodes
- `system:node:<nodeName>` - per-node token, preferred

state:
CSI incorrectly sets fsgroup for all volume types

fsgroup is only intended for RWO volumes because it recursively changes the permissions of all the directories in the volume. This can cause problems for nfs-type volumes because multiple pods could access the same volume and have the permissions changed out from underneath.
Determine whether or not the plugin supports fsgroup either via:
- access mode. This is still a bit ambiguous for nfs volume types, that can theoretically support rwo, especially since Kubernetes does not do any sort of access mode enforcement.
- a new csi capability

state:
Eviction should be able to request eviction asynchronously

`kubectl drain` got stuck because we had PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) with `spec.minAvailable: 1` and the deployment only had one replica -> allowed disruptions was always 0.
Instead of `kubectl drain` getting stuck, it should activly start a new pod on a different node if the deployment allows for it (deployment.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge). This should be built into to eviction API.
If a missconfiguration of PodDisruptionBudget prevents a drain, `kubectl drain` or the eviction API should warn about it.
- Create a deployment with `spec.replicas: 1`
- Create PDB with `spec.minAvailable: 1` and select the pod of the deployment
- Try to evict the pod from its node via eviction api or `kubectl drain`

state:
Eviction should be able to request eviction asynchronously

`kubectl drain` got stuck because we had PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) with `spec.minAvailable: 1` and the deployment only had one replica -> allowed disruptions was always 0.
Instead of `kubectl drain` getting stuck, it should activly start a new pod on a different node if the deployment allows for it (deployment.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge). This should be built into to eviction API.
If a missconfiguration of PodDisruptionBudget prevents a drain, `kubectl drain` or the eviction API should warn about it.
- Create a deployment with `spec.replicas: 1`
- Create PDB with `spec.minAvailable: 1` and select the pod of the deployment
- Try to evict the pod from its node via eviction api or `kubectl drain`

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: not a bug.

state:
kubelet: HTTP liveness probes should not be run when no connection to the APIServer exists

We are running `etcd` as a static pod with an HTTP liveness probe. For some reason, our `etcd` container died. The `kubelet` then attempted to restart it, but could not succeed as it could not determine that the `etcd` container was alive. When `etcd` was down, obviously the API could not respond with data, so when the prober routine constructed a liveness probe, it had no `PodStatus` and could not determine the IP to probe on:

Critical line of logging is:

When no connection to the API server exists and we cannot read `PodStatus` to determine the IP at which to reach the liveness probes, we should not execute the probes.
Going to be hard to do, not really sure.

state:
modified subpath configmap mount fails when container restarts

When a container uses a configmap which is mounted with the `subPath` option, the configmap is changed and then the container (but not the pod) restarts the mounting of the configmap fails:

# change something in the configmap
kubectl edit extra-cfg
kubectl exec podname kill 1
kubectl describe podname

Warning Failed 5s kubelet, kworker-be-intg-iz2-bap006 Error: failed to start container "puppetdb": Error response from daemon: OCI runtime create failed: container_linux.go:348: starting container process caused "process_linux.go:402: container init caused \"rootfs_linux.go:58: mounting \\\"/var/lib/kubelet/pods/b9ffd644-af98-11e8-a05e-246e96748774/volume-subpaths/extra-cfg/puppetdb/2\\\" to rootfs \\\"/var/lib/docker/overlay2/c8790b7f3f690c1ef7a582672e2d153062ff6b4ed1ee21aab1158897310fd3d1/merged\\\" at \\\"/var/lib/docker/overlay2/c8790b7f3f690c1ef7a582672e2d153062ff6b4ed1ee21aab1158897310fd3d1/merged/etc/puppetlabs/puppetdb/conf.d/extra.ini\\\" caused \\\"no such file or directory\\\"\"": unknown

(The pod this happens on consists of multiple containers, I have not tested yet if it also happens in a single container pod.)

One has to delete the pod to fix the problem.

state:
Reduce the set of metrics exposed by the kubelet

### Background
In 1.12, the kubelet exposes a number of sources for metrics directly from [cAdvisor]([link] This includes:
* [cAdvisor prometheus metrics]([link] at [`/metrics/cadvisor`]([link]
* [cAdvisor v1 Json API]([link] at [`/stats/`, `/stats/container`, `/stats/{podName}/{containerName}`, and `/stats/{namespace}/{podName}/{uid}/{containerName}`]([link]
* [cAdvisor machine info]([link] at [`/spec`]([link]

The kubelet also exposes the [summary API]([link] which is not exposed directly by cAdvisor, but queries cAdvisor as one of its sources for metrics.

The [Monitoring Architecture]([link] documentation describes the path for "core" metrics, and for "monitoring" metrics. The [Core Metrics]([link] proposal describes the set of metrics that we consider core, and their uses. The motivation for the split architecture is:
* To minimize the performance impact of stats collection for core metrics, allowing these to be collected more frequently
* To make the monitoring pipeline replaceable, and extensible.

### Current kubelet metrics that are not included in core metrics
* Pod and Node-level Network Metrics
* Persistent Volume Metrics
* Container-level (Nvidia) GPU Metrics
* Node-Level RLimit Metrics
* Misc Memory Metrics (e.g. PageFaults)
* Container, Pod, and Node-level Inode metrics (for ephemeral storage)
* Container, Pod, and Node-level DiskIO metrics (from cAdvisor)

Deprecating and removing the Summary API will require out-of-tree sources for each of these metrics. "Direct" cAdvisor endpoints are not often used, and have even been broken for multiple releases ([link] without anyone raising an issue.

volume A/D controller: move CRDs to yaml

In #68260 validations have been added to the CRDs. There was also the request to move the CRDs into yaml files:

@user requested the CRD be defined in a yaml file in the original API PR, and I agree with that request. Reviewing and tracking changes to API type definitions made in code like this is difficult and error prone.

However, to not block [1.12]([link] this won't be done right now. As soon as 1.12 is out the door the CRDs should be moved to yaml files.

It should also be discusses how moving to yaml should actually be done:
- Using literally a file? How to managed this *runtime* dependency?
- Using go-bindata or similar to convert the yaml int o code at compile time in some code generation phase?

----

state:
Improve dependency injection for volume plugins

Today many of in-tree volume plugin's dependencies are injected through the VolumeHost interface, but there are several pain points:
* It's difficult to see a list of dependencies for each plugin.
* Volume plugins have to embed nil checks for their VolumeHost dependencies directly in the code path that uses them. This makes plugins more prone to bugs.
* If a particular dependency is missing, there is no way to explicitly configure whether initialization of the caller component (e.g. kubelet, controller manager) should fail, or just skip plugin initialization. For different caller situations either option is possible.
* Today, returning an error in the volume plugin's `Init()` call when a dependency is missing causes the caller component to fail.

Investigate whether it makes sense to improve this dependency injection mechanism.

state:
Kubelet does not launch static pods while waiting for bootstrapping

The kubelet currently blocks trying to attempt to get a bootstrap client before it starts its worker loops for running static pods, which means a static pod that provides functionality on a node that bootstrapping may need (talking to an HSM, calling out externally, providing a plugin for bootstrapping, or even running a control plane pod) is blocked. There is no actual functionality in the Kubelet that depends on this (waiting for bootstrap has no use case value), it's just a historical legacy of how the code evolved. As people start to leverage bootstrapping and rotation, it becomes more obvious how this doesn't work in practice.

In the long run we want bootstrap credentials to be pluggable and extensible so that an HSM or other trust store on the machine can deal with the problem. Having secret key material for bootstrapping stored on disk that allows you to join a cluster is undesirable, and having a callout to make that flow less error prone is very desirable for both cloud and metal provisioned environments.

In addition, the bootstrapping and client cert rotation flows are slightly duplicated today - using the client cert to rotate itself means that when a client cert expires (very possible with quicker rotations if the api goes down for a period of time) the bootstrap credential is consulted - but that could be arbitrarily far in the future and means we tend to fail in those cases (bootstrap credential expired). Since the long term desire is for bootstrap to be out of process, it would be better for us to continually go back to bootstrap on cert expiration rather than retrying our flow.

For 1.13, we should fix the kubelet to not pause when bootstrapping and instead delegate to the rotation flow to provide that credential.

state:
Support an image pull credential flow built on bound service account tokens

ImagePullSecret is a mechanism to provide kubelet with credentials to pull images for pods running as a specific service account. This provides segmentation of image access between tenants of a cluster. Now that Kubernetes has a more featureful service acccount token issuer, we can leverage bound service account tokens rather than static secrets to authenticate kubelet to docker registries.

Strawman flow:
1. Pod running as service account `foo` with image `bar.io/baz` is bound to a node
1. Kubelet on node requests a service account token for service account `foo` with audience `bar.io`
1. (Optional) Kubelet does an [OAuth token exchange]([link] which is a general approach to what we [already do in CRI]([link]
1. Kubelet passes resulting token to as a `registry_token` (which is just an access token of type Bearer) to the CRI.

@user talked about this in the pod-identity-wg meeting a while ago.

state:
Plugin watcher getting notified of every Kubelet directory event

The Plugin Watcher is setup to trigger on file activities when they occur in the subdirectory that it scans. During startup, the Watcher is passed (from within the Kubelet) the Kubelet's root plugin directory as a location to scan for newly added plugins - [link]

Because the kubelet's plugins subdirectory is also used by existing in-tree drivers (including csi) as a location to store plugins artifacts, the Plugin Watcher is getting triggered by directory/file activities occurring in that subdirectory that has nothing to do with plugin registration as shown in the output below:

The Plugin Watcher should not be getting triggered by file/directory activities not related to plugin registration/unregistration. One possibility is to have the Watcher scan one directory below plugins like `/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/registration` or something similar
Run plugin watcher with a CSI driver.

The Plugin Watcher is setup to trigger on file activities when they occur in the subdirectory that it scans. During startup, the Watcher is passed (from within the Kubelet) the Kubelet's root plugin directory as a location to scan for newly added plugins - [link]

Because the kubelet's plugins subdirectory is also used by existing in-tree drivers (including csi) as a location to store plugins artifacts, the Plugin Watcher is getting triggered by directory/file activities occurring in that subdirectory that has nothing to do with plugin registration as shown in the output below:

The Plugin Watcher should not be getting triggered by file/directory activities not related to plugin registration/unregistration. One possibility is to have the Watcher scan one directory below plugins like `/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/registration` or something similar
Run plugin watcher with a CSI driver.

cc @user @user

Routing determination: node.

state:
CSI: races in CSISkipAttach tests

This is somewhat related to #68261.

[CSISkipAttach tests]([link] do these things:

1.
1. Create CSIDriver CRD (in BeforeEach).
2. (Optionally) create CSIDriver instance.
3. Create a pod and check that VolumeAttachment was (not) created.
2.
1. Delete pod
2. Delete CSIDriver instance
3. Delete CSIDriver CRD (!!!)

What happens in A/D controller (and in kubelet too):

a. Kubelet and A/D controller create informer on CSIDriver. When the CRD does not exists, it tries periodically every second until the CRD is created.
b. When creating a pod, A/D controller looks into the informer cache if it has CSIDriver for that volume. If not, it creates VolumeAttachment.

Thing is that A/D controller (and kubelet) informer does **not** react to CSIDriver CRD deletion. It keeps watching the old CSIDriver CRD and it won't get events when new CRD and its CRs are created. So A/D controller still sees the CSIDriver created by the first test.
With #69331 merger, run the cluster:

Run e2e tests:

In addition, the test does not give kubelet/A/DController enough time to get a newly created CSIDriver, so it's racy even if CSIDriver CRD was installed only once.

state:
CSI: `readOnly` field is not passed to CSI NodePublish RPC call

As per the CSI spec, `readOnly`is passed to ControllerPublishVolumeRequest that should be passed to NodePublish as well..

Ref: [link]

For CSI driver that do not support Controller Publish/Unpublish, the `readOnly` flag is missing from the nodePublish RPC request.
`readOnly` flag is passed to both, ControllerPublish and NodePublish calls.
CSI driver that doesn't support ControllerPublish call should be able to validate from NodePublish call that the `readOnly` flag is not passed to the driver.

state:
Have kubelet pass pod annotations directly to CNI plugins

Currently, if a CNI network plugin needs access to [annotations]([link] that are configured on a pod, it needs to do a GET/read of the pod manifest from the Kubernetes API server, based on the pod's name.
With the introduction of [CNI release 0.4.0]([link] (which supports CNI API version 0.2.0), it should be possible to make changes to kubelet such that pod annotations (and possibly labels) can be dynamically inserted into the CNI network configuration that is passed to CNI plugin binaries via stdin. In many cases, this would eliminate the need for CNI plugins to perform Kubernetes API reads of pod manifests.

This can be achieved by using the new [args field]([link] in the CNI network configuration. This field is intended to allow runtimes (e.g. kubelet) to dynamically insert per-container (per-pod, in the case of Kubernetes) configuration when a container/pod is being created.

The [CNI conventions for the args field]([link] currently suggest the use of a "labels" field to convey mappings to the plugin:

It's not clear whether this "labels" field should be used ("overloaded") for Kubernetes pod annotations... maybe the CNI maintainers would prefer that we create a new "annotations" field in parallel with "labels".

The use of this feature would also require the use of CNI version 0.4.0 binaries, so we should consider bumping up the Kubernetes reference version for CNI from 0.3.0.
Refer to code [here]([link] This is approximately where changes would be needed.
Use of this feature will require CNI versions 0.4.0 or newer. The Kubernetes reference version for CNI should be bumped from 0.3.0 to 0.4.0 at some point.

state:
Kubelet VolumeManager incorrectly marks volume as not "in use" (i.e. safe to detach) while a mount or format is pending

While debugging an issue with a volume getting detached prematurely, @user discovered an issue: the Kubelet VolumeManager incorrectly marks volume as not "in use" (i.e. safe to detach) while a mount or format is pending.

For context, attach/detach controller will not proceed with a detach (after pod referencing a volume is deleted) while the volume is still marked as "in use" by kubelet. Kubelet marks a volume as "in use" before it starts mounting or formating the volume.

The problem is:

* If a pod referencing a volume is deleted while a mount (or format) is pending, then kubelet will go ahead and remove that pod from its "desired state of the world" cache (normally this waits for pod's containers to terminate, but in this case the containers never even started because mount is still pending, i.e. format, is still pending).
* Kubelet volume_manager's `GetVolumesInUse()` method ([link] reports the volume as no longer in use because it is not in desired or actual state (it does not check pending operations <-- this is the bug).
* Attach/detach controller sees the pod delete, checks and sees the volume is not marked as "in use" and proceeds with the detach (incorrectly), but a mount (or format) operation may be pending.
Kubelet volume_manager's `GetVolumesInUse()` method ([link] should count volumes that have pending operations (mount or otherwise) as "in use" (even if they are not in actual or desired state).
While mount is pending (because format is taking a long time, for example), delete the pod referencing the attachable volume.

state:
CSI Readonly issues

Kubernetes readonly flags are a mess (see [link] and readonly flags are broken in the beta implementation of CSI.

We should explicitly define and implement what the mapping of Kubernetes readonly flags is for CSI before moving CSI to GA.
*Current (CSI beta) behavior:*

1. PVC/PV access modes may be `ReadOnlyMany`.
* PVC Access Mode
* Set by end user.
* Controls "required access mode" of volume to provision.
* Passed to CSI via `CreateVolumeRequest.volume_capabilities`.
* external-provisioner ([link]([link]
* PV Access Mode
* Set by provisioner: Copy of PVC access modes.
* Used for PV/PVC binding.
* If PV is created without error, the assumption is that the provisioned volume satisfied all the PVC access modes, so PV access mode should just be copied from the PVC access mode ([link]
2. `Pod.spec.volumes.persistentVolumeClaim.readOnly` boolean
* Specified by end user.
* Controls if volume is **mounted** readonly.
* Passed to CSI via `NodePublishVolumeRequest.readonly`.
* kubelet ([link]([link]
3. `PersistentVolume.spec.CSIPersistentVolumeSource.readOnly` boolean
* Specified by CSI provisioner: but not currently set (so always defaults to false).
* See [link]([link]
* Controls if volume is **attached** readonly.
* Passed to CSI via `ControllerPublishVolumeRequest.readonly`.
* external-attacher ([link]([link]
4. `Pod.spec.containers.volumeMounts[x].readOnly` boolean.
* Specified by end user.
* Controls if last mile bind **mount** in to container is readonly
* Controlled entirely by Kubernetes and container via CRI. Not passed to CSI.
* See [link]([link]

Number 3 is NOT doing the right things. Problems include:
* 3 is being used but never set -- and suffers from all the problems pointed out in [link]

*Proposal:*

1. Add new `csiControllerPublishVolumeReadOnly` `StorageClass` parameter to CSI `external-provisioner`.
* This will enable control of the `PersistentVolume.spec.CSIPersistentVolumeSource.readOnly` boolean for newly provisioned volumes.

Disable cpu quota(use only cpuset) for pod Guaranteed

Disable cpu quota when we use cpuset for guaranteed pods.
For now, kubelet default adds cpu quota and share for all cases when `cpuCFSQuota` is open, even if *cpuset* will be set in guaranteed pod case.

My question is why not make a `if` statement when we add cpuQuota config, if it's *guaranteed* case, just set `cpuQuota=-1`?

state:
Kubelet should not consume Environment Variables

The kubelet uses a [versioned, kubernetes-style configuration]([link] As part of this migration, folks in sig-node [removed using the global flag set]([link] in favor of explicitly defining the flags the kubelet accepts. Environment variables similarly share a global, unversioned namespace.

The kubelet should call `os.Clearenv` when it starts up to maintain control of its api surface and thereby ensure we follow api compatibility guarantees. If there are environment variables we need, we should parse them before `os.Clearenv`, and pass them as explicit configuration to the consumer.

cc @user @user [team]

The kubelet should call `os.Clearenv` when it starts up to maintain control of its api surface and thereby ensure we follow api compatibility guarantees. If there are environment variables we need, we should parse them before `os.Clearenv`, and pass them as explicit configuration to the consumer.

state:
Kubelet node status based on CRD Installation

As we move to using CRD's more we have use cases for not letting the Kubelet be schedulable until certain CRD's have been installed or certain initialization actions have been performed with them. It would be nice to have a generic feature that hooks into Kubelet Node Status Ready Condition that can check whether certain CRD's are installed or not and post an error (and make Kubelet NotReady) if those CRD's are not available.

This becomes more important as many core (required for functionality) new Kubernetes API's are being made into CRDs. Without the CRD installed some core functionality will not work so we need a mechanism to ensure that the CRDs exist.

Functionality has a dependency on: #70910

state:
CSINodeInfo lister not syncing existing objects

The CSINodeInfo lister here:
[link]
is used in the external-attacher to get NodeID. If `CSINodeInfo` already exists before external-attacher is started, the object corresponding to the target node is missing for at least a few minutes.
[link]

The node lister inside the external-attacher, which is initialized the same way as the CSINodeInfo lister, syncs existing objects just fine. Calling the API directly works.
Lister initialization:
[link]

I suspect it's a bug in listers and informers associated with CRDs.

Caused one of the test failures in #70760; other possibly related discussion around the use of CRD informers in CSI: #68261

Once this bug is fixed, [link] needs to be reverted

[link]

Lister initialization:
[link]

state:
Allow CSI Drivers that support BOTH 0.x and 1.x to use old plugin dir

CSI allows 0.x drivers only in the deprecated kubelet plugin dir.
CSI allows 1.x drivers only in the new kubelet plugin dir.

If a driver implements both 0.x and 1.x (which is unlikely since the side car containers do not support this), kubelet requires the driver live in new kubelet plugin dir.

So CSI drivers that implement both 0.x and 1.x if they want a seamless transition between k8s 1.12 to 1.13 would need to deploy in both old and new dir.
@user argues that this is adding churn for CSI authors. He recommends allowing any driver that implements 0.x (even if it implements 1.x) to use either new or old (not just new).

If release team approves, PR is small and I can get prepare it pretty quickly.

state:
Orphaned pod cleanup removed all data in subPaths of a local volume with path on root drive

Network for all nodes of kubernetes cluster (29 hosts) was turned off for a day. Once the network was brought back, we've scaled down a statefulset that mounts a `subPath` from local volume which `path` on a root drive and then scaled it back up to previous number of replicas. kubelet on 26 out of 29 hosts proceeded with removing all data from subpaths of the pod. In fact, it was ongoing, such that when we'd create a file on a mounted subpath within the container, the file would be cleaned up within a couple of seconds. The issue would continue until volume-subpath was manually unmounted (with `unmount` command).

Ended up removing 3rd of all of our data (we have 3 drives per host and one was wiped) for the whole cluster.

Equivalent definition. Note that *host path of local volume has to be on root drive*:

Kubelet logs (filtered out logs from other pods) during the issue:

Expected no data loss for peristent local volumes.
Unfortunately was not able to reproduce. But this bug hit 26 out of 29 nodes simultaneously. Need some way to create a case where a pod becomes orphan and "volumes" folder gets somehow removed (similar to issue [link] Then there is a code path that can lead to data loss:

We are in orphan pod cleanup and `volumes` directory is missing (not sure why it's printed twice):
[link]

No error returned and empty volumes list, so we go into this case which proceeds removing pod directory and `volume-subpaths` along with it even thought they might still be mounted (not sure why):
[link]

`IsLikelyNotMountPoint` checks if device is the same, but we use root drive for local volume, so the device is the same, so it's not a mount point so ok for removing (this is a bug IMHO).
[link]
k8s version upgrades went from 1.9.6 -> 1.11.1 -> 1.12.1 -> 1.12.2 -> 1.13.0 without restarting the pods.
