state:
Support configurable ProjectedVolumeToken rotation period on kubelet

A kubelet configuration parameter for modifying the rotation period on ProjectedVolumeTokens.
The current default is hardcoded to begin rotation attempts [after 80% of the token's lifetime or 24 hours]([link] whichever is occurs first. This is a safe default for a 24 hour period, but shorter periods might necessitate more frequent rotation. The API server requires a [minimum token lifetime of 10 minutes]([link] so perhaps kubelet could accept a range of 20% to 80% of the token's lifetime. The 20/80 numbers are arbitrary, but it would be nice to allow this to be configurable

See kubernetes/enhancements#542

When a node restarts, and the kubelet cannot reach the apiserver, dockerd restarts all the containers in the node.

dockerd logs shows the following:

when inspecting containers created by the kubelet we see that we create containers with the following restart policy:

state:
memory leak in kubelet 1.12.5

After upgrading to kubernetes 1.12.5 we observe failing nodes, that are caused by kubelet eating all over the memory after some time.

![image]([link]

I use image `k8s.gcr.io/hyperkube:v1.12.5` to run kubelet on 102 clusters and since a week we see some nodes leaking memory, caused by kubelet.

I investigated some of these kubelets with strace and pprof.
With 3s of running strace I saw >= 50 openat() calls to the same file from the same threadid (pid) from kubelet:

If I do pprof kubelet it shows client_go metrics and compress is taking over most of the compute time.

Memory profile png:
![mem_profile001]([link]

**The reflector metrics seem to be the problem**:

I expect that kubelet does not need so much memory
I don't know
One of the affected clusters has only 120 Pods and 3 Pods are in CrashLoopBackOff state, one pod since 6 days on an affected node which was investigated.

After upgrading to kubernetes 1.12.5 we observe failing nodes, that are caused by kubelet eating all over the memory after some time.

![image]([link]

I use image `k8s.gcr.io/hyperkube:v1.12.5` to run kubelet on 102 clusters and since a week we see some nodes leaking memory, caused by kubelet.

I investigated some of these kubelets with strace and pprof.
With 3s of running strace I saw >= 50 openat() calls to the same file from the same threadid (pid) from kubelet:

If I do pprof kubelet it shows client_go metrics and compress is taking over most of the compute time.

Memory profile png:
![mem_profile001]([link]

**The reflector metrics seem to be the problem**:

I expect that kubelet does not need so much memory
I don't know
One of the affected clusters has only 120 Pods and 3 Pods are in CrashLoopBackOff state, one pod since 6 days on an affected node which was investigated.

state:
Slow volume attach for single ReadOnlyMany volume across multiple nodes

A GCE PD volume is used in read-only mode (through a PVC & PV pair in ReadOnlyMany mode) by over 100 pods running across tens of nodes. Volume attachment sometimes takes over 30min for some of these pods.
Attaching should take seconds instead of minutes.
* Provision a read-only GCE PD, and the associated PVC & PV.
* Run a Job with parallelism of 100+ pods in a cluster with tens of nodes (we tested with 50+), and use the PD inside all pods.
Generally attach/detach calls are parallelized (through OperationExecutor), but calls with the same volume name are serialized. This was done as a way to prevent races between attach and detach calls for the same volume. However, it's sufficient to provide this guarantee for each node, as long as the volume is Read[Write|Only]Many.

[link]

state:
Expose kube-proxy metrics on 0.0.0.0 We'd like to change the Kube Proxy MetricsBindAddress default from 127.0.0.1 to 0.0.0.0. Currently the kube-proxy metrics are exposed by default on 127.0.0.1 interface. It makes it impossible to export kube proxy metrics to prometheus server via prometheus operator. I've sent [link] to change the bind address in tests, but we believe that changing the default might be actually a better idea. Other components (e.g. [kube-scheduler]([link] use 0.0.0.0 as the default metrics bind address.
I'm happy to send a PR to do that, but would like to get your opinion first.

state:
Many ConfigMaps and Pods slow down cluster, until it becomes unavailable (since 1.12)

I schedule multiple jobs in my cluster. Each job uses a different ConfigMap which contains the configuration for that job.

This worked well on version 1.11 of Kubernetes. After upgrading to 1.12 or 1.13, I've noticed that doing this will cause the cluster to significantly slow down; up to the point where nodes are being marked as NotReady and no new work is being scheduled.

For example, consider a scenario in which I schedule 400 jobs, each with its own ConfigMap, which print "Hello World" on a single-node cluster would.

On v1.11, it takes about 10 minutes for the cluster to process all jobs. New jobs can be scheduled.
On v1.12 and v1.13, it takes about 60 minutes for the cluster to process all jobs. After this, no new jobs can be scheduled.
I did not expect this scenario to cause my nodes to become unavailable in Kubernetes 1.12 and 1.13, and would have expected the behavior which I observe in 1.11.
The easiest way seems to be to schedule, on a single-node cluster, about 300 jobs:

I can consistently reproduce this issue in a VM-based environment, which I configure using Vagrant. You can find the full setup here: [link]
Happy to provide further information as needed

Init containers are not looked at when calculating quality of service class

A pod that has init container with request for cpu and memory, and containers that make no request for cpu or memory reports a BestEffort QoS class. This is incorrect.

[link]
Containers that make requests independent of lifecycle phase should impact quality of service calculation.

Found in 1.12, looks to still be present in 1.14 dev.

state:
Volumes fail to clean up when kubelet restart due to race between actual and desired state

We have tests to delete pods while kubelet restarts, the test is a little bit flaky because the following race condition
1. stop kubelet, delete pod gracefully and restarts kubelet
2. pod's volumes are first put into the volume desired state. Then populator will try to remove it because pod is deleted. However, it is normally failed because we check whether actual state already has the volume record or not.
3. actual state verify volume is attached and have a record of it, but it does not record it as mounted yet
4. desired state remove the volume right after step 3 happened.
5. reconciler never has a chance to umount volume because actual state does not has it as mounted (only has it as attached)

I think in step 3, we should check actual state has this volume as mounted or not, instead of just checking whether it exists or not (attached).

state:
Remove kube-proxy's automatic clean up logic

Remove any logic in kube-proxy that tries to automatically clean up proxy rules based on the proxy mode. Only attempt to clean up if `--cleanup` is set.
This is a continuation of a discussion from [link] There's a lot of complexity that comes with switching the proxy mode on kube-proxy because it tries to delete proxy rules created from other proxy modes. This has a lot of side-effects and we should be encouraging users to reboot thier nodes along with switching proxy modes. One example of this can be found [link]

state:
go-inotify leaks file descriptors

There are a couple of places where github.com/sigma/go-inotify is being used.
Unfortunately this package can leak file descriptors since `inotify_init` is called without `IN_CLOEXEC`.

This package seems to be a fork from an old golang.org/x package (which was removed) and hasn't been updated at all except for the fork itself.
(ping @user, maybe you would take a patch for this?)

fsnotify is recommend here, however fsnotify does not support all of the inotify watch flags being used, plus it adds a bunch that we aren't really interested in. Since fsnotify is more of a cross-platform package, I'm not sure how feasible it is to include support for these.

state:
Test coverage for pod quality of service

There is no complete test coverage for the Resource quality of service. There is only one test case is there for Guaranteed QoSClass. There is few important things to cover the test case,
Please refer the QOS [proposal doc]([link]
Test cases to cover :
- Excess CPU resources will be distributed based on the amount of CPU requested. For example, suppose container A requests for 600 milli CPUs, and container B requests for 300 milli CPUs. Suppose that both containers are trying to use as much CPU as they can. Then the extra 100 milli CPUs will be distributed to A and B in a 2:1 ratio (implementation discussed in later sections)
- Pods will be throttled if they exceed their limit. If limit is unspecified, then the pods can use excess CPU when available
- Pods will get the amount of memory they request, if they exceed their memory request, they could be killed (if some other pod needs memory), but if pods consume less memory than requested, they will not be killed (except in cases where system tasks or daemons need more memory)
- When Pods use more memory than their limit, a process that is using the most amount of memory, inside one of the pod's containers, will be killed by the kernel
- Test case for Burstable and BestEffort

state:
pvc_protection_controller queries local cache instead of apiserver(s)

After studying [link] I thought of an optimization and checked the current implementation to see if it is there. Instead I found that the current implementation makes a critical mistake: it only checks the local cache and never the live apiserver(s) (see [link] Following is a scenario in which the current implememtation allows the removal of a PVC while it is in use by a Pod. Start in a state where the PVC exists, has the finalizer, and is bound. Next a Pod API object is created. Then the Pod is scheduled and the relevant kubelet is notified and begins work on that Pod. That kubelet queries an apiserver, which queries the etcd cluster holding PVC objects (which may or may not be the same as the etcd cluster holding Pod objects), and finds out that the PVC exists and is not being deleted. The kubelet finishes creating and starting the Pod. Then some client requests deletion of the PVC. Its DeletionTimestamp is set. Then the pvc_protection_controller is notified about this change to the PVC. Note that I did _not_ say that the pvc_protection_controller has by now been notified about the creation or scheduling of the Pod. This is possible, because we have no guarantee about ordering of notifications about different Kinds of objects. The pvc_protection_controller queries its Pod informer's local cache of Pod information and does not find the new Pod. The pvc_protection_controller then removes the Finalizer from the PVC, and soon the PVC API object is removed.
I expected to see that [link] follows the community design doc or includes an optimization to avoid the apiserver check if the local cache shows usage of the PVC.

Instead I found that the current implementation makes a critical mistake: it only checks the local cache and never the live apiserver(s) (see [link] Following is a scenario in which the current implememtation allows the removal of a PVC while it is in use by a Pod. Start in a state where the PVC exists, has the finalizer, and is bound. Next a Pod API object is created. Then the Pod is scheduled and the relevant kubelet is notified and begins work on that Pod. That kubelet queries an apiserver, which queries the etcd cluster holding PVC objects (which may or may not be the same as the etcd cluster holding Pod objects), and finds out that the PVC exists and is not being deleted. The kubelet finishes creating and starting the Pod. Then some client requests deletion of the PVC. Its DeletionTimestamp is set. Then the pvc_protection_controller is notified about this change to the PVC. Note that I did _not_ say that the pvc_protection_controller has by now been notified about the creation or scheduling of the Pod. This is possible, because we have no guarantee about ordering of notifications about different Kinds of objects. The pvc_protection_controller queries its Pod informer's local cache of Pod information and does not find the new Pod. The pvc_protection_controller then removes the Finalizer from the PVC, and soon the PVC API object is removed.
I expected to see that [link] follows the community design doc or includes an optimization to avoid the apiserver check if the local cache shows usage of the PVC.

Routing determination: storage. Bug assessment: a bug.

E2E Proposal: Verify tcpSocket property of v1.Probe along with success and failure threshold.

A E2E to verify `core.v1.tcpSocketAction` resource along with probe's important properties like `successThreshold`, `failureThreshold`, and `periodSeconds`.

Note: following default values are in effect `delay=0s timeout=1s period=10s #success=1 #failure=3`
To improve API coverage based on [label] and their important properties.
[link]

E2E behavior could be:
Create a pod with a container having `tcpSocket` based readiness and liveness probes provided with successThreshold, failureThreshold and periodSeconds values and container should not accept any connection after ~30 sec of it's start. Container MUST be ready after `successThreshold * periodSeconds` (<~30s) is reached. Container MUST NOT be in ready state after `failureThreshold * periodSeconds` (>~30s) is reached.

Note: May need to implement connection closing mechanisam at certain time for `gcr.io/kubernetes-e2e-test-images/liveness:1.1` image to test failureThreshold for `tcp` requests.

Kubelet Bandwidth Limiting Not Working

I tried to set up bandwidth limiting by booting a cluster with `kops`, which by default sets up kubenet. I used the annotations

- kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth: xM
- kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth: xM

and then used `iperf3` to test the ingress and egress bandwidths, with no effect.

Does anyone know if this feature is still supported in kubenet? And if so what are the steps I need to take to boot a cluster that can use pod annotations to do tc shaping.
Per [#2856]([link] traffic shaping should be implemented on Kubenet as of 4/12/2018.
There are a lot of issues regarding traffic shaping not working. None have a concrete answer of how to get it to work on kubenet:
- [#2856]([link]
- [#41471]([link]

Relevant:
- [PR #11988]( [link] I believe this is where it was first implemented.

state:
Deprecate kubelet cAdvisor-based endpoints

The cAdvisor port, which exposed the raw cAdvisor UI & API was removed in Kubernetes 1.12.

Now, we should also begin the deprecation process for the Kueblet API endpoints that are backed by the cAdvisor API. These are legacy endpoints, that expose undocumented APIs that don't conform to Kubernetes API standards. They no longer have any internal usage, as we moved core components to the summary API, and soon to the core metrics API. The cAdvisor APIs also tie us to cAdvisor internally, which we would eventually like to move to an implementation detail.

The endpoints I propose deprecating, and eventually removing are:
- `/spec`
- `/stats/*` _except_ `/stats/summary`
- `/metrics/cadvisor`

state:
Slow connect (TCP retransmits) via NodePort

In out archutecture we have some kinda external (out-of-cluster) Ingress Controller, based on HAProxy + self-written scripts for Kubernetes service discovery (2 instances). ~60 Kubernetes services exposed via NodePort on 8 Kubernetes nodes. Each node runs kube-proxy in iptables mode.

Everything worked fine. But after cluster got more load (HTTP requests per second / concurrent connections), we are experiencing slow connects to services exposed via NodePort because of TCP retransmits.

For now have 4k RPS / 80k concurrent peak. TCP retransmits starts at ~1k RPS / 30k concurrent.

But most strange thing in this situation - retransmit count not same for haproxy/kube-node pair.
For example, haproxy1 have retransmits from kube-nodes 1,2,3 and 8, but haproxy2 have almost zero retransmits from that nodes. Instead haproxy2 have retransmits from kube-nodes 4,5,6 and 7. As you can see, it is like mirrored.

See attachments for clarification. HAProxy configured with 100ms connect timeout, so it redispatches connection on timeout.
![haproxy1]([link]
![haproxy2]([link]
No TCP retransmits, fast connects.
Commit 50-60 deployments + NodePort-exposed services on few nodes. Load with 1k+ RPS, 30k+ concurrent cons. Observe slow connects (1s, 3s, 6s...)
Intercluster communication via flannel w/o cni in hostgw mode.

Tried different sysctls on nodes and haproxies. Tried ipvs mode and got much more TCP retransmits.
Also tried with iptables 1.6.2 with latest flanneld to fix NAT bugs according to this article: [link]

For test installed on kube-nodes out-of-cluster reverse-proxy to pass traffic from outside to kubernetes services and pods - no problems. Also no problems with HostPort-exposed services.

For now have 4k RPS / 80k concurrent peak. TCP retransmits starts at ~1k RPS / 30k concurrent.

But most strange thing in this situation - retransmit count not same for haproxy/kube-node pair.

![haproxy1]([link]
![haproxy2]([link]

state:
Garbage collect VolumeAttachment objects to trigger detach

*Background:* The attach/detach controller create `VolumeAttachment` objects for CSI Volumes to indicate that a volume needs to be attached to a node. It deletes the object to indicate that the volume should be detached.

*Problem:* If the Attach/Detach controller crashes, and in the meantime the pod using that volume is deleted, when the AD controller restarts, it won't know that the volume was previously attached and should be cleaned up.
*Proposal:* We should have the AD controller periodically list all `VolumeAttachment` objects and for any that are not accounted for, update its internal actual/desired state caches so that the volume is gracefully detached.

state:
Autodetect IP family for e2e testing

Introduce a mechanism that allows ~~detecting~~ specifying the IP protocol version used in the e2e testing.
This is a followup on #70248, my understanding is that in order to discriminate between IPv4 or IPv6 we have to use the test labels and this adds complexity to the testing automation and doesn't allow to send this information to the context of the tests.

Having a mechanism to ~~detect~~ specify the IP protocol will simplify the testing for IPv4 and IPv6 and will allow reusing most of the code.

Autodetect IP family for e2e testing

Introduce a mechanism that allows ~~detecting~~ specifying the IP protocol version used in the e2e testing.
This is a followup on #70248, my understanding is that in order to discriminate between IPv4 or IPv6 we have to use the test labels and this adds complexity to the testing automation and doesn't allow to send this information to the context of the tests.

Having a mechanism to ~~detect~~ specify the IP protocol will simplify the testing for IPv4 and IPv6 and will allow reusing most of the code.

Routing determination: network. Bug assessment: not a bug.

CVE-2019-11245: container uid changes to root after first restart or if image is already pulled to the node

[CVSS:3.0/AV:L/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L]([link] 4.9 (medium)

In kubelet v1.13.6 and v1.14.2, containers for pods that do not specify an explicit `runAsUser` attempt to run as uid 0 (root) on container restart, or if the image was previously pulled to the node. If the pod specified `mustRunAsNonRoot: true`, the kubelet will refuse to start the container as root. If the pod did not specify `mustRunAsNonRoot: true`, the kubelet will run the container as uid 0.

CVE-2019-11245 will be **fixed** in the following Kubernetes releases:

* v1.13.7 in [link]
* v1.14.3 in [link]

Fixed by #78261 in master

### Affected components:

* Kubelet

### Affected versions:

* Kubelet v1.13.6
* Kubelet v1.14.2

### Affected configurations:

Clusters with:
* Kubelet versions v1.13.6 or v1.14.2
* Pods that do not specify an explicit `runAsUser: <uid>` or `mustRunAsNonRoot:true`

### Impact:

If a pod is run without any user controls specified in the pod spec (like `runAsUser: <uid>` or `mustRunAsNonRoot:true`), a container in that pod that would normally run as the USER specified in the container image manifest can sometimes be run as root instead (on container restart, or if the image was previously pulled to the node)

* pods that specify an explicit `runAsUser` are unaffected and continue to work properly
* podSecurityPolicies that force a `runAsUser` setting are unaffected and continue to work properly
* pods that specify `mustRunAsNonRoot:true` will refuse to start the container as uid 0, which can affect availability
* pods that do not specify `runAsUser` or `mustRunAsNonRoot:true` will run as uid 0 on restart or if the image was previously pulled to the node

### Mitigations:

This section lists possible mitigations to use prior to upgrading.

CVE-2019-11245: container uid changes to root after first restart or if image is already pulled to the node

[CVSS:3.0/AV:L/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L]([link] 4.9 (medium)

In kubelet v1.13.6 and v1.14.2, containers for pods that do not specify an explicit `runAsUser` attempt to run as uid 0 (root) on container restart, or if the image was previously pulled to the node. If the pod specified `mustRunAsNonRoot: true`, the kubelet will refuse to start the container as root. If the pod did not specify `mustRunAsNonRoot: true`, the kubelet will run the container as uid 0.

CVE-2019-11245 will be **fixed** in the following Kubernetes releases:

* v1.13.7 in [link]
* v1.14.3 in [link]

Fixed by #78261 in master

### Affected components:

* Kubelet

### Affected versions:

* Kubelet v1.13.6
* Kubelet v1.14.2

### Affected configurations:

Clusters with:
* Kubelet versions v1.13.6 or v1.14.2
* Pods that do not specify an explicit `runAsUser: <uid>` or `mustRunAsNonRoot:true`

### Impact:

If a pod is run without any user controls specified in the pod spec (like `runAsUser: <uid>` or `mustRunAsNonRoot:true`), a container in that pod that would normally run as the USER specified in the container image manifest can sometimes be run as root instead (on container restart, or if the image was previously pulled to the node)

* pods that specify an explicit `runAsUser` are unaffected and continue to work properly
* podSecurityPolicies that force a `runAsUser` setting are unaffected and continue to work properly
* pods that specify `mustRunAsNonRoot:true` will refuse to start the container as uid 0, which can affect availability
* pods that do not specify `runAsUser` or `mustRunAsNonRoot:true` will run as uid 0 on restart or if the image was previously pulled to the node

state:
kube-proxy prints misleading error on successful --cleanup

`kube-proxy --cleanup` logs a nil error on success, EG:

`server.go:475] <nil>`.
kube-proxy shouldn't log an error on success. Either a nil error should be interpreted as success, or an explicit exit boolean should be returned & evaluated.
Run `kube-proxy --cleanup` in master/1.15, or 1.14.2+.
Code indicates that this is a problem ever since exiting was introduced (kube-proxy previously hung). It calls log.Fatal() on the return result, under the now-false assumption that an exit -> a crash.

state:
Flexvolume master driver is blocking controller-manager from moving to distroless

There is an effort underway to move to core k8s component images to distroless. One side effect is that shell access is unavailable inside these containers.

Dummy Flexvolume drivers in e2e tests are written as shell scripts, and it's possible that many drivers are written this way as well. These drivers are a problem for controller managers going distroless - the driver Init() call will fail.

Going forward here are some of the possible options:

state:
Calculate oom_score_adj in a CPU-agnostic way, taking in consideration Pod Priority too

I would like to start a conversation to understand if we may improve `GetContainerOOMScoreAdjust` to:

1. Calculate the `oom_score_adj` in a CPU-agnosticy way
2. Take in account Pod Priority too
Currently, the `kubelet` sets a `oom_score_adj` value for each container based on the Pod QoS:

- `Guaranteed`: `-998`
- `BestEffort`: `1000`
- `Burstable`: `min(max(2, 1000 - (1000 * memoryRequestBytes) / machineMemoryCapacityBytes), 999)`

The QoS class depends both on the CPU and memory requests/limits, which means the `oom_score_adj` also depends on the CPU resources and not just on the memory resources, while OOM score is a purely memory management thing. Moreover, `oom_score_adj` is also Pod priority agnostic (except that critical pods always get `-998`, regardless their QoS class) which can cause higher priority pods to get evicted before lower priority pods under node memory pressure.

state:
kubelet won't retry PodSandbox creation for pods with restart policy "Never"

If a pod's restart policy is "Never", and kubelet failed to create the PodSandbox (for whatever reason) once, the pod will be stuck at "ContainerCreating" forever.
Since the user/application containers were never created, kubelet should retry the PodSandbox creation.

The fact that the pod remains in a ContainerCreating state while kubelet explicitly does nothing to resolve the situation also confuses the user.
I don't have an easy way to trigger a podsandbox creation failure off the top of my head, but this should be doable by messing with the CNI binaries/configurations.

When using kubelet config file, `resolverConfig` option is not used by kubelet.
kubelet config option `resolverConfig` is used to set resolver configuration file by kubelet.
kubelet config file:

state:
Improve logging when AD controller lets kubelet attach volumes

Add a lower-level log (2) and/or pod event (info level) whenever the attach detach controller decides to skip processing a volume and let kubelet handle the attaching.
The typical volume attach handling is done by the attach detach controller running in the master.
It used to be handled by kubelet, but was moved to a single controller in the 1.3 timeframe, and this configuration is not being used or supported in most configurations anymore. I would also like to deprecate this option, but that's [another discussion]([link]

However, the mechanism to transition to controller attach detach uses Node annotations is not a reliable mechanism to communicate configuration between master and nodes, as the Node objects can be modified and annotations modified or dropped. In these situations, it would be useful to surface a more visible message to make it easier for users to debug.

state:
Add e2e test(s) for volume scheduling limits

Right now, we have e2e test for [volume scheduling limits]([link] that executes only CSI mock driver with artificial limit of 2 volumes per node.

We need a test with real CSI driver(s).

Proposal:

* Allow individual test storage drivers to specify if they support CSI limits.
* Add a test that picks a random node and creates as many pods with a PV that the volume can handle (128 on GCE!).
* Check that the node can't handle any other volume.
* Make this test part of [CSI external test suite]([link]

* Add similar test(s) for in-tree volume plugins.
* Make sure the tests work with in-tree volume plugins migrated to CSI.

state:
winkernel kube-proxy problems when IPv6DualStack is enabled (ie, in 1.21)

Ran winkernel kube-proxy in 1.21 (where `IPv6DualStack` is now enabled by default). It fails:

`F0408 17:17:11.043472 1316 server.go:489] unable to create proxier: unable to create ipv4 proxier: Could not find host mac address for 0.0.0.0, hostname: e2e-wmcow-bpfpl, clusterCIDR : 10.132.0.0/24, nodeIP:0.0.0.0`

Manually specifying `--bind-address` gets it past that problem but then fails with:

`F0408 21:22:41.744719 1804 server.go:489] unable to create proxier: unable to create ipv6 proxier: Could not find host mac address for ::, hostname: winworker-pbvb6, clusterCIDR : 10.132.0.0/24, nodeIP:::`

(Note that this is a single-stack IPv4 cluster.)

Enabling the feature gate should not change the end-user-visible behavior for people who are not using the gated feature.

There are (at least) two problems:

1. When `IPv6DualStack` is disabled, the startup code calls `utilnode.GetNodeIP(client, hostname)` to get the node IP and passes that to `winkernel.NewProxier`, but when `IPv6DualStack` is enabled, it passes `nodeIPTuple(config.BindAddress)` instead, which will always pass at least one unspecified (`0.0.0.0`/`::`) IP to `NewDualStackProxier`. But the winkernel proxier code doesn't deal with unspecified IPs, at least when using an "overlay" network; it requires that the passed-in IP be an actual IP address on some interface. (It's possible that it should be using something like `utilnet.ResolveBindAddress()` from apimachinery to convert the possibly-unspecified bind address to a local IP.)
2. The winkernel kube-proxy startup code always creates a metaproxier with IPv4 and IPv6 sub-proxiers if `IPv6DualStack` is enabled, but then fails if it can't create either of those proxiers.

state:
Generic Ephemeral Volumes do not work with OwnerReferencesPermissionEnforcement admission plugin

This test fails when OwnerReferencesPermissionEnforcement admission plugin is enabled:

`[sig-storage] CSI Volumes [Driver: csi-hostpath] [Testpattern: Generic Ephemeral-volume (default fs) (late-binding)] ephemeral should create read/write inline ephemeral volume`

After the test creates a pod with an ephemeral volume, ephemeral volume controller in kube-controller-manager fails to create a PVC for it:

The controller must have permissions to `update pods/finalizers` to be allowed to set `pvc.ownerReferece` with `blockOwnerDeletion` to Pods.

The test passes.

With `hack/local-up-cluster.sh`:

1. `
ENABLE_ADMISSION_PLUGINS="NamespaceLifecycle,LimitRanger,ServiceAccount,DefaultStorageClass,DefaultTolerationSeconds,Priority,MutatingAdmissionWebhook,ValidatingAdmissionWebhook,ResourceQuota,OwnerReferencesPermissionEnforcement" ALLOW_PRIVILEGED=true LOG_LEVEL=4 hack/local-up-cluster.sh
`
2. `kubetest --test --test_args="--ginkgo.focus=hostpath.*Generic.Ephemeral.*late-binding.*read/write"`

After the test creates a pod with an ephemeral volume, ephemeral volume controller in kube-controller-manager fails to create a PVC for it:

The controller must have permissions to `update pods/finalizers` to be allowed to set `pvc.ownerReferece` with `blockOwnerDeletion` to Pods.

The test passes.

With `hack/local-up-cluster.sh`:

1. `
ENABLE_ADMISSION_PLUGINS="NamespaceLifecycle,LimitRanger,ServiceAccount,DefaultStorageClass,DefaultTolerationSeconds,Priority,MutatingAdmissionWebhook,ValidatingAdmissionWebhook,ResourceQuota,OwnerReferencesPermissionEnforcement" ALLOW_PRIVILEGED=true LOG_LEVEL=4 hack/local-up-cluster.sh
`
2. `kubetest --test --test_args="--ginkgo.focus=hostpath.*Generic.Ephemeral.*late-binding.*read/write"`

Routing determination: storage. Bug assessment: a bug.

state:
Data caching issue for snapshot tests

The volume snapshot controller tests can result in an empty VolumeSnapshot being taken if NodeUnstageVolume occurs after the VolumeSnapshot is taken. Previously there was a change made in Windows to ensure that NodeUnstageVolume finishes before continuing with the test; however, this needs to also to be included in other distros as well. NodeUnpublish, which removes the bind mount, does not force the caches to flush.

Tests - [link]

The CI jobs should pass when running with a non-hostpath driver.

I'm uncertain on why we've seen an increase in these failures, but running the following tests with a non-hostpath driver appear to flake regularly:
* [Testpattern: Pre-provisioned Snapshot (retain policy)] snapshottable[Feature:VolumeSnapshotDataSource] volume snapshot controller should check snapshot fields, check restore correctly works after modifying source data, check deletion
* [Testpattern: Pre-provisioned Snapshot (delete policy)] snapshottable[Feature:VolumeSnapshotDataSource] volume snapshot controller should check snapshot fields, check restore correctly works after modifying source data, check deletion
* [Testpattern: Dynamic Snapshot (retain policy)] snapshottable[Feature:VolumeSnapshotDataSource] volume snapshot controller should check snapshot fields, check restore correctly works after modifying source data, check deletion
* [Testpattern: Dynamic Snapshot (delete policy)] snapshottable[Feature:VolumeSnapshotDataSource] volume snapshot controller should check snapshot fields, check restore correctly works after modifying source data, check deletion

Pod resources reports no ID for the NUMA node 0

During access to pod resources API, it reports devices from NUMA node 0 without NUMA ID.
For example

The device from NUMA node 0

The device from NUMA node 1

Topology for the device on the NUMA node 0 should be reported correctly

1. Be sure that you have configured some device plugin((GPU, SR-IOV)) and the node has some device on the NUMA node 0(GPU, SR-IOV)
2. Create the pod with the above node selector and that requests the device.
3. Under the node, run a simple go binary that will get container resources via pod resources API

4. Check the above pod resources.

The problem happens because of the topology presentation,

Because ID represented by int64 and the default value for int64 is 0, it ignored during serialization.
From proto3 documentation:

Possible solutions will be:
- represent ID as a string
- do not use nested struct and just have

Dual-stack updates w/ PreferDualStack changes IP assignments

1) start with a single stack cluster
2) create a PreferDualStack service
3) configure API server with a 2nd service CIDR
4) Confirm the above service is not dual-stack
5) Add a label to the above service
6) Observe that the service becomes dual-stack

I think the correct answer is to have a "repair loop" that upgrades (and downgrades!) PreferDualStack Services to match the config.

I think this is a GA blocker.

state:
GPU limits being omitted

Crude example based on the NVIDIA cuda vectorAdd sample container.

The yaml file contents below deploys a pod demonstrating that multiple containers in a single pod can access the same GPU on the K8s node concurrently.

Screenshots of an on-premises execution and a quick diagram of the GPU node, Pod & Container layout follow the yaml file below.

Should it be possible to deploy multiple containers in a single pod and access the same GPU on the K8s node concurrently?
Is this by design and is it an expected behavior?

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: cuda-vector-add
spec:

state:
Corrupted filesystems on failed reconstruction

On a busy machine, kubelet was restarted while a pod was deleted in the API server. Newly started kubelet tried to reconstruct the volume, but it failed with:

Everything went wrong from here. Since kubelet can't reconstruct the volume, it only unmounts the pod local mount, leaving the global mount still mounted. And kubelet removed the volume from `volumesInUse`, therefore allowing the mounted volume to be detached + attached somewhere else. In case of FibreChannel or iSCSI, that don't have 3rd party attach, the volume ends up mounted on two different nodes and the volume gets corrupted. In clouds, the volume may get stuck attached to the node (because some clouds refuse to detach mounted volumes) or it gets force-detached, possibly corrupting the volume.

Exact sequence:

\+ the next node sync removed the volume from `volumesInUse`.

The volume is not corrupted.
Ideally, the volume is unmounted from global mount using UnmountDevice, however, it's not possible without reconstructed volume.

I injected error to [ConstructVolumeSpec of FibreChannel]([link]
I don't know how to reproduce it without it - it's hard to get `GetMountRefs` / `ConsistentRead` to return an error.

Everything went wrong from here. Since kubelet can't reconstruct the volume, it only unmounts the pod local mount, leaving the global mount still mounted. And kubelet removed the volume from `volumesInUse`, therefore allowing the mounted volume to be detached + attached somewhere else. In case of FibreChannel or iSCSI, that don't have 3rd party attach, the volume ends up mounted on two different nodes and the volume gets corrupted. In clouds, the volume may get stuck attached to the node (because some clouds refuse to detach mounted volumes) or it gets force-detached, possibly corrupting the volume.

Exact sequence:

\+ the next node sync removed the volume from `volumesInUse`.

The volume is not corrupted.
Ideally, the volume is unmounted from global mount using UnmountDevice, however, it's not possible without reconstructed volume.

I injected error to [ConstructVolumeSpec of FibreChannel]([link]
I don't know how to reproduce it without it - it's hard to get `GetMountRefs` / `ConsistentRead` to return an error.

state:
Move pod resources API related tests from the memory manager to pod resource test suite

First, memory-related pod resource tests were introduced under the memory manager test suite to avoid over-complication of the pod resource test suite, because pod resource tests do not have a clear separation between setup, test, and teardown phases and
adding some new tests that will configure hugepages, create VMs with relevant memory and hugepages resources will rise the cyclomatic complexity of the pod resource test suite(check if hugepages configured, if yes choose one, if no choose the other, similar to SR-IOV device configuration).

But we should move tests once we will improve the pod resource tests and make it more flexible for adding new tests.

state:
Short running pods take very long to teardown

In master we continue to see instances of short running pods failing to terminate quickly, due to races between sources of truth.

[link] stops e2e tests from "cheating" and bypassing kubelet shutdown, and as a result some tests fail predictably (garbage collection lots of short running pods for testing various behaviors). The linked comment shows a pod that is racing between container start and pod delete. The problem is that dispatchWork invokes `podAndContainersAreTerminal()` on the containerstart event, but the cache that `podAndContainersAreTerminal` checks is not yet up to date (that's handled inside UpdatePod / syncPod).

In general, the pod worker is the one who should be managing shutdown. We added optimizations to dispatchWork to skip the pod worker, and we historically had a race condition where the pod worker was shut down too early and thus termination never happened, but the right thing to do is to stop trying to optimize the pod worker knowing the state of the pod (it's job is to sync the pod) and instead make sure that a) the pod worker is running until a pod is deleted from api (which should be true today) and b) if we need to reduce latency of shutdown, we should do so by ensuring the pod worker gets that update.

The failures here are a significant violation of our performance goals around pods, and our e2e tests are demonstrating the failures pretty cleanly, so we need to put this race condition to bed.

[link] can trigger the issue trivially, so for now using that to debug failure reasons.

We recently upgraded our k8s node from cgroup v1 to cgroup v2 hierarchy and saw that few io related metrics from kubelet (/metrics/cadvisor) are showing erroneous values. for example - `container_fs_writes_bytes_total` or `container_fs_writes_total` always has zero value for all cgroups within that node even though one pod is heavily writing to some pvc in that node. e.g

We expected to see correct values as specified by `io.stat` file under container's cgroup v2 hierarchy.

Simply provision a k8s node with below environment and enable cgroup v2 with following commands during boot.

We've tried kubelet version (v.1.19.8) on another node having cgroup v1 hierarchy with exactly same workload and saw that above metrics are giving values as expected, but they remains zero for cgroup v2 enabled node. We are using kubelet version 1.19.8 which has dependency of cadvisor version v0.37.4. To debug it, I’ve tried increasing the verbosity of kubelet logs --v=5, but there were no surprises there. state:
Kubelet JSON logging performance test

With Kubelet logs fully migrated to structured logging we can measure macro performance improvements related to using JSON logging format. We should use this data to motive more cluster administrators to save on resources.

Requirements:
* Test different logging format to compare. Formats --logging-forma=text, --logging-format=json
* Test different logging verbosity levels: --v=0 (default), and --v=4
* Test Kubelet standard flow (run container, terminate etc)
* Repeat test in small clusters or run larger cluster to collect enough data

My first idea would be to utilize pull-kubernetes-e2e-gce-100-performance scenario to create repeatable way to collect Kubelet metric data. Before starting tests we should consult with SIG Scalability/Node how to best measure compare Kubelet performance.

Goal: Motivate further investment in JSON by being able to say "Switching to JSON logging in kubelet saves average of X% CPU and Y% of Memory" in release announcements.

[team]

Needed to graduate JSON to Beta.

state:
Kubelet JSON logging performance test

With Kubelet logs fully migrated to structured logging we can measure macro performance improvements related to using JSON logging format. We should use this data to motive more cluster administrators to save on resources.

Requirements:
* Test different logging format to compare. Formats --logging-forma=text, --logging-format=json
* Test different logging verbosity levels: --v=0 (default), and --v=4
* Test Kubelet standard flow (run container, terminate etc)
* Repeat test in small clusters or run larger cluster to collect enough data

My first idea would be to utilize pull-kubernetes-e2e-gce-100-performance scenario to create repeatable way to collect Kubelet metric data. Before starting tests we should consult with SIG Scalability/Node how to best measure compare Kubelet performance.

Goal: Motivate further investment in JSON by being able to say "Switching to JSON logging in kubelet saves average of X% CPU and Y% of Memory" in release announcements.

To get kicked out of the pod after the container runtime specified time is reached.
- configure your kubectl client to 1.21
- `kubectl exec -it <any pod> -- sh`
- wait however long your container runtime is set to and see that it doesn't kick you out.

Kubelet does not update its node's leaseDurationSeconds

After creating my cluster, I tweaked one kubelet's config to change its NodeLeaseDuration to 100 seconds. The kubelet echoed the new config to the journal and changed its behavior to renew its lease every 25 seconds --- but it did _not_ update the `spec.leaseDurationSeconds` field of its Lease, that still says "40".

I expected the Lease to reflect the newly configured duration.

I think the above is pretty direct.

state:
Device manager silently fails to restore checkpoint after upgrading to 1.20+

After upgrading kubelet from version <= 1.19 to version >= 1.20, the device manager will fail to restore its state from the checkpoint. The change was introduced in [link] .

The restore fails silently (it actually writes a warning in the logs, but keeps going). Because of this the device manager state is inconsistent up until the device plugins register themselves again, which can take minutes, depending on the specific device plugin. We seen up to 5 minutes on real clusters the for SRIOV device plugin.

Because of the inconsistent state, the kubelet will **NOT** update the device availability to zero, so the scheduler will send pods towards the inconsistent kubelet.
At admission time, the device manager allocation will not trigger, again because of the incosistent state, so pods will be admitted without device plugins actually being allocated to them.

Any of the following wouls be acceptable
1. the kubelet recovers the checkpoint state correctly
2. the kubelet sets its own state as inconsistent, so pods aren't scheduled until the node heals
3. the kubelet sets its own state as inconsistent, so pods aret scheduled, but aren't admitted until the node heals

1. run pods requesting devices on <= 1.19 kubelet
2. drain the node
3. upgrade the kubelet to a version >= 1.20
4. run pods on the upgraded node typically as soon as the node gets Ready

The issue was discovered first in openshift, but turns out is not openshift specific.

The bug triggers only after a upgrade, so kubelet is stopped, updated (<= 1.19 to >= 1.20) and started again.
There are no more know ways to trigger this bug.

The updated kubelet fails to restore the checkpoint data. See this excerpt from the logs

The kubelet keep going, but this means the internal devicemanager maps will be **completely** empty. The expected state after recovery is that the *key* of the relevant devices will be present.

state:
Support for 1:N mapping between hostPort and containerPort in Deployment Spec

Currently when we specify a deployment spec with hostNetwork is true and the application in a container listens to multiple ports, the hostPort should be assigned for each of those port.

ports:
- containerPort: 8090
hostPort: 8090
- containerPort: 8091
hostPort : 8091

It would be nice to have range of containerPort for a given hostPort. Something like this below:
ports:
- hostPort: 8090
containerPort: 8090-8200

To add, we are not using the service resource here because these are security applications where it should need host network namespace and avoid SNAT/DNATing. Pod can create successfully because /etc/resolv.conf is not an essential file in filesystem. (see

1. mv /etc/resolv.conf somewhere else

state:
CSI volume is not re-labeled when the first NodePublishVolume fails

Using a CSI volume on a Linux machine with SELinux in enforcing mode. I noticed when the volume is used in a pod and the first NodePublishVolume for that pod fails (e.g. timeout), the volume does not get correct SELinux labels.

The volume gets correct SELinux labels.

With a hacked CSI driver that returns error on the first NodePublishVolume.
1. Run a pod with a CSI volume.
2. See the first NodePublishVolume fails (e.g. DeadlineExceeded).
3. See that a subsequent NodePublishVolume succeeds.
4. See the pod is Running.
5. Check SELinux label of the volume

Got `system_u:object_r:unlabeled_t:s0`, where `system_u:object_r:container_file_t:s0:c15,c25` was expected.

state:
Kubelet panic in syncTerminatedPod

When testing #102344 against OpenShift CI, I discovered a panic in the kubelet: [link]

Further investigation revealed that it is possible for `syncTerminatedPod` to panic under certain circumstances: [link]

We hit this case when `update.Options.RunningPod != nil` (podStatus remains nil) and `update.WorkType == TerminatedPodWork` (nil will be passed along to `syncTerminatedPod`). I'm not sure why exactly that would happen but it seems possible.

Don't panic!

Unclear, I've been trying to trace the code/find evidence of this happening in k8s CI but haven't found a match yet. ([link] would be nice :smile:)

state:
Race condition in prober_manager

Ref: [link]

Prober_manager triggers a manual run of readinessProbe after startupProbe succeeds, a race condition might reset `ready=false` even after readinessProbe succeeds.
Ready state takes another success of readinessProbe to register.

Ready state updates immediately after the manual readinessProbe successful run.

Flake #99979

Related to #103593

state:
The CPU manager does not work correctly for the guaranteed pod with multiple containers

The CPU manager removes the allocation for previous containers under the guaranteed pod once the next container allocation started.

The CPU manager test fails because of it

[link]

The CPU manager should keep previous containers allocations.

- Start the guaranteed pod with two containers
- Verify the CPU pining for the first container

I think the problem introduced by recent refactor under [link]

So what happens:

- the CPU manager allocates the CPU for the first container
- Part of the second container allocation the CPU manager calls to [removeStaleState]([link]
- The kubelet does not recognize our new pod as running one and as a result, `removeStaleState` removes the first container from the state file

The issues affect the memory manager as well.

state:
Kubelet reporting 137 exit code for a container whose exit code 0 was previously known

I have pods with a `RestartPolicy: Never` that perform a task, wait for a sigterm, clean up and then exit. These pods have only one container inside them. I have observed on kubernetes > 1.20.0, that after issuing a graceful delete, sometimes these pods will be stuck in `Terminating`. Upon describing the pod, I can see the following state:

I have confirmed from the `containerd` logs (the container runtime I am using) and with `strace`, that the pods are receiving a single `sigterm` and then exiting, with an exitCode of 0. I have been patching log statements into kubelet and I am now confident I understanding _what_ is happening, though I do not know why. All of the following statements relate specifically to commit `4aa451e8458a7cbf78ed464e9e47e87d424541ce`, which I believe is the sha for kubernetes `1.21.1`.

In [link] upon receiving a `pleg.ContainerDied` event for the pod sandbox, which for `containerd` is a container, [link] is called. This leads to us calling [link] and the returned `podStatus` is passed to [link] This takes us to [link] where we immediately call `convertStatusToAPIStatus` with the `podStatus` arg. This function calls [link] and we end up setting the ExitCode to 137 [link] Why does that happen? Well, it turns out that `podStatus.ContainerStatuses` is an empty slice at this point in time.

I have pods with a `RestartPolicy: Never` that perform a task, wait for a sigterm, clean up and then exit. These pods have only one container inside them. I have observed on kubernetes > 1.20.0, that after issuing a graceful delete, sometimes these pods will be stuck in `Terminating`. Upon describing the pod, I can see the following state:

I have confirmed from the `containerd` logs (the container runtime I am using) and with `strace`, that the pods are receiving a single `sigterm` and then exiting, with an exitCode of 0. I have been patching log statements into kubelet and I am now confident I understanding _what_ is happening, though I do not know why. All of the following statements relate specifically to commit `4aa451e8458a7cbf78ed464e9e47e87d424541ce`, which I believe is the sha for kubernetes `1.21.1`.

In [link] upon receiving a `pleg.ContainerDied` event for the pod sandbox, which for `containerd` is a container, [link] is called. This leads to us calling [link] and the returned `podStatus` is passed to [link] This takes us to [link] where we immediately call `convertStatusToAPIStatus` with the `podStatus` arg. This function calls [link] and we end up setting the ExitCode to 137 [link] Why does that happen? Well, it turns out that `podStatus.ContainerStatuses` is an empty slice at this point in time.

state:
kube get pods --watch doesn't always report terminal status with exitCode during Deployment update

When updating an existing Deployment (`kubectl replace -f deployment.yaml`), new pods are being created and old pods are killed. We are constantly doing `kubectl get pods --watch` to do some internal monitoring, however sometimes (cca 30-50% of the cases) we don't receive the final update (for the old pod that is being stopped). Expecting somthing like:

Instead the last status update for such pod is weird:

(complete logs below)
We really need to know the exitCode of all terminated containers/pods during upgrade.

Receive the exitCode (included in the final pod status update notification) for all pods during Deployment upgrade.

It is hard to consistently reproduce, but it happens to us with almost every Deployment update for at least one pod.

Deployment spec: [deployment.yml]([link]
I am attaching 3 logs ( all done via `kubectl get pods --output json --watch-only --output-watch-events | jq 'del(.object.metadata.managedFields)'`):

- [Initial creation of the Deployment]([link] really interesting)

- [Logs from deployment upgrade that is OK]([link] (changed resources.limits.memory to trigger the upgrade), using `kubectl replace` that is without problems. All pods correctly reported the final terminated status with exitCode. This log is mainly for complete picture, nothing much interesting there. All pods starts terminating (MODIFIED event with deletionTimestamp appears, then they shift from `state.running` to `state.terminated` with attached exit code.

- [Logs from second (faulty) upgrade]([link] <--- THIS is the important one. Again just changed memory using `kubectl replace` And one pod doesn't report the exitcode at all.

Inconsistent reset of changes to kubernetes endpoints

If you change some attributes of the kubernetes endpoint in the default namespace, they are not reset

##### Attributes that are reset (correctly)
* IP address

##### Attributes that are not reset (incorrect)
* Port
* Port name
* Protocol

If you change those attibutes of the kubernetes endpoint in the default namespace it is not reset to the correct value. This differs from the IP address which is reset rapidly.

All attributes to be reset to the correct values.

##### Example of what I expect to happen
Here's an example of the IP being reset to 192.168.65.4 rather than being left at the wrong values (1.1.1.1)

Example to patch the port to some nonsense that won't work

To reset to default

Example to patch the port name

To reset to default

Example to patch the protocol

To reset to default

The resetting behaviour of the IP address prevents #97076 being used to MITM traffic to the kubernetes API, so that's good.

state:
Graceful Node Shutdown regression in 1.21 → 1.22

Shutdown a node gracefully. E.g. with `systemctl reboot`.

Expected to see pods being evicted, and pods being started on another nodes.

Let a deployment create one pod, configure Graceful Node Shutdown as described in [link] then just `systemctl reboot` that node. Then, the pod will get a state of `Terminated` or `Completed`, but no new pod is being created and scheduled on a different node. Then, when the node comes back, the terminated pod stays in such a state:

Effectively, the pod is running on the node which has been rebooted gracefully, but is in a `Terminated` state.

This worked as expected in v1.21

# cat /etc/os-release
PRETTY_NAME="Debian GNU/Linux 11 (bullseye)"
NAME="Debian GNU/Linux"
VERSION_ID="11"
VERSION="11 (bullseye)"
VERSION_CODENAME=bullseye
ID=debian
HOME_URL="[link]
SUPPORT_URL="[link]
BUG_REPORT_URL="[link]

# uname -a
Linux k8s-node07 5.10.0-8-armmp #1 SMP Debian 5.10.46-4 (2021-08-03) armv7l GNU/Linux

Shutdown a node gracefully. E.g. with `systemctl reboot`.

Expected to see pods being evicted, and pods being started on another nodes.

Let a deployment create one pod, configure Graceful Node Shutdown as described in [link] then just `systemctl reboot` that node. Then, the pod will get a state of `Terminated` or `Completed`, but no new pod is being created and scheduled on a different node. Then, when the node comes back, the terminated pod stays in such a state:

Effectively, the pod is running on the node which has been rebooted gracefully, but is in a `Terminated` state.

This worked as expected in v1.21

# cat /etc/os-release
PRETTY_NAME="Debian GNU/Linux 11 (bullseye)"
NAME="Debian GNU/Linux"
VERSION_ID="11"
VERSION="11 (bullseye)"
VERSION_CODENAME=bullseye
ID=debian
HOME_URL="[link]
SUPPORT_URL="[link]
BUG_REPORT_URL="[link]

state:
1.22 regression: Kubelet rejects pods that use resources that should be freed by completed pods

There appears to be a change of behavior / possible regression in k8s 1.22 with respect to pod lifecycle behavior.

We've started to see some cases when multiple pods are being created (often as part of a k8s job) the following will happen:

1. Multiple pods get created by e.g. job controller (e.g. say 5). Each pod in job requests majority of node memory so only one such pod can fit on node at a time.
2. Scheduler schedules [first] pod to node, rest (4 pods) stay in pending
3. Kubelet accepts first pod, runs it to completion
4. Next pod get scheduled to the node
5. Kubelet rejects the pod during pod admission, e.g. with `OutOfMemory`, despite the fact that the first pod has already completed successfully
6. This results in many of pods backing the job getting into Failed phase and having to be recreated by job controller. The job can often get into BackofLimit exceeded to hitting backoffLimit.

The root issue seems to be a mismatch of when kubelet actually considers the pod to complete and what it reports to API server (which causes the followup pods to be scheduled to it). I'm still investigating further, but this may be related to the pod lifecycle changes in 1.22 -- [link]

I've created a e2e test as minimal repro of this behavior -- [link]

state:
kubelet is creating a 0 byte file for each pod restart and is causing nodes to run out of inodes on filesystem

For each restart of the pod, kubelet seems to write a 0 byte file into the `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-id>/containers/<container-name>/`:

On k8s clusters where many pods are stuck in `CrashLoopBackOff` state kubelet will create millions of these 0 byte files, which can lead to nodes running out of inodes on a filesystem where `/var/lib/kubelet` is located. For example, in our clusters `/var/lib/kubelet` is on a small `/` filesystem with 512K inodes allocated and we found instances where the above described kubelet behavior exhausted inodes:

kubelet should keep the latest file (if it is needed) and delete files for any previous pod restarts.

Start a broken pod that you know will go into `CrashLoopBackOff`. Login into a node where the pod gets scheduled and look at the files in the `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-id>/containers/<container-name>/` directory.

No.

kubectl get pods command shows status AppArmor for pod on k8s v1.22

I recently upgraded to k8s version 1.22 and made the following observations. I deployed hello-apparmor.yaml example from the kubernetes tutorial on [securing pods with AppArmor]([link]
hello-apparmor.yaml

Since I had not loaded corresponding apparmor profile yet I got this output using `kubectl describe pods`:

And `kubectl get pods -A` output:

So to correct that I applied the desired apparmor profile(k8s-apparmor-example-deny-write). After doing so I get the following outputs:
`sudo aa-status`

`kubectl describe pods`

`kubectl describe pods`

I followed the same steps on k8s version 1.21 and couldn't produce the issue. I think we should get `Running` instead of `AppArmor` and the message shouldn't be displayed since the profile is already applied.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Deploy a pod with apparmor annotations.
2. Enforce the associated apparmor profile.
1. I checked whether profile is actually being enforced using `kubectl exec -ti hello-apparmor -- /bin/sh` and found that the profile is indeed enforced on the pod containers.

Here I tried creating newfile and apparmor blocks it since the profile denies write.
2. This doesn't go away even after waiting for several hours.

state:
Improve unit tests for Kubelet configuration APIs

There are two main issues right now with the test coverage for the Kubelet configuration APIs (internal type defined by [pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go]([link] and serializable type at [staging/src/k8s.io/kubelet/config/v1beta1/types.go]([link]

1. There are no unit tests for [pkg/kubelet/apis/config/v1beta1/defaults.go]([link]

We should at minimum have unit tests that populate defaults for the most minimal config, e.g. [pkg/apis/core/v1/defaults_test.go]([link]

2. The validation tests in [pkg/kubelet/apis/config/validation/validation_test.go]([link] are not targeted

These just throw together a bunch of different validation issues and then count the errors. In theory, if one thing breaks but another is fixed, the tests won't fail. These should be completely refactored in order to test *specific* validation behaviours, e.g. as in [pkg/apis/core/v1/validation/validation_test.go]([link]

If you are a relatively new contributor, please give the [API conventions]([link] and [API change]([link] docs a read as they will help provide context for you to dive in.

There are two main issues right now with the test coverage for the Kubelet configuration APIs (internal type defined by [pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go]([link] and serializable type at [staging/src/k8s.io/kubelet/config/v1beta1/types.go]([link]

1. There are no unit tests for [pkg/kubelet/apis/config/v1beta1/defaults.go]([link]

We should at minimum have unit tests that populate defaults for the most minimal config, e.g. [pkg/apis/core/v1/defaults_test.go]([link]

2. The validation tests in [pkg/kubelet/apis/config/validation/validation_test.go]([link] are not targeted

These just throw together a bunch of different validation issues and then count the errors. In theory, if one thing breaks but another is fixed, the tests won't fail. These should be completely refactored in order to test *specific* validation behaviours, e.g. as in [pkg/apis/core/v1/validation/validation_test.go]([link]

If you are a relatively new contributor, please give the [API conventions]([link] and [API change]([link] docs a read as they will help provide context for you to dive in.

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: not a bug.

state:
Remove DynamicKubeletConfig from node tests

Deprecation issue: [link]

Currently, our e2e tests have a dependency on the deprecated DynamicKubeletConfiguration feature. At minimum, we use the feature to set the KubeletConfiguration, and we check metrics from it (e.g. [link]

We've also seen that the use of this feature in our serial tests is unreliable. Sometimes the kubelet fails to restart, which causes the tests to crash/fail: [link]

The node e2e test suite was written before the component config APIs existed, and so right now the only way to configure a kubelet for tests is with extra command line flags, passed through our current test harness. The only way it's possible to set KubeletConfiguration values that don't have a corresponding command line flag is with a test code change using the DynamicKubeletConfiguration feature. It would be much better to refactor to just support a custom KubeletConfiguration provided at launch time.

Suggested path forward:

- [ ] Update our test runner such that we can provide a KubeletConfiguration file, rather than configuring jobs with command-line flags
- [ ] Determine some mechanism to either update the config and restart the kubelet during test runs, or guidelines for how to manage custom KubeletConfigs in test jobs that need to exercise features outside of the default set
- [ ] Remove all use of the DynamicKubeletConfiguration from e2e tests

state:
CPUManager releases CPUs of init containers while they are being reused in app containers

+ CPUManager releases CPUs of init containers while they are being reused in app containers.

+ Certainly kubelet should not release any of CPUs which are being used in containers.

+ Start kubelet using static policy.
+ Create a pod with 1 init container(request 4cpu) and 1 app container(request 2cpu).
+ After pod started(Running), we can see 2 CPUs used by app container are inherited from init container which is fine.
+ Then manually remove init container, you will see the CPUs once used by init container are all released even though some of them are being reused in app container.

- It seems this was introduced in PR #90419.

#### Others:
- This issue is fixed by #104837.

state:
CPUManager releases CPUs of init containers while they are being reused in app containers

+ CPUManager releases CPUs of init containers while they are being reused in app containers.

+ Certainly kubelet should not release any of CPUs which are being used in containers.

+ Start kubelet using static policy.
+ Create a pod with 1 init container(request 4cpu) and 1 app container(request 2cpu).
+ After pod started(Running), we can see 2 CPUs used by app container are inherited from init container which is fine.
+ Then manually remove init container, you will see the CPUs once used by init container are all released even though some of them are being reused in app container.

- It seems this was introduced in PR #90419.

#### Others:
- This issue is fixed by #104837.

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.

state:
Orphaned pod found, but error not a directory occurred when trying to remove the volumes dir

One of our nodes had a hard reboot. After this, the following message was occurring in the kubelet logs every 2 seconds:

Indeed, the orphaned pod directory exists and contains 1 stale volume directory with a file in it (probably explaining the "not a directory" error):

Deleting this file manually leads to immediate resolving of the Kubelet error 2 seconds later:

I know that the Kubelet tries to clean up orphaned pod directories, and various issues have been fixed regarding this in the past, such as figuring out stale mounts and deleting old directories (#60987 for example).

However, it looks like when there are files present, it fails to remove the stale directory.

I think, but have not attempted, it can be reproduced by these steps:

1. start a Pod with a mounted PVC
2. manually create a file inside a Pod's `volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/pvc-...` directory
3. hard-reboot the machine, so that the kubelet gets no chance to clean up the Pod directory, i.e. directory becomes orphaned
4. (If creating the file of step 2 was not possible before, it can also be done after the reboot, but before the kubelet comes up.)
5. observe error in the Kubelet logs.

The CSI provider used is Hetzner Cloud (hcloud-csi-driver:1.6.0), I'm not sure if it's responsible for creating the file.

state:
kubelet does not restart static pods when apiserver is down

HandlePodCleanups is responsible for restarting static pods, but handle pod cleanups will not run until the apiserver reports in. If the apiserver or any components it depends on is running as a static pod, it is possible for the static pod to never restart.

Reproduce:

1. Start a cluster
2. Run a static pod with a static UID on a node
3. Terminate the apiservers
4. Restart the kubelet of the node with the static pod
5. Change the configuration of the static pod on disk

Expect: static pod with static uid should restart

HandlePodCleanups should be able to SyncKnownPods to pod worker and restart static pods independent of whether the apiserver is running.

We are missing e2e tests that simulate down apiserver and stress static pods, which could have caught this.

state:
containerd pod and mirror pods sometimes remain after deleting the manifest

We have a test that creates a static pod on every node and a daemonset that later deletes the manifests for those files. Sometimes the mirror pod and the containerd pod remain. We've seen this when transient failures communicating with the apiserver caused a failure in calico like:

There were no further references to the pod in the kubelet logs after that.

Restarting kubelet seems to clean up the pods. It looks like kubelet takes one shot at deleting the pod and doesn't try again until kubelet is restarted.

Kubelet should successfully delete the containerd resources and mirror pod once connectivity is restored. We don't see the node go NotReady, so a retry might have succeeded right away.

* Create pod manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests
* Wait to see mirror pod in `kubectl get pods`
* Delete manifest file - and somehow cause a failure like seen above
* `kubectl get pod` and `crictl pods` still list the pod

state:
CSI Volume staging path contains PV name

When two CSI PVs point to the same volume in the storage backend, kubelet can't start pods that use these two PVs on the same node.

Both PVs have the same VolumeHandle and kubelet is smart enough to recognize that they're the same volume (because they have the same unique volume ID). It calls `NodeStage` only once, however, the staging path contains name of one of the PVs, say PV1: `/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/pv/pvc-f5fa91c3-bf91-42a9-a8a3-da516e0371f0/globalmount/`

[link]

One of the CSI volume `SetUpAt` calls then fails, because it uses PV2 to compute the staging path and that path does not exist.

Both pods should just start.

Using CSI HostPath volume, PV1 (dynamically provisioned for simplicity):

PV2 (basically edited PV1):

PVC1, PVC2, Pod1 and Pod2 are trivial, nothing special there.

state:
CSI Volume staging path contains PV name

When two CSI PVs point to the same volume in the storage backend, kubelet can't start pods that use these two PVs on the same node.

Both PVs have the same VolumeHandle and kubelet is smart enough to recognize that they're the same volume (because they have the same unique volume ID). It calls `NodeStage` only once, however, the staging path contains name of one of the PVs, say PV1: `/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/pv/pvc-f5fa91c3-bf91-42a9-a8a3-da516e0371f0/globalmount/`

[link]

One of the CSI volume `SetUpAt` calls then fails, because it uses PV2 to compute the staging path and that path does not exist.

Both pods should just start.

Using CSI HostPath volume, PV1 (dynamically provisioned for simplicity):

PV2 (basically edited PV1):

PVC1, PVC2, Pod1 and Pod2 are trivial, nothing special there.

Routing determination: storage. Bug assessment: a bug.

EndpointSlice Mirroring Controller does not cleanup EndpointSlices when a Selector is added to a Service

1. Service with Selector is created
2. Selector is removed
3. Both Endpoints and EndpointSlice controllers do not clean up Endpoint(Slice)s
4. EndpointSlice mirroring controller starts mirroring the Endpoints resource originally created by the Endpoints controller
5. Selector is added back to the Service
6. Pods backing Service change
7. EndpointSlice created by mirroring controller still references original IP from step 4

At least one of the following:

1. The Endpoints and EndpointSlices to be cleaned up when the Service has the selector removed ([link]
2. The mirrored EndpointSlice to be removed when the Service has a selector added back

state:
node_e2e: Cleanup configuration and rename jenkins/ directory

Currently, node_e2e configuration exists in the `jenkins/` directory underneath node_e2e. This directory is a hangover from the time before Kubernetes migrated to Prow. This directory is regularly a point of contention when adding new features to tests, and causes confusion to people trying to make changes to them.

We should remove the unused portions of this directory and rename it to something more useful (`e2e_node/configuration`?) to simplify future changes while maintaining the current developer workflow.

This is going to involve coordinating a couple of things between k/k and k/test-infra to ensure that we do not cause a break in tests during the migration process and to not break running tests against older release branches.

My naive suggestion for handling this would be:

- [ ] Remove unused code from jenkins/
- [ ] Create a copy of the jenkins/ directory with the new name
- [ ] Update test-infra to reference the new paths, duplicating configurations where necessary to preserve jobs for older branches
- [ ] Remove the jenkins/ directory

(@user / @user might have better suggestions for how to handle this?)

- [ ] Update test-infra to reference the new paths, duplicating configurations where necessary to preserve jobs for older branches
- [ ] Remove the jenkins/ directory

Kubelet credential provider is in alpha since 1.20 release, we need to add e2e tests to move it to beta.

**Current e2e tests for intree credential providers:**
[1] [link] (uses intree docker config credential provider)
[2] [link] (uses intree gcp credential provider)
[3] [link] (uses intree gcp credential provider)

The job pull-kubernetes-e2e-gce-ubuntu-containerd fails with replica sets private image tests if external credential provider is enabled by default

**Problems in adding e2e tests for external credential providers**
- The credential provider binary and config file needs to be installed on node VM before Kubelet starts, external cloud providers credential providers like GCP only supported to install with external cloud providers
- Tests using intree docker config provider are part of node conformance tests

**Work needs to be done**
1. Provide a way to run existing node conformance tests[1] with external credential provider
A sample-credential-provider repo needs to be created under k8s-sigs which can be build and installed via node e2e tests to run existing node conformance tests

2. Migrate the replica set tests [2] & [3] to out of tree gcp credential provider
Need help from gcp cloud provider team to work on this.

state:
kube-proxy only looks at Addresses[0] in EndpointSlice

An `EndpointSlice` can contain up to 1000 `Endpoints`, which can each contain up to 100 `Addresses`. Or at least, that's what the docs say, but actually, kube-proxy (or more specifically, `pkg/proxy/endpointslicecache.go`) only looks at the first Address in each Endpoint:

(This is compatible with how `EndpointSliceController` works, since it would only generate multi-Address Endpoints if a pod had multiple `PodIPs` of the same address family, which is not allowed. But it's not compatible with manually-generated EndpointSlices.)

Either all `Addresses` are used, or else the docs state that only `Addresses[0]` is used and the field is an array solely for historical reasons.

(This is compatible with how `EndpointSliceController` works, since it would only generate multi-Address Endpoints if a pod had multiple `PodIPs` of the same address family, which is not allowed. But it's not compatible with manually-generated EndpointSlices.)

Either all `Addresses` are used, or else the docs state that only `Addresses[0]` is used and the field is an array solely for historical reasons.

Routing determination: network. Bug assessment: a bug.

state:
Add an e2e test validating pod statuses on container state wipe

I changed some behaviour to be more resilient to this failure mode in [link] but we don't have an e2e to validate it.

We should write an e2e to verify that, when the container runtime statuses are wiped (e.g. with crio-wipe on a node running CRI-O), we preserve the following behaviours:

1. Any deleted pod will never go Running -> Pending.
2. A non-daemonset API pod will never go Running -> Pending.
3. Static pods (with the same UID) are allowed to go Running -> Pending if the node rebooted.
4. If a daemonset pod doesn't have init containers, it will never go Running -> Pending.
5. Daemonset pods with init containers are allowed to go Running -> Pending if the node rebooted.

See also [link]

state:
Test should be demoted from Conformance: [sig-node] Events should be sent by kubelets and the scheduler about pods scheduling and running

Related:
- Noticed this as part of [link]
- Opened in response to: [link]

According to our [rules for Conformance tests]([link] the `[sig-node] Events should be sent by kubelets and the scheduler about pods scheduling and running` e2e test is ineligible for Conformance. Specifically, the test in question is looking for guaranteed delivery of Events from specific sources (kubelet and default scheduler). This cannot be reasonably expected of all Kubernetes clusters, and thus the test should be demoted from Conformance.

For historical context:
- It looks like this has been part of Conformance sometime since sometime prior to 2015-10-17 (we introduced the [Conformance] tag in 1.2, ref: [link]
- We overhauled Conformance testing policy (including exclusion of Events) on 2018-10-08 (ref: [link] )

If I wanted to be a language lawyer about this, I could say the policy covers ineligibility for _promotion_ but said nothing about the existing corpus of tests. But I think this was just an honest oversight when we reviewed the existing Conformance tests.

Due to the very nature of what this test is verifying, I don't think it's possible to rewrite to avoid Events. Thus, I think it should be demoted from Conformance. SIG Node is free to continue to treat this as release-blocking, but it's not something we can reasonably expect of any Kubernetes cluster

state:
Test should be demoted from Conformance: [sig-node] Events should be sent by kubelets and the scheduler about pods scheduling and running

Related:
- Noticed this as part of [link]
- Opened in response to: [link]

According to our [rules for Conformance tests]([link] the `[sig-node] Events should be sent by kubelets and the scheduler about pods scheduling and running` e2e test is ineligible for Conformance. Specifically, the test in question is looking for guaranteed delivery of Events from specific sources (kubelet and default scheduler). This cannot be reasonably expected of all Kubernetes clusters, and thus the test should be demoted from Conformance.

For historical context:
- It looks like this has been part of Conformance sometime since sometime prior to 2015-10-17 (we introduced the [Conformance] tag in 1.2, ref: [link]
- We overhauled Conformance testing policy (including exclusion of Events) on 2018-10-08 (ref: [link] )

If I wanted to be a language lawyer about this, I could say the policy covers ineligibility for _promotion_ but said nothing about the existing corpus of tests. But I think this was just an honest oversight when we reviewed the existing Conformance tests.

Due to the very nature of what this test is verifying, I don't think it's possible to rewrite to avoid Events. Thus, I think it should be demoted from Conformance. SIG Node is free to continue to treat this as release-blocking, but it's not something we can reasonably expect of any Kubernetes cluster

because conformance

state:
Volumes are detached while they're still mounted on a node

A/D controller tries to detach volumes that are still mounted after 6 minutes. The conditions to trigger the detach are: [link]

I.e. all containers are finished. But that does not guarantee that volumes are unmounted. When a CSI driver can't unmount a volume for 6 minutes, the volume is force detached by A/D controller, corrupting the volume and leaving volume mounts on the node in a bad state. Note that the node is perfectly healthy, it just can't unmount a volume from whatever reason.

A/D controller detaches volumes after a Pod is deleted from the API server, i.e. the volumes are unmounted or someone force-deleted the pods.

Very artificial reproducer:

1. Run a Pod with an attachable CSI volume.
2. On the node, make the volume mount busy, e.g.:

Every unmount of the volume fails and kubelet/the CSI driver periodically retry.
3. Delete the pod
4. After 6 minutes, see the volume is detached without unmounting first.

KCM logs:

Note that the Pod is still in the API server:

And the node is healthy:

Note that some CSI drivers (e.g. the cloud ones) do not allow detaching a volume while it's still mounted. Not all CSI driver have such possibility and they rely on Kubernetes not to call ControllerUnpublish before NodeUnpublish / NodeUnstage succeeds.
