The new grpc probe feature introduced a new field for grpc probes that has an inconsistent name between json and proto and needs to be changed before release goes out. Otherwise this inconsistency will be stayed forever as it will be close to impossible to change field names.

See thread: [link]

Field [link] to be called `grpc` (all lower case).

this is just a schema change

Routing determination: network. Bug assessment: a bug.

state:
No traffic disable handled by graceful node shutdown

The graceful-node-shutdown feature has been there, it handled preStop and grace period cases, but traffic may still be routed into this pod during shutdown.

No further traffics are routed when node gets shutdown: pod IP should be moved into NotReady address list of Endpoint

Create a nginx deployment and a LoadBlance service with one or more replicas, keep simulating traffics, then try to reboot a node that runs nginx pod, the 503 error or other errors may be returned.

state:
Container status not updated after termination cause by pod deletion

Reproduction steps below, but at a high level:
1. I have a pod with 2 containers. I kill the pod. terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 30s
2. Container 1 terminates immediately. Container 2 terminates after 30s.
3. Immediately after the removal, pod is updated with deletionTimestamp
4. Container 1 terminates, but pod status does NOT change at all.
5. 30s later, container 2 terminates and pod dies.

After container 1 terminates, the containerStatus is updated to indicate the terminated container is no longer running.

Apply this pod:

echo container exits immediately, sleep does not until SIGKILL.

Next, run `kubectl delete foo`.

Observe that after a few seconds (up to 30s), the container status is not updated:

Kubelet logs, with -v6:
[kubelet.txt]([link]

state:
Container status not updated after termination cause by pod deletion

Reproduction steps below, but at a high level:
1. I have a pod with 2 containers. I kill the pod. terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 30s
2. Container 1 terminates immediately. Container 2 terminates after 30s.
3. Immediately after the removal, pod is updated with deletionTimestamp
4. Container 1 terminates, but pod status does NOT change at all.
5. 30s later, container 2 terminates and pod dies.

After container 1 terminates, the containerStatus is updated to indicate the terminated container is no longer running.

Apply this pod:

echo container exits immediately, sleep does not until SIGKILL.

Next, run `kubectl delete foo`.

Observe that after a few seconds (up to 30s), the container status is not updated:

Kubelet logs, with -v6:
[kubelet.txt]([link]

state:
Kubelet spamming 'Unable to fetch pod log stats' log messages after running cronjobs

I have a cronjob that runs a Python script every 5 minutes. After the cronjob finishes running, I start seeing a bunch of log messages in my systemd journal like the following:

Those directories in /var/log don't exist as they belong to old pods that have finished running.

These messages keep increasing in volume as time passes (almost received a 1000 of those messages at one time, after which I had to reboot the node to fix the issue). It almost looks like the kubelet is not cleaning up the old pods for some reason. I can't see these old pods when I run `kubectl get pods -A`, so I'm assuming their is some issue with the kubelet's cleanup process.

kubelet (or cadvisor) shouldn't try to read logs for pods that don't exist.

Setup a short lived cronjob running every 5 minutes and observe the logs (Kubernetes v1.22.4, CRI-O v1.22.1, Ubuntu 20.04)

state:
Exclusive CPUs not removed from deleted Pod and put back in the defaultCPUSet.

The `CPUManager` has logic to periodically cleanup stale state and reclaim exclusive CPUs from pods that have recently terminated. It does this by querying the system for a list of `activePods()` and reclaiming CPUs from any pods it is tracking that are not in this list.

This works fine for most pods, but special care needs to be taken to ensure that CPUs are not accidentally reclaimed from pods that have not started yet. Allocation of CPUs to the containers of a pod happens during pod admission (i.e. before the pod is added to the `activePods()` list), so a simple state variable (`pendingAdmissionPod`) is used to indicate which pod is currently being admitted and exclude it from cleanup. Since pod admission is serialized, only one pod will ever be pending admission at a given time, and only a single variable is necessary to track this (i.e. whenever a new pod enters the admission loop to have exclusive CPUs granted to it, `pendingAdmissionPod` is overwritten to point to the new pod, clearing way for the previous one to have its state cleaned up when appropriate).

Unfortunately, this simple procedure can cause problems because `pendingAdmissionPod` is never reset to `nil` after the **last** pod is admitted. This is usually fine, because the next time a pod comes in for admission, it will be overwritten to point to the new pod. But if no new pods come in, then it continues to point to the last pod that we attempted to admit (forever essentially), making it so that we can never cleanup its state if it gets deleted at some point in the future (because it is always treated as an "active" pod so long as it is pointed to by `pendingAdmissionPod`).

I don't think this issue is critical, since in any practical setting pods will be started and stopped all the time, clearing way for the state of previously admitted pods to be cleaned up.

state:
System maximum PID inconsiderate of sysctl 'threads-max'

PIDPressure is not set to true when the system has insufficient pid resource.

PIDPressure is set to true correctly when the system is insufficient in pid resource.

See cause below

The max pid is not solely controlled by `/proc/sys/kernel/pid_max` which is referred by [pidlimit]([link] But it is also controlled by `/proc/sys/kernel/threads-max` (whichever is smaller).

However, they have different semantics resulting in the same constraint to how many processes/threads can be running on the system.

4. Should CRI API allow "optional features like suggested here: [link] Would this needs to be tested as part of k8s e2e to make sure k8s doesn't depend on "optional" APIs.

Also we need to define the deprecation and feature removal policies.

We need to define clear rules of working with CRI API.

CRI API versioning policies

We need to define the CRI API versioning policies:

1. Do we bump the version of API when methods and optional fields are added? [discussion example]([link]
2. Does CRI API need to indicate that the new methods are optional (not part of a conformance) for a new features that are in alpha/beta?
3. Define the release cycle for the features going thru alpha/beta stages that require CRI API changes and implementation in various runtimes.
4. Should CRI API allow "optional features like suggested here: [link] Would this needs to be tested as part of k8s e2e to make sure k8s doesn't depend on "optional" APIs.

Also we need to define the deprecation and feature removal policies.

We need to define clear rules of working with CRI API.

Routing determination: node.

request: backport cadvisor v0.40.0 to older branches

I'm running k3s with kube `1.21.x` and I am currently impacted by google/cadvisor/pull/2868 which was fixed in cadvisor `v0.40.0`. All maintained branches are currently running cadvisor `v0.39.0` except `1.23.x` which is under the latest cadvisor.

Bump all supported branches of Kubernetes to cadvisor > `0.40.0`.

* Deploy the [Concourse Helm chart]([link]
* Deploy a test pipeline using the [concourse tutorial]([link]
* Introspect the metric endpoint `kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/${NODE}/proxy/metrics/cadvisor`
* Container metrics will disappear after few minutes and `container_scrape_error` will start emit `1`.

Concourse workers run a lots of short lived containers using containerd. They causes cadvisor to cache miss when pulling latest container metrics and hence, completely interrupt the metric gathering.

The kubelet logs will start tracing this logs when the problem occurs:

state:
POD fails to attach correct sriov device on ungraceful node reboot

POD with sriov nic device attached to it fails to attach correct sriov device up on node is hard rebooted after volumes are attached to it. The node is a VM in openstack cloud provider environment and the PCI address of the sriov VF changes on node hard reboot when additional volumes are attached to the VM.

Moreover, the same scenario works with graceful node reboot.

This is seen in the logs:

state:
Kubelet reports Ready=true for pod and containers conditions during kubelet level evictions

In 1.22+, when kubelet evicts a pod, it updates the pod status to api-server marking the pod phase as failed / succeeded. However, the kubelet continues to report Ready=true pod condition until the all of the containers are fully terminated by the container runtime.

As a result, since the pod is still considered ready, external controllers (e.g. the endpoint controller), utilize the pod ready condition and will continue to send traffic to these pods marked in terminal phase. These pods are often not ready to serve traffic since they are in progress of being shutdown.

This is regression from prior to 1.22, since prior to 1.22, kubelet did not send any pod/container conditions to the api-server for evicted pods.

xref: [link] for difference between kubelet status for evicted pods before and after 1.22

One of the areas where this issue manifests is with Kubelet graceful shutdown. In 1.22+, if a pod takes a long time to shutdown, during the entire shutdown process the kubelet will report Ready=true condition, and traffic will be sent to the pod.

Additionally, If the node is shutdown before the pod fully terminates, the pod will be stuck in this state where Phase=Failed, but Ready=true. As a result, the pod will be seen incorrectly as ready by services and will be sent traffic (which the pod will likely be unable to handle due to either the pod being in progress of terminating or the node already being shutdown).

I suspect this is issue not only for graceful shutdown, but for any type of kubelet initiated eviction.

Kubelet should maintain the same behavior as prior to 1.22. Kubelet should report Ready=false condition at the same time as marking Phase=Failed for evicted pods. Having pods in terminal phases (i.e. Failed / Succeeded), but Ready=true should not be a possible status update from kubelet to api-server.

state:
"kubectl logs --follow" has not printed new logs after log rotation.

When running `kubectl logs pod-name --follow`, new logs are not output to the logs command after the log file has grown and rotated.

Even after log rotation, new logs are output to `kubectl logs pod-name --follow`.

The following steps will reproduce it.

1. Deploy a Pod that continues to output to stdout.
2. Run `kubectl logs pod-name --follow`.
3. Wait a while and the log file will be rotated. The waiting time depends on the environment.
4. New logs will not be output to logs command.

state:
Waiting containers are marked as Terminated on pod failure

A pod failed due to an initContainer failure and the main container was marked as `Terminated`:

The main container should stay in `Waiting` since it hasn't started (as described [in the docs]([link] "_A container in the Terminated state began execution and then either ran to completion or failed for some reason_").

Create a pod with an initContainer that will fail. After the pod fails, inspect the main container status and you should see it in `Terminated` state instead of the `Waiting` expected state.
I believe it might be a regression from [link] that was [backported in v1.22.3]([link] since we removed the `|| status.ContainerStatuses[i].State.Waiting != nil` check that was making sure only previously-running containers could end up as `Terminated`.

I noticed there was a test added in [kubernetes/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager_test.go#L639]([link] as part of this PR so I'm not sure if this change was intentional (and undocumented) or just overlooked.

This is problematic since many systems expect `Terminated` containers to have started as documented in the docs. A workaround might be to rely `containerStatuses[i].state.terminated.startedAt` in addition to `containerStatuses[i].state.terminated` but I'm curious to know if this was an intentional change and the documentation should be updated or if it's a regression that should be fixed.

This is problematic since many systems expect `Terminated` containers to have started as documented in the docs. A workaround might be to rely `containerStatuses[i].state.terminated.startedAt` in addition to `containerStatuses[i].state.terminated` but I'm curious to know if this was an intentional change and the documentation should be updated or if it's a regression that should be fixed.

state:
Log sampled successful probe execution with higher verbosity

It will be useful to log successful probes execution details with higher verbosity once in a while. With the default verbosity no information on successful probe execution is reported. Which is fine as it typically very verbose and rarely needed. However if somebody investigating a problem with probes and cannot make sense why they are not failing when expected to fail, logs would be very interesting.

One suggestion may be to log successful probe execution logs with higher verbosity once in 15 minutes or so. This will make sure that logs are not too verbose, while allowing troubleshooting without changing verbosity to higher level.

state:
device manager can incorrectly recover devices on node restart

The following behaviour was reproduced on openshift 4.10 ("Kubelet version" kubeletVersion="v1.23.3+54654d2") but I believe the root cause is on kubernetes.

Let's consider a pod requiring resources, among them a device (point in case: dpdk network device)

the pods starts and run just fine up until the node is restarted. On restart, the device manager correctly recover its state from the checkpoint data:

As expected, the device plugin capacity is set to zero until the device plugin correctly re-register itself:

A bit later, the recovery process from the apiserver begins:

we can see already that the workload pod (testpmd) is going to be recovered BEFORE the device plugin. When the workload pod
enters the admission flow (as per recovered pods), because the devicemanager restored its state and has data about this pod, we see:

When the topology manager requests device allocation, we end up in the devicemanager's [devicesToAllocate]([link] function. This function checks if there already a pre-allocated device (and there is, thanks to the recovered data), and if so exits early, skipping the health check which would have failed, because the device plugin has not re-registered itself yet.

The end result is that containers can be admitted and start running without the requested device actually available, causing runtime errors in the workload.

The kubelet should reject the admission of the pod until the device plugins re-registered themselves; then the pods requiring devices should be processed again. This seems the only meaningful way to recover pods while taking in consideration the actualy health of the devices.

The behaviour here depends on the order on which pods are recovered, so it's essentially a race.

1. run a test pod requiring devices. Make sure this test pod clearly fails if the requested devices are not available
2. restart the node (can take few attempts)
3.

Let's consider a pod requiring resources, among them a device (point in case: dpdk network device)

the pods starts and run just fine up until the node is restarted. On restart, the device manager correctly recover its state from the checkpoint data:

As expected, the device plugin capacity is set to zero until the device plugin correctly re-register itself:

A bit later, the recovery process from the apiserver begins:

we can see already that the workload pod (testpmd) is going to be recovered BEFORE the device plugin. When the workload pod
enters the admission flow (as per recovered pods), because the devicemanager restored its state and has data about this pod, we see:

When the topology manager requests device allocation, we end up in the devicemanager's [devicesToAllocate]([link] function. This function checks if there already a pre-allocated device (and there is, thanks to the recovered data), and if so exits early, skipping the health check which would have failed, because the device plugin has not re-registered itself yet.

The end result is that containers can be admitted and start running without the requested device actually available, causing runtime errors in the workload.

The kubelet should reject the admission of the pod until the device plugins re-registered themselves; then the pods requiring devices should be processed again. This seems the only meaningful way to recover pods while taking in consideration the actualy health of the devices.

The behaviour here depends on the order on which pods are recovered, so it's essentially a race.

1. run a test pod requiring devices. Make sure this test pod clearly fails if the requested devices are not available
2. restart the node (can take few attempts)
3.

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.

state:
Confusing log from kubelet crash when `--container-runtime-endpoint` is wrong

I installed Docker, [link] and Kubernetes release 1.24. I used `hack/local-up-cluster.sh` to start a single-node local cluster, without specifying `CONTAINER_RUNTIME_ENDPOINT`, so it defaulted to `unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock` --- which is indeed a thing, but is the _wrong_ thing (I eventually worked out that I need to point Kubernetes at `unix:///run/cri-dockerd.sock` instead). The kubelet came up briefly, issued a bunch of I messages, and a couple of W and a couple of E, then a usage message, and exited. Since the last thing in the log was the usage message, I figured the problem was something syntactic on the command line. I eventually realized that is not true.

I expected the kubelet log to give me a clearer idea of why it is exiting, not mislead me.

Run a kubelet with `--container-runtime-endpoint` pointing to an _unsuitable_ container runtime.

state:
Kubelet removes non-Kubernetes images.

We also hit by this issue. We're using Flatcar Linux which is quite barebone so we are using a few containers to augment it. Unfortunately kubelet removes the images when they are not in active use. For example we a have a cronjob which uses an image we pulled and specially tagged. That images isn't used by any pods at all but kubelet choose to remove it under disk pressure. It is very annoying.

It would be nice to have a setting which says that "you can touch images only if the tag is starting with this prefix" or similar.

Even if you are using another Linux distribution then you might want to install something which isn't available in the distribution itself. Using a container is a very likely way to go and you don't expect that something which never belonged to the Kubernetes cluster will be removed by kubelet. It's very unintuitive.

Kubelet won't remove images which aren't belongs to it.

* Pull some images from the command line.
* Fill up the local disk to create a DiskPressure "situation".
* Wait until kubelet removes the images - by the documentation it does in every five minutes.

We are still using Kubernetes 1.21 as because of the faulty etcd-client lib used in 1.22 and 1.23 we cannot upgrade our clusters. The fix appeared in 1.24 but never backported to 1.22 or 1.23 which left us no possible upgrade paths.

For example we a have a cronjob which uses an image we pulled and specially tagged. That images isn't used by any pods at all but kubelet choose to remove it under disk pressure. It is very annoying.

It would be nice to have a setting which says that "you can touch images only if the tag is starting with this prefix" or similar.

Even if you are using another Linux distribution then you might want to install something which isn't available in the distribution itself. Using a container is a very likely way to go and you don't expect that something which never belonged to the Kubernetes cluster will be removed by kubelet. It's very unintuitive.

Kubelet won't remove images which aren't belongs to it.

* Pull some images from the command line.
* Fill up the local disk to create a DiskPressure "situation".
* Wait until kubelet removes the images - by the documentation it does in every five minutes.

I created this new ticket because the old one (#103255) I found gets closed by k8s-ci-robot.

We are still using Kubernetes 1.21 as because of the faulty etcd-client lib used in 1.22 and 1.23 we cannot upgrade our clusters. The fix appeared in 1.24 but never backported to 1.22 or 1.23 which left us no possible upgrade paths.

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.

state:
kubelet: fix to prevent concurrent map read and map

When we add custom annotations to PodSandboxConfig.Annotations in function generatePodSandboxConfig， kubelet crashes with errror:
kubelet[2257292]: fatal error: concurrent map read and map write

The role of function generatePodSandboxConfig(located at kuberuntime_sandbox.go) is to create SandboxConfig that is used to RunSandbox. In some scenarios, we want to pass custom annotations to runtime through PodsandboxConfig.Annotations .

In kubelet, multiple goroutins access *v1.Pod fetched from podManager at the same time with no lock. For example, syncPod goroutin and volumeManager goroutin get *v1.Pod from podManager， when there is writing pod.Annotations operations, kubelet will panic.

So, in function generatePodSandboxConfig，a deep copy of pod.Annotations should be performed.

Kubelet process won't panic when we add custom annotations to PodSandboxConfig.

Writing podSandboxConfig.Annotations in function generatePodSandboxConfig

We have a HorizontalPodAutoscaler configured on all of our fleet. The issue arises when we are scaling down, a node is being drained and a pod on that node is part of the `FC` service. We get around ten exceptions each time, Sentry reporting `AbortedException`s in FC and `CompletionException`s with "Socket timed out" in the `OS` service, which calls `FC`.

The timeline each time is roughly the following:

Kubernetes logs that a node is being shut down, and lists the pods to be rescheduled, and announces they're being deleted:

3-5 seconds later, the exceptions begin:

(no root cause reported).

The errors end within a few seconds. 30 seconds later we get the readiness/liveness probes failing:

We can see on the FC pod logs that it continues serving requests (some requests complete successfully) until 11:29:56.

Eventually pod does shut down, usually with a KillContainerException because the heap dump process hasn't terminated in time.

So far we have no idea why these errors occur. We have grace period configured:

and we have a preStop hook in each container too:

We are also using an internal GCP load balancer on this service, but we haven't established any link between it and the errors.

So shutdowns should be as graceful as possible, but they aren't. Any idea what's going on?

Expect the node draining and shutdowns to be graceful.

Try the kubernetes settings listed - but they should work just fine. Let me know if you need any additional info to repro.

We get around ten exceptions each time, Sentry reporting `AbortedException`s in FC and `CompletionException`s with "Socket timed out" in the `OS` service, which calls `FC`.

The timeline each time is roughly the following:

Kubernetes logs that a node is being shut down, and lists the pods to be rescheduled, and announces they're being deleted:

3-5 seconds later, the exceptions begin:

(no root cause reported).

The errors end within a few seconds. 30 seconds later we get the readiness/liveness probes failing:

We can see on the FC pod logs that it continues serving requests (some requests complete successfully) until 11:29:56.

Eventually pod does shut down, usually with a KillContainerException because the heap dump process hasn't terminated in time.

So far we have no idea why these errors occur. We have grace period configured:

and we have a preStop hook in each container too:

We are also using an internal GCP load balancer on this service, but we haven't established any link between it and the errors.

So shutdowns should be as graceful as possible, but they aren't. Any idea what's going on?

Expect the node draining and shutdowns to be graceful.

Try the kubernetes settings listed - but they should work just fine. Let me know if you need any additional info to repro.

state:
Node lifecycle controller makes api calls under lock

During scale testing, as sig-scalability, we observed that node-lifecycle-controller ([link] was unable to process nodes in reasonable time due to lock contention.

Example log:

The difference between log timestamp 19:06:29.860 and decision timestamp 19:06:09.872955473 is around 20s.
As a part of method `processTaintBaseEviction` I can see that `markNodeForTainting` was executed, which takes `evictorLock`.
My suspicion is that it was waiting on this lock for ~20s. I can see that this lock might be taken by other goroutines that execute api calls under lock, for example [link]

The whole `monitorNodeHealth` loop took around 40 minutes in total for one pass through all nodes in this cluster.

I expected node-lifecycle-controller to process nodes in reasonable time

This test was run on large cluster and we removed significant portion of nodes - around 4k nodes out of 15k nodes.

Related issue that was opened before: [link]
Related comment in code: [link]

state:
Node lifecycle controller makes api calls under lock

During scale testing, as sig-scalability, we observed that node-lifecycle-controller ([link] was unable to process nodes in reasonable time due to lock contention.

Example log:

The difference between log timestamp 19:06:29.860 and decision timestamp 19:06:09.872955473 is around 20s.
As a part of method `processTaintBaseEviction` I can see that `markNodeForTainting` was executed, which takes `evictorLock`.
My suspicion is that it was waiting on this lock for ~20s. I can see that this lock might be taken by other goroutines that execute api calls under lock, for example [link]

The whole `monitorNodeHealth` loop took around 40 minutes in total for one pass through all nodes in this cluster.

I expected node-lifecycle-controller to process nodes in reasonable time

This test was run on large cluster and we removed significant portion of nodes - around 4k nodes out of 15k nodes.

Related issue that was opened before: [link]
Related comment in code: [link]

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.

Kubelet was not able to attach + mount an iSCSI PV when it has IPv6 server address.

Volume is mounted + attached.

Set up iSCSI target that's reachable over IPv6 and create a PV for it.

For example:

Kubelet logs:

Notice `[]` around the IP address. Various iSCSI files in /sys and /dev/disk/by-path do not have these square brackets and kubelet is then not able to find the iSCSI host in /sys. That's where `Could not get SCSI host number for portal` comes from.

When running a cluster and enabling feature gate `PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI`, resource usage doesn't report any values:

When retrieving logs from metric server, we can see several errors with code 500 when it calls the `/stats/summary` API:

Resource usage reports values:

state:
The logic of oom_score_adj doesn't work well for sidecar containers

I was debugging a OOM failure recently and noticed some unexpected behavior for how the kubelet is setting `oom_score_adj`.

From the [Node-pressure Eviction documentation]([link] this is how setting `oom_score_adj` is described for burstable QoS pods:

min(max(2, 1000 - (1000 * memoryRequestBytes) / machineMemoryCapacityBytes), 999)

The documentation also states the intention of this calculation is:

This means that containers in low QoS pods that consume a large amount of memory relative to their scheduling requests are killed first.

However the calculation actually does the opposite. For processes that request a small amount of memory the `(1000 * memoryRequestBytes) / machineMemoryCapacityBytes` ratio approaches zero, meaning the calculation ends up being: `min(max(2, 1000 - 0), 999) = 999`

Similarly, when the requested memory increases and the ratio approaches the total size of the machine the calculation becomes: `min(max(2, 1000 - 1000), 999) = 2`

This means that containers that are using the smallest amount of the machine get the highest score adjustment which makes the smallest processes killed first. I observed this in practice while looking at the kernel's OOM logs. These are the set of processes the OOM killer was logging:

Provide output of Pod-Healthcheck per API

Provide an easy way to view the detailed HTTP-response of a httpGet liveness/readyness-check of pods, in case of error 500.

This can then be used in the dashboard: [link]

If you use a web-framework with a health-endpoint like springboot or dropwizard, the endpoint will provide you with detailed information of what makes the healthcheck fail.

In case of error Kubernetes dashboard only shows a response of 500. To get the details you have to

* Have logging configured correctly which might not always be the case
* Disable the liveness-probe to be able to start the container, then call the healthcheck-endpoint yourself, where you also have to go into the container if the service is not yet setup correctly.

state:
When using --serialize-image-pulls=true "Successfully pulled image" Event outputs misleading time

While going over Kubernetes events I noticed that image pulls for some small images were taking several minutes according to the "Successfully pulled image" event. From investigating this is misleading as the actual pull time is much smaller but due to --serialize-image-pulls=true being the default in the observed cluster and other pods being initialized at the time, the reported pull time ends up accounting for time while waiting for other pods to finish pulling.

I expected to see the time it takes to download the image itself from a registry. Customers seem to rely on this metric for this information and we have received some complaints as a result where customers noted slow pull times as a result of misunderstanding the current behavior of this metric.

Start with a K8s cluster with --serialize-image-pulls=true (default) - For my check I used default minikube v1.26.1

1. Create pod-large where pod-large pulls any large image (the image cannot be locally cached)

2. Right after step 1 (within seconds) create pod-small where pod-small pulls any small image

Check the output for the event after running: `kubectl describe pod pod-small`

Note that despite the small size, pull time for the image in pod-small is several minutes, we should instead see it take seconds (which is how long the pull actually takes). To note this is the case you can try pulling another small image like alpine that isnt cached locally and compare after the above are done.

Here is the code that pulls an image in kubernetes and logs the event:
[link]

As can be seen from it, it's not true pull time, just time from invoking the puller to receiving a result. The serial puller is using a Golang channel as a queue and will just wait until a previous image is done pulling as I noted before, thus it will end up recording the amount of time in the queue + pull time yielding a misleading metric.

From investigating this is misleading as the actual pull time is much smaller but due to --serialize-image-pulls=true being the default in the observed cluster and other pods being initialized at the time, the reported pull time ends up accounting for time while waiting for other pods to finish pulling.

I expected to see the time it takes to download the image itself from a registry. Customers seem to rely on this metric for this information and we have received some complaints as a result where customers noted slow pull times as a result of misunderstanding the current behavior of this metric.

Start with a K8s cluster with --serialize-image-pulls=true (default) - For my check I used default minikube v1.26.1

1. Create pod-large where pod-large pulls any large image (the image cannot be locally cached)

2. Right after step 1 (within seconds) create pod-small where pod-small pulls any small image

Check the output for the event after running: `kubectl describe pod pod-small`

Note that despite the small size, pull time for the image in pod-small is several minutes, we should instead see it take seconds (which is how long the pull actually takes). To note this is the case you can try pulling another small image like alpine that isnt cached locally and compare after the above are done.

Here is the code that pulls an image in kubernetes and logs the event:
[link]

As can be seen from it, it's not true pull time, just time from invoking the puller to receiving a result. The serial puller is using a Golang channel as a queue and will just wait until a previous image is done pulling as I noted before, thus it will end up recording the amount of time in the queue + pull time yielding a misleading metric.

state:
kube-proxy should report events when the proxier failovers

kube-proxy should report k8s events of critical cases instead of just logging, e.g., kube-proxy failovers to iptables proxier when it should be running ipvs proxier, see [link]

There might be other critical cases need sysadmin's attention, maybe we should check everywhere.

The background is: we recently had kube-proxy’s ipvs scheduling algorithm changed, but one of the nodes didn’t have the corresponding kernel module. When the kube-proxy agent restarts, it failed to enable ipvs proxier, and failovered to iptables proxier. As a result, the ipvs rules and iptables rules are mixed together, causing network issues. I think this kind of failover is rather important, should be reported as k8s events.

state:
Service NodePorts can be accessed via LB IPs (iptables, at least)

Create a single-port Service of type LB. It gets nodeport 31234.

Wait for an LB IP to be assigned.

Access that LB IP on 31234 - it works as long as firewalls don't stop it.

This is because the NodPorts chain doesn't necessarily check IPs (hence why it is the last chain). It finds port 31234 and forwards it to the Service.

I think we need to add rules to "KUBE-PROXY-FIREWALL" to allow valid IP+port combos and then drop other uses of those IPs. Or something.

@user since you are elbow-deep in that area.

state:
Service NodePorts can be accessed via LB IPs (iptables, at least)

Create a single-port Service of type LB. It gets nodeport 31234.

Wait for an LB IP to be assigned.

Access that LB IP on 31234 - it works as long as firewalls don't stop it.

This is because the NodPorts chain doesn't necessarily check IPs (hence why it is the last chain). It finds port 31234 and forwards it to the Service.

I think we need to add rules to "KUBE-PROXY-FIREWALL" to allow valid IP+port combos and then drop other uses of those IPs. Or something.

@user since you are elbow-deep in that area.

state:
Each time a pod exits, kubelet cpu usage increases with cgroups v2

When a pod exits, there is some problem in the cgroup cleanup. The containerd cgroup within the kubelet cgroup does not get deleted, and then the kubelet keeps trying to delete the kubelet cgroup, which fails because of the child cgroup. The kubelet continues to try to delete the cgroup every 1 second or so. As pods start and stop, the number of cgroups in this state grows, and the kubelet process itself gradually consumes more and more cpu, until it gets to 100% of available.

Here are snippets of the /var/log/syslog for a single example. This is for the case of kubelet cgroup /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/kubepods-burstable-podde737447_24b2_4f9e_a805_ad1161a169fb.slice which contains a sub-cgroup cri-containerd-67620447e632a1b3edb19fe05a2b44211cffb996bf6ba5ff52811a8bf32eb8b7.scope.

state:
Change in semantics for the device plugin registration process

The following refactoring of the kubelet's devicemanager was done as part of the 1.25 release: [link]

As part of this, a change in semantics was (unintentionally) introduced which is breaking at least one 3rd party plugin. The logic required to go back to the old semantics is fairly straight forward. However, it's not obvious that we should actually go back to the old semantics because (at least in my opinion) the new semantics are actually more correct.

Previously, the kubelet's devicemanager would do the following upon receiving a plugin registration request:
1. Register the plugin
2. Launch a go-routine to connect to the gRPC service being served by the plugin (with a timeout of 10s)
3. Return

This gave the plugin the opportunity to first register itself with the kubelet and then (within a 10s time window) start its gRPC server.

The new semantics are similar, except that no go-routine is launched to connect to the gRPC service. The connection is attempted synchronously. This means that the plugin must now start serving its gRPC server *before* registering itself with the kubelet. Otherwise the registration call will fail.

As mentioned before, this change was not necessarily intentional, but it's also not clear if it should be reverted. It brings the device plugin's custom registration process more in line with the kubelet's standard registration process and the order is actually a bit more intuitive. Why bother registering if you aren't able to start serving your API?

The first plugin to report this problem was the KubeVirt plugin and a discussion of the issue can be found here:
[link]

The question now is -- should we revert the kubelet code to the old semantics to avoid breaking plugins that rely on this (somewhat awkward) ordering. Or do we leave the new semantics in place and send out an announcement of this (potentially) breaking change?

state:
kube-proxy loses track of some changes if iptables-restore fails

In each iteration of `syncProxyRules`, kube-proxy (iptables backend) does:

Specifically:
1. It has to call `proxier.serviceMap.Update(proxier.serviceChanges)` first, to update `proxier.serviceMap` with the pending changes, so that it will build the correct set of iptables rules.
2. Calling `proxier.serviceMap.Update(proxier.serviceChanges)` also returns information about stale services, and has the side effect of clearing `proxier.serviceChanges`.
3. If `iptables-restore` fails, then `syncProxyRules` returns before it uses the stale service information that was returned by `proxier.serviceMap.Update()`
4. When `syncProxyRules` runs again, `proxier.serviceChanges` will no longer contain the previous set of changes, and so `proxier.serviceMap.Update()` will only return the set of services that have become stale since the last, failed, `syncProxyRules`. The conntrack changes that should have been applied in the last `syncProxyRules` have been lost forever.

(This also applies to `endpointsMap`/`endpointsChanges`. Also, in the past this would have applied to creating/destroying NodePort listeners in addition to doing conntrack cleanup.)

I don't think this will be trivial to fix, and given that the bug has always existed but never been reported (and given that iptables-restore is _supposed to_ never fail), and given that kpng is on the horizon (somewhere?) maybe it's not worth trying to fix this in the current kube-proxy, but we need to at least make sure that kpng doesn't have the same bug. @user

state:
Awkward pod status message for admission errors due to node-pressure condition

When a Pod admission fails due to node-pressure condition then the Pod's `status.message` looks like this:
"Pod The node had condition: [DiskPressure]."
The "Pod The node..." reads awkward.

A message like: "The node had condition: [DiskPressure].".

1. Run a job with a pod on a single node cluster, when the node is under disk pressure (then it is tainted with `node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressure:NoSchedule`). The Pod gets stuck in the `Pending` phase.
2. Untaint the node by kubectl command line: `kubectl taint node $nodeName node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressure:NoSchedule-`
3. The Pod is scheduled but admission by Kubelet fails as the taint is re-added shortly after its manual removal.

Then, the status of the Pod contains the awkward message.

state:
Starting in 1.25 clusters, services of type=LB and xTP=Local sometimes does not update node backends on load balancers

When upgrading nodes from 1.24 to 1.25, on a cluster where master is already at 1.25, I notice that my Service `type=LoadBalancer` and `xTP=Local` have an incorrect set of nodes after the nodes have been upgraded. The set contains only the old nodes that no longer exist resulting my service being unavailable through my load balancer.

I would expect that the load balancer to be properly updated with the new set of nodes after the upgrade.

1. Create 1.25 Cluster with 1.24 nodes
2. Deploy a service of `type=LoadBalancer` and `xTP=Local`
3. Upgrade the 1.24 nodes to 1.25
4. After upgrade is finished look at the node list for the Load Balancer.

The existing logging is not enough to diagnose the issue. I added some more logs and ran the KCM at log level =5 to find the root cause.

There was a change introduced to reduce the number syncs for `xTP=Local` services: #109706. With this change, there are situations where the `xTP=Local` never gets updated.

The following is the chain of events.
1. Node is created or deleted and causes `triggerNodeSync()`:

[link]

2. Inside `nodeTriggerSync()`, the nodeLister (line 264) filters for Ready only nodes so it does not have the new node or still contains the deleted node, which means that `c.needFullSync = false` when line 281 is executed.

[link]

3. Following down the chain of functions that are called (across goroutines communicating with nodeSyncCh), we end up at `nodeSyncInternal`. Because `c.needFullSync = false`, we will only do a sync of services that were marked for retry. If the state previously was good, this means `c.servicesToUpdate` has 0 services before entering `updateLoadBalancerHosts`.
[link]

4. Nodes are queried again from the NodeLister. But this time the new node or the deleted node is reflected.
[link]

5. nodeSyncService is then parallelized based on the length of services.

state:
Regression in winkernel proxier that causes stale load balancing proxy rules

There is a regression in v1.24.0 (and above) that causes stale HNS load balancer proxy rules anytime a backend pod is deleted. Each subsequent deletion will leave behind an additional external VIP load balancing rule that references endpoints which no longer exist.

This can cause occasional connectivity issues and timeouts, if a stale load balancing rule is matched and it redirects traffic to an endpoint which no longer exists.

We are under the impression this may have been introduced [here.]([link] (creds to @user for identifying this.)

I expect all load balancing rules created by winkernel proxier (aka HNS load balancer) to be referencing valid backends (aka HNS endpoints)

1. Create a Kubernetes cluster v1.24 or higher with Windows nodes.
2. Create a Kubernetes Service with type "LoadBalancer" on Windows.
3. Delete one or more pods of the Service.
4. Observe stale load balancing rule left behind referencing endpoint that was already deleted.

This issue can be discovered by establishing multiple connections to the service, after pods were deleted. Some of the requests will fail.

This issue can be monitored using the following script:
[link]

Execute as follows:
`.\networkhealth.ps1 -OutputMode Stdout`

It will print something along the lines of:

Another way to inspect this manually is using the following PowerShell:

In the $refs, you would see multiple entries (indicating there are duplicate HNS load balancer proxy rules with the same VIP) and that some of the references are invalid (ie not showing up in the get-hnsendpoint output)

### Workaround
1. You can force all pods of a given service onto a single Node. This will still cause duplicated load balancer entries, but the connections should all succeed as the right rule should be matched.
2. Use K8s version <v1.24.0
3. `Restart-service kubeproxy`. This will remove all the rules and re-create them.

state:
Regression in winkernel proxier that causes stale load balancing proxy rules

There is a regression in v1.24.0 (and above) that causes stale HNS load balancer proxy rules anytime a backend pod is deleted. Each subsequent deletion will leave behind an additional external VIP load balancing rule that references endpoints which no longer exist.

This can cause occasional connectivity issues and timeouts, if a stale load balancing rule is matched and it redirects traffic to an endpoint which no longer exists.

We are under the impression this may have been introduced [here.]([link] (creds to @user for identifying this.)

I expect all load balancing rules created by winkernel proxier (aka HNS load balancer) to be referencing valid backends (aka HNS endpoints)

1. Create a Kubernetes cluster v1.24 or higher with Windows nodes.
2. Create a Kubernetes Service with type "LoadBalancer" on Windows.
3. Delete one or more pods of the Service.
4. Observe stale load balancing rule left behind referencing endpoint that was already deleted.

This issue can be discovered by establishing multiple connections to the service, after pods were deleted. Some of the requests will fail.

This issue can be monitored using the following script:
[link]

Execute as follows:
`.\networkhealth.ps1 -OutputMode Stdout`

It will print something along the lines of:

Another way to inspect this manually is using the following PowerShell:

In the $refs, you would see multiple entries (indicating there are duplicate HNS load balancer proxy rules with the same VIP) and that some of the references are invalid (ie not showing up in the get-hnsendpoint output)

### Workaround
1. You can force all pods of a given service onto a single Node. This will still cause duplicated load balancer entries, but the connections should all succeed as the right rule should be matched.
2. Use K8s version <v1.24.0
3. `Restart-service kubeproxy`. This will remove all the rules and re-create them.

Routing determination: network. Bug assessment: a bug.

This is required to [GA the feature]([link] but it's also useful in general.

To the best of my knowledge, it's very hard to observe the behavior of cpumanager without peeking into the pod and/or use the podresources interface (kubelet >= 1.24). But even for the latter, no well known components expose metrics consuming this information.

I believe anyway kubelet some expose some basic metrics about cpumanager behaviour, while deferring more fine grained metrics to external components (NFD, node_exporter, is fine)

state:
Pod with tolerationSeconds 0 for taint "unreachable" would be scheduled and evited frequently while node became ready from not ready

1. create a cluster with 1 master and 2 nodes
2. create a statefulset which has affinity with one of 2 nodes

3. stop kubelet on the pod running node
4. after pod was evicted, start the kubelet again to make node ready
5. see the controller-manager logs

7. see the kube-scheduler logs

The reason is that while the node becomes ready from not ready, `nc.doNodeProcessingPassWorker` would remove NoSchedule taint immediately, but the NoExecute taint would be removed by `nc.monitorNodeHealth()` which may be some seconds later, so we can see the pod was evicted and scheduled frequently until the NoExecute taint was removed.

the following taints should be removed simultaneously while node not-ready -> ready

see above

state:
Forbidden accessing or modifying other pod's cgroup in privileged container

I created a `privileged` pod on K8S v1.24.0. Use `kubectl exec` to enter the pod's shell, i noticed that the whole host cgroupfs was mount at `/sys/fs/cgroup` with `rw` mode. And i can get other pod's cgroup, even modify it!

Created `privileged` pod on K8S v1.25.2, same results. Created `privileged` pod on K8S v1.22.0 and v1.23.0, i can only access and modify the cgroup of the current pod, which is what i expect.

BTW, my OS is ubuntu-22.04 (kernel v5.15.0) with cgroup v2. When i tested in ubuntu-18.04 (kernel v4.15.0) with cgroup v1, K8S v1.24.0/v1.25.2/v1.23.0/v1.22.0 worked as expect!

Forbidden accessing or modifying other pod's cgroup in privileged pod on K8S v1.24.0 (or higher).

step1. Use OS ubuntu-22.04 (or other distributions with cgroup v2)
step2. Create K8S cluster v1.24.0 (or higher) by kubeadm (follow the doc [kubeadm)]([link]
step3. Install CNI plugin (i use calico)
step4. Create a privileged pod use the below manifest, and discover its `/sys/fs/cgroup`

state:
dynamic resource allocation: trigger re-scheduling of specific pods

There are several scenarios where the current approach is too coarse:
- The scheduler plugin marks ResourceClaim changes as triggers for all pods. It should only do that for pods that actually use claims.
- When ResourceClaims are missing, trying to schedule the pod repeatedly is a waste. Perhaps use "PreEnqueue" + unschedulable pods? See [link]

Less impact on normal pod scheduling.

state:
dynamic resource allocation: use generated name for ResourceClaim from template

Right now, the name is specified as `<pod name>-<claim source name inside pod spec>`. That's easy and deterministic, but may lead to conflicts with ResourceClaims that were created earlier, either automatically or manually.

Let's investigate the alternative: generate the name and let code which needs to know it search the API server or in a local cache via some label.

Avoids conflicts.

state:
Support topology aware routing (node and zone)

Currently there is no way to achieve topology aware routing (`kubernetes.io/hostname`, `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, `topology.kubernetes.io/region`) and define _deterministic_ rules like the ones offered from the already deprecated and removed [`ServiceTopology`]([link]
- Prefer endpoints on the same node, fall back on any available endpoint if none are available for this node: `["kubernetes.io/hostname", "*"]`.
- Prefer enpoints on the same zone, but fallback on any available endpoint if none are available within this zone: `["topology.kubernetes.io/zone", "*"]`.
- Prefer endpoints on the same node, fall back to endpoints in the same zone, followed by the same region, and failing otherwise: `["kubernetes.io/hostname", "topology.kubernetes.io/zone", "topology.kubernetes.io/region"]`. This may be useful, for example, in cases where data locality is critical.

The `ServiceTopology` feature was deprecated (and removed in K8s 1.22) in favor of [`TopologyAwareHints`]([link]
Note: This feature, specifically the alpha topologyKeys API, is deprecated since Kubernetes v1.21. Topology Aware Hints, introduced in Kubernetes v1.21, provide similar functionality.

Although that the docs write that TopologyAwareHints "provide similar functionality", this is not reflecting the reality. TopologyAwareHints is a feature that is applicable only in particular use cases and is not a replacement for the feature offering of ServiceTopology.

Drawbacks of TopologyAwareHints:
- Sometimes the CPU-balance heuristic is wrong. For example, if we know that the whole zonal CPU pool does not model the set of clients which will access a service, then we may erroneously disable hints. (ref [link]
- Hints do not work at low-endpoint counts. (ref [link]
- Hints are not deterministic.
- ...

- Prefer enpoints on the same zone, but fallback on any available endpoint if none are available within this zone: `["topology.kubernetes.io/zone", "*"]`.
- Prefer endpoints on the same node, fall back to endpoints in the same zone, followed by the same region, and failing otherwise: `["kubernetes.io/hostname", "topology.kubernetes.io/zone", "topology.kubernetes.io/region"]`. This may be useful, for example, in cases where data locality is critical.

The `ServiceTopology` feature was deprecated (and removed in K8s 1.22) in favor of [`TopologyAwareHints`]([link]
Note: This feature, specifically the alpha topologyKeys API, is deprecated since Kubernetes v1.21. Topology Aware Hints, introduced in Kubernetes v1.21, provide similar functionality.

Although that the docs write that TopologyAwareHints "provide similar functionality", this is not reflecting the reality. TopologyAwareHints is a feature that is applicable only in particular use cases and is not a replacement for the feature offering of ServiceTopology.

Drawbacks of TopologyAwareHints:
- Sometimes the CPU-balance heuristic is wrong. For example, if we know that the whole zonal CPU pool does not model the set of clients which will access a service, then we may erroneously disable hints. (ref [link]
- Hints do not work at low-endpoint counts. (ref [link]
- Hints are not deterministic.
- ...

state:
Projected ConfigMap Update Delay

Recent Kubernetes versions (1.25, 1.24 and main) exhibit a delay on ConfigMap update for the time taken to render the changes to the volume on the filesystem. Recent test [runs]([link] (`Projected configMap updates should be reflected in volume`) display a time of upwards to 1m to update the projected volume on the filesystem.

The delay is noticeable and can be improved. Ideally, a ConfigMap update should take around ~10s.

Related Issues:
[link]

I expect a ConfigMap update within the API to be rendered to the filesystem within a pod within around 10s.

CI is exhibiting the issue with the `Projected configMap updates should be reflected in volume` test.

state:
CSI migration for Cinder volumes is missing

[link] removed OpenStack cloud provider + related volume plugin from Kubernetes 1.26, but it also removed CSI migration for OpenStack Cinder volumes. All volumes with `pv.spec.cinder` are now unusable.

When a PV should be dynamically provisioned, I get an event:

In-tree Cinder volume should be silently translated by `staging/src/k8s.io/csi-translation-lib` to CSI volumes and provisioned / attacher / mounted by corresponding CSI driver.

Use Kubernetes 1.26 with in-tree Cinder PV, i.e. with `pv.spec.cinder` set.

Better security if a node gets compromised.

Prevent a plugin from blocking kubelet.

state:
Scheduling Pods with dynamic resources and using the Pod `.spec.nodeName` field fails

The combination of using the Pod spec nodeName field with the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin (currently feature-gated) doesn't work. No surprise really as the nodeName field effective bypasses the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin running, and something rather clever would need to be invented to make things to work. But this is still a bit of a regression compared to the old device plugin model which doesn't have a similar limitation. @user as the author of the dynamic resources feature can explain what could maybe be created to fix this.

Granted, forcing scheduling even with a device plugin resource may or may not succeed at the node level depending on the availability of said plugin resources at the node, but with dynamic resources the failure seems to be currently guaranteed.

The use-case for this is such that the Kubernetes scheduler is effectively being preceded by some other scheduler which runs earlier (say, some HPC framework) which is giving the Pods the node names and somehow knows that there will be enough resources, and then the workloads ought to land in the specified node and the container related work is then handled normally from there on. So basically Kubernetes wouldn't do much in terms of scheduling, but takes over from there.

TBH I expected it to fail and it did. The resource claims won't work, since the scheduler plugin isn't getting a chance to do its thing.

Just use DRA with Pod spec nodeName field, one needs a DRA driver obviously.

state:
the volume is not detached after the pod and PVC objects are deleted

Hello, I've recently been testing the reliability of storage for k8s **v1.25.0.** A strange phenomenon occurs occasionally during the test: the volume cannot be detached after the PVC and pod are deleted(the reclaimPolicy of pv is delete）.
So I first went to check the corresponding `pv` and `volumeAttachment` objects and found that they both existed. Then I checked the kube-controllerManager and kubelet logs and found that kubelet logs kept printing:

`I1125 10:28:42.931263 3908451 reconciler.go:389] "Starting operationExecutor.UnmountDevice for volume \"pvc-1a4bcff1-f11d-456c-b91a-1aaa5c3ea5db\" (UniqueName: \"kubernetes.io/csi/xxx^f2ee34c4-f297-49cb-8730-4442ceb1df4f\") on node \"192.168.x.x\" "`

But I found that at the beginning, the volume was unmountDevice succeed, as shown in the following kubelet log:

it is so wired !

Then I added some log variables to the unmountDetachDevices method:

The results show that

And I've drawn up a time-series chart of the contents of the log.
![xxx]([link]

Let's go back to the unmountDetachDevices method.

According to the above-mentioned log content, the first `unmountDetachDevices` operation successfully changes `DeviceMountState` of the corresponding attachedVolume to `DeviceNotMounted`, **but the `attachedVolume.DeviceMayBeMounted()` function in the subsequent `unmountDetachDevices` operation still uses stale DeviceMountState.**

## In my opinion:
1. Ensure that the unmountDevice operation is not performed after the first unmountDevice operation succeeds.
2. If multiple unmountDevice operations are allowed, ensure that the correct pvname can be obtained in the `getDriverAndVolNameFromDeviceMountPath` method.

the volume is detached after the pod and PVC objects are deleted

This problem can be reproduced by repeatedly deleting and recreating pods that require PVC in k8s 1.25.0 cluster

state:
(usage - inactive file) greater than capacity causing eviction

`free` shows the total memory is 32Gi and used only 6Gi.
Free is 12Gi
Shared 1.6Gi
buff/cache 13Gi
available 19Gi

4.19.90-23.8.v2101.ky10.aarch64
- [link] This is a script to calculate memory.available from [link]

- workingset memory(70Gi) = memory.usage_in_bytes(80Gi) - inactive file (10Gi)
- - this will be including active file memory
- availabel = capacity (32Gi) - working set memory(70Gi) = - 38Gi < 0

With the script, we got a negative value available in bytes which is obviously a bug of the operation system Kylin.

No eviction if the problem is that memory.usage_in_bytes greater than memory.capacity_in_byte.

Before the OS fixes the bug, can kubelet stop evicting pods when `usage_in_bytes` is not properly set? fixes

Yes.

And the workaround is to drop cache and the usage_in_bytes and active file/inactive file will become correct.

**Eviction is so dangerous if the condition checking is based on wrong data.**

Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, DaemonSet require restartPolicy=Always but don't NEED to

Since forever, these APIs all require "restartPolicy: Always". There's not really a REASON for that, as far as I can see.

For example, suppose we allowed "Never" or "OnFailure". If a Pod were to "finish", a Deployment, ReplicaSet, or StatefulSet will all start a new pod on some node, and a DaemonSet will start a new pod on the same node. The primary difference would be that the WHOLE POD restarts - including initContainers. That seems like it could be useful.

This seems mostly like deleting code:

...and then fixing tests and probably adding some new ones. Unfortunately, StatefulSet validation has this in `ValidatePodTemplateSpecForStatefulSet()`:

Which means that the template is not really being validated right now. Sigh.

It may be that a "keystone" container ([link] would be required to really make this work. I wanted to file this while it was in front of me.

Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, DaemonSet require restartPolicy=Always but don't NEED to

Since forever, these APIs all require "restartPolicy: Always". There's not really a REASON for that, as far as I can see.

For example, suppose we allowed "Never" or "OnFailure". If a Pod were to "finish", a Deployment, ReplicaSet, or StatefulSet will all start a new pod on some node, and a DaemonSet will start a new pod on the same node. The primary difference would be that the WHOLE POD restarts - including initContainers. That seems like it could be useful.

This seems mostly like deleting code:

...and then fixing tests and probably adding some new ones. Unfortunately, StatefulSet validation has this in `ValidatePodTemplateSpecForStatefulSet()`:

Which means that the template is not really being validated right now. Sigh.

It may be that a "keystone" container ([link] would be required to really make this work. I wanted to file this while it was in front of me.

state:
pod LifecycleHandler should support a `sleep` option

Many people use `exec` to run `sleep` in their container. This works, but it's kludgey and requirtes them to have a sleep binary in the image. We should offer sleep as a first-class thing.

I hacked up a quick POC. This is obviopusly incomplete (no tests, no feature gate, poor API docs, etc) but could be a starting point for someone who wants to contribute. I assume it would have to sit in Alpha for a while to deal with back-rev kubelets, so the sooner it gets in the sooner it van be used.

This might warrant a micro KEP, but that's not something to be afraid of. Happy to help if someone wants to pick this up.

state:
pod_startup_latency_tracker doesn't track the lastFinishedPulling time

It can be observed in any kubelet log, just pick one from a random job in CI, per example

The `lastFinishedPulling` time is always `0001-01-01 00:00:00 +0000`, that is the golang zero time IIRC.
In addition, when the image is already present, neither `firstStartedPulling` and `lastFinishedPulling` are set.

I think that the fix has to be something like this

but this means that we are lacking testing on these, feature, I'd expected to see at least 2 new tests in

`pkg/kubelet/util/pod_startup_latency_tracker_test.go`
`pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager_test.go`

envFrom not working in ephemeral containers: failed to sync secret cache

I have the following deployment:

I am working on an automated script (written in Go) that, among other things, does the following:

* Creates a Secret resource

* Lists pods and creates one ephemeral container for each one of them with the Secret added as env variable using `envFrom`:

When I run it, the ephemeral container is created but never started, it is left in `Waiting` state with Reason `CreateContainerConfigError`.

The code seems to be correct since I can see the Secret is referenced in the Environment Variables.

Checking the events I can see the following:

Type | Reason | Age | From | Message
--|--|--|--|--
Warning | Failed | 3s | kubelet | Error: failed to sync secret cache: timed out waiting for the condition

It seems the cache is not synced when an ephemeral container is created in a pod and therefore its creation fails because the Secret is not present in the cache.

Based on that previous assumption, I tried referencing the secret in the regular container defined in the deployment.

Running the same code that creates the ephemeral container is now run successfully and it creates the container with the secret as an environment variable.

I would expect the ephemeral container to be created and successfully started with the appropriate environment variable containing the data in the secret.

Using the code provided in the explanation of the issue should be enough to reproduce the problem.

state:
VolumeZone scheduling plugin should handle csi migration

In [link] we discovered that our plan for eventually removing the [VolumeZone]([link] scheduling plugin when CSI migration is GA is not possible because the plugin also applies to non-migratable volume types.

However, if we leave the plugin as is, then even migratable PVs will be broken if we remove beta topology labels from Nodes in the future. This is because the plugin does not have any handling for migrated volumes.

I suggest we add CSI migration handling to the VolumeZone plugin. I think we just need to detect if the volume is migrated, and if so, skip the VolumeZone processing. For migrated volumes, we translate `PV.Labels` into `PV.NodeAffinity` so they end up getting processed by the [VolumeBinding]([link] plugin.

In a cluster with csi migration for a specific intree volume type enabled,
1. create an intree PV with beta topology labels
2. remove the beta topology label from a node
3. try to schedule a pod using that pv

However, if we leave the plugin as is, then even migratable PVs will be broken if we remove beta topology labels from Nodes in the future. This is because the plugin does not have any handling for migrated volumes.

I suggest we add CSI migration handling to the VolumeZone plugin. I think we just need to detect if the volume is migrated, and if so, skip the VolumeZone processing. For migrated volumes, we translate `PV.Labels` into `PV.NodeAffinity` so they end up getting processed by the [VolumeBinding]([link] plugin.

In a cluster with csi migration for a specific intree volume type enabled,
1. create an intree PV with beta topology labels
2. remove the beta topology label from a node
3. try to schedule a pod using that pv

state:
Eviction Manager should check the disk usage of dead containers

Under the condition of disk pressure, Eviction-manager checks disk usage of only living containers, which causes that it evicts wrong pods.

For example:
Pod A has 1 living container whose disk usage is 5 GB
Pod B has 1 living container whose disk usage is 0 GB and 1 dead container whose disk usage is 10 GB

When disk pressure occurs, Eviction manager attempts to evict Pod A prior to Pod B

The Eviction Manager should also check the disk usage of dead containers and therefore in above example, it should evict Pod B prior than Pod A.

1. Deploying two pods having yaml

2. Writing a 5 GB file to local disk on Pod A

3. Writing 10 GB file to local disk on Pod B, then kill Pod's process once for creating a dead container

Checking the status of both pods

Now Pod A has 1 living container using around 5GB of disk space and Pod B has 2 containers, 1 living container using very low disk space and 1 dead container having 10GB disk space

4. Checking the disk space of Pod A

5. Checking the disk space of Pod B

6. Creating a disk pressure on node

7. Checking the pod status

Pod A was Evicted first inspite of having less disk space than Pod B
Also, checking the logs, PodA's eviction rank was higher than PodB's

state:
Eviction Manager should check the disk usage of dead containers

Under the condition of disk pressure, Eviction-manager checks disk usage of only living containers, which causes that it evicts wrong pods.

For example:
Pod A has 1 living container whose disk usage is 5 GB
Pod B has 1 living container whose disk usage is 0 GB and 1 dead container whose disk usage is 10 GB

When disk pressure occurs, Eviction manager attempts to evict Pod A prior to Pod B

The Eviction Manager should also check the disk usage of dead containers and therefore in above example, it should evict Pod B prior than Pod A.

1. Deploying two pods having yaml

2. Writing a 5 GB file to local disk on Pod A

3. Writing 10 GB file to local disk on Pod B, then kill Pod's process once for creating a dead container

Checking the status of both pods

Now Pod A has 1 living container using around 5GB of disk space and Pod B has 2 containers, 1 living container using very low disk space and 1 dead container having 10GB disk space

4. Checking the disk space of Pod A

5. Checking the disk space of Pod B

6. Creating a disk pressure on node

7. Checking the pod status

Pod A was Evicted first inspite of having less disk space than Pod B
Also, checking the logs, PodA's eviction rank was higher than PodB's

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.

state:
Volume populators should use resource instead of kind

While discussing the ReferenceGrant kep, I learned that there is a distinction between "resource" and "kind". The biggest takeaway is that "group + kind" is not uniquely identifiable for arbitrary resources (for in-tree apis we can enforce).

refs:
[link]
[link]

The implications are that we should be using `resource` instead of `kind` in `PVC.dataSourceRef` and `VolumePopulator.sourceKind`.

We need to resolve this before volume populators goes GA.

state:
NodeExpandVolume gets called, even if CSI plugin returned NodeExpansionRequired=false in ControllerExpandVolumeResponse

In case of online volume expansion of raw block volumes, some of the CSI plugins may not need file system resize or any related handling and thus NodeExpandVolume API call can be skipped for the same. In order to do this, plugin must set NodeExpansionRequired to false, in ControllerExpandVolumeResponse.
However, it is observed that kubelet does call NodeExpandVolume API, after successful resize done by CSI plugin in ControllerExpandVolume API call with NodeExpansionRequired=false in response.
Even though CSI plugin can skip handling in NodeExpandVolume API as per its requirement, is it expected to get this API call from kubelet when NodeExpansionRequired set to false by plugin in ControllerExpandVolumeResponse?

During CSI volume online expansion, if CSI plugin returns NodeExpansionRequired=false in ControllerExpandVolumeResponse, to indicate no FS resize handling needed, then kubelet should not call NodeExpandVolume API for such volume(s).

The issue is seen with vSphere CSI driver, while expanding vSphere raw-block volume (volumeMode: Block), already in use by one pod(raw-block-pod). However, the issue may not be specific to vSphere CSI driver.

Kubelet logs on node where raw-block-pod was running:

`Jan 23 05:46:53 k8s-node-803-1673532986 kubelet[389705]: I0123 05:46:53.362905 389705 operation_generator.go:2217] "MountVolume.NodeExpandVolume succeeded for volume \"pvc-ad41ea4d-725b-42d7-acb5-9aea7679d17d\" (UniqueName: \"kubernetes.io/csi/csi.vsphere.vmware.com^81b5bb35-d858-4f43-b8a0-8dcafa967934\") pod \"raw-block-pod\" (UID: \"4ac3bfad-cf20-425d-a22c-6533d7a91a41\") k8s-node-803-1673532986" pod="default/raw-block-pod"
`

state:
CSI migration race condition can cause unexpected detach and data loss

After the cluster was updated to enable PD CSI Driver, there was a race condition where AD Controller (kube-controller-manager) started to [populate the desired state of world]([link] BEFORE the PD CSI Driver was up, thus AD Controller gave us the error

Then AD Controller triggered the disk detach because the disk/volume was not populated in the desired state of world.

Unfortunately the disk was in use during this detach and got corrupted.

Since cluster upgrades can cause the controller manager and CSI drivers to start at different times, the AD controller needs to be more conservative when detaching

We have not been able to reproduce this, it came up from a customer.

state:
De-share `InitContainer` type from `Container`

In order to simplify future KEPs and allow more flexibility on adding new fields and behaviors on Containers I suggest we fork the type of `InitContainer` and regular `Container`.

This de-sharing will be very helpful with the Sidecar containers KEP [link] where we want to introduce a new field on Init containers, but not on any other containers.

There will be more requests for change of these types going forward and de-sharing of types will simplify discussions and improve velocity of features development.

It will also allow us to have a better documentation of Init Containers type - today the same documentation for each field is used.

## Existing approach

We already have a precedence in code where `EphemeralContainer` is a separate type from `Container`. The way it's implemented is by introducing a collection `EphemeralContainerCommon` that contains all the same fields as a regular `Container` so it can be casted to the `Container` type. See the [type definition]([link] and a [test]([link]

This approach simplified the development in some places, but made types heavily interdependent so no new fields can be added to the `Container` type without updating `EphemeralContainer` as well.

## Proposed

The proposal is to completely split these types making them a separate types that cannot be casted to one another.

This will require some changes in interfaces, mostly for the various resource managers. Those interfaces will be extended to provide separate API methods for `InitContainer` and a regular `Container`.

There are a few places that may need to iterate over all containers making similar changes. If those patterns common across the code, we will implement helper functions that would simplify this iterating exposing only common fields, to the iterator function, not the entire `Container` class.

## Risks

There are two types of risks - risk of having separate types going forward vs.

state:
De-share `InitContainer` type from `Container`

In order to simplify future KEPs and allow more flexibility on adding new fields and behaviors on Containers I suggest we fork the type of `InitContainer` and regular `Container`.

This de-sharing will be very helpful with the Sidecar containers KEP [link] where we want to introduce a new field on Init containers, but not on any other containers.

There will be more requests for change of these types going forward and de-sharing of types will simplify discussions and improve velocity of features development.

It will also allow us to have a better documentation of Init Containers type - today the same documentation for each field is used.

## Existing approach

We already have a precedence in code where `EphemeralContainer` is a separate type from `Container`. The way it's implemented is by introducing a collection `EphemeralContainerCommon` that contains all the same fields as a regular `Container` so it can be casted to the `Container` type. See the [type definition]([link] and a [test]([link]

This approach simplified the development in some places, but made types heavily interdependent so no new fields can be added to the `Container` type without updating `EphemeralContainer` as well.

## Proposed

The proposal is to completely split these types making them a separate types that cannot be casted to one another.

This will require some changes in interfaces, mostly for the various resource managers. Those interfaces will be extended to provide separate API methods for `InitContainer` and a regular `Container`.

There are a few places that may need to iterate over all containers making similar changes. If those patterns common across the code, we will implement helper functions that would simplify this iterating exposing only common fields, to the iterator function, not the entire `Container` class.

## Risks

There are two types of risks - risk of having separate types going forward vs.

Routing determination: node.

state:
Clarify ContainerStatus.Started null value and initialize the value for Init containers

This issue is to discuss whether we can change the `Started` field of `ContainerStatus` from pointer to non-pointer bool value. The pointer type is inconsistent with other field `Ready`. The semantic of `Started` being `null` is undefined and it is not ideal if users will use `Started` field `null` value as indication of a spacial condition beyond what `false` indicates. So if there is a process of making field non-pointer after skew period has passed, it would be great to follow it.

The field was introduced as a pointer following [this suggestions]([link]

If this is optional, it needs to be a pointer. We can't add non-optional fields, ergo this should be a pointer. Otherwise an old client will not set it and it will be false, which is super confusing.

The field long passed it's skew inconsistency period.

The field is set by prober_manager: [link]

## Current behavior

The PR: [link] improves the documentation for the `Started` field of `ContainerStatus`. We never declared when `null` value means for the `ContainerStatus`.

For regular container:
- Field is `null` before the `prober_manager` starts.
- Field is `false` once `prober_manager` started.
- Field is `true` when no startup probes defined or once startup probe succeeded.

For Init and ephemeral containers:
- Field is always `null` as those do not start the `prober_manager`.

`StartedAt` field of `Status` type is always populated for both - regular and Init containers. It is populated earlier than `Started` will be set by `prober_manager`. So there is period of time when `StartedAt` has a date and `Started` is `null`.

There is also `Ready` field on `ContainerStatus` that is not a pointer. It will be `false` from the Pod creation and will change to `true` while readiness probes succeed.

## Changes for sidecar containers

state:
Clarify ContainerStatus.Started null value and initialize the value for Init containers

This issue is to discuss whether we can change the `Started` field of `ContainerStatus` from pointer to non-pointer bool value. The pointer type is inconsistent with other field `Ready`. The semantic of `Started` being `null` is undefined and it is not ideal if users will use `Started` field `null` value as indication of a spacial condition beyond what `false` indicates. So if there is a process of making field non-pointer after skew period has passed, it would be great to follow it.

The field was introduced as a pointer following [this suggestions]([link]

If this is optional, it needs to be a pointer. We can't add non-optional fields, ergo this should be a pointer. Otherwise an old client will not set it and it will be false, which is super confusing.

The field long passed it's skew inconsistency period.

The field is set by prober_manager: [link]

## Current behavior

The PR: [link] improves the documentation for the `Started` field of `ContainerStatus`. We never declared when `null` value means for the `ContainerStatus`.

For regular container:
- Field is `null` before the `prober_manager` starts.
- Field is `false` once `prober_manager` started.
- Field is `true` when no startup probes defined or once startup probe succeeded.

For Init and ephemeral containers:
- Field is always `null` as those do not start the `prober_manager`.

`StartedAt` field of `Status` type is always populated for both - regular and Init containers. It is populated earlier than `Started` will be set by `prober_manager`. So there is period of time when `StartedAt` has a date and `Started` is `null`.

There is also `Ready` field on `ContainerStatus` that is not a pointer. It will be `false` from the Pod creation and will change to `true` while readiness probes succeed.

## Changes for sidecar containers

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: not a bug.
