state:
kubelet: PreStop Hooks can hang termination of a pod beyond pod's termination grace period

Termination grace period includes the termination time of prestop hooks and containers in the pod. The total time that the pod terminates should always be < termination grace period seconds.

A misconfigured pod with a preStopHook that hangs indefinitely and pod ignoring SIGTERM can result in the pod taking 2X (double) the termination grace period seconds to terminate.

The time to terminate the pod should always be <= termination grace period seconds including prestop hook execution time as documented in [link]

1) Apply the following pod

2)

3) Observe it actually took ~120s to terminate the pod not ~60s as would be expected.

The kubelet logs for the pod [link]

The issue is that we are not taking into account the time taken by execution of the prestop hook when calculating the time remaining to kill the remaining containers in the pod.

state:
Give an indication in container events for probe failure as to whether the failure was ignored due to FailureThreshold

Probes of all kinds currently support FailureThreshold (and SuccessThreshold), these properties allow a user to specify that Kubernetes should not take action in response to a failed probe unless it fails a successive number of times.

This is useful for end-users as it allows them to mitigate the effects of any probes that "flake" by requiring successive failure.

When a probe fails in Kubernetes, we emit a container event indicating this here: [link] and end-users can consume these events via the API for their own purposes. This event is emitted regardless of whether the FailureThreshold has been reached or not.

Currently when a user consumes a probe failure event they have no way of knowing whether the event resulted in action on the control plane (because the event can be ignored due to FailureThreshold, and information on this is not included in the event). This can lead to users assuming there is a problem and a container/pod was restarted when nothing occurred.

I think we should expose the keepGoing value from [link] in the emitted event somehow, my preferred solution is to emit the probe failure event in the worker rather than where it currently sits in [link] - there is also the option of passing some information down the stack into the prober from the worker (such as making the FailureThreshold/SuccessThreshold decision in the prober) but I'm worried about separation of concerns, happy to hear what other folks think :)

Also of note is that FailureThreshold/SuccessThreshold is the only filter I can see where a probe can be ignored after being run (and therefore emitting a container event)

I’m happy to write this PR once we’re confident in our approach :)

state:
API: ResourceRequirements usage in Container and PVC

The same ResourceRequirements struct is used in two only loosely related entities (Container and PersistentVolumeClaim). Extending ResourceRequirements for dynamic resource requirement had the unintended effect that the new `Claims` field also became available in a PersistentVolumeClaim.

Extending one should not affect the other.

[link]

We just ran across this while reviewing [link]

The ResourceRequirements type is also used within the PersistentVolumeSpec type (which is also used indirectly in pod specs via ephemeral volumes), and the "clear if feature-gate is disabled" logic is only wired to podspec-handling. That means in 1.26 PVC objects or PodSpecs with ephemeral volumes defined can persist data in this field even if the feature is disabled.

Can you open a PR to clear this field in PVC and ephemeral volume create/update flows, and file a follow-up issue to consider splitting the type used in PVCs so it doesn't continue inheriting work done that is targeted at pods?

API: ResourceRequirements usage in Container and PVC

The same ResourceRequirements struct is used in two only loosely related entities (Container and PersistentVolumeClaim). Extending ResourceRequirements for dynamic resource requirement had the unintended effect that the new `Claims` field also became available in a PersistentVolumeClaim.

Extending one should not affect the other.

[link]

We just ran across this while reviewing [link]

The ResourceRequirements type is also used within the PersistentVolumeSpec type (which is also used indirectly in pod specs via ephemeral volumes), and the "clear if feature-gate is disabled" logic is only wired to podspec-handling. That means in 1.26 PVC objects or PodSpecs with ephemeral volumes defined can persist data in this field even if the feature is disabled.

Can you open a PR to clear this field in PVC and ephemeral volume create/update flows, and file a follow-up issue to consider splitting the type used in PVCs so it doesn't continue inheriting work done that is targeted at pods?

TODO:

- [x] clear this field in PVC and ephemeral volume create/update flows
- [ ] splitting the type

na

Routing determination: storage.

state:
Refactor prober_manager to update the runtime state vs. API state

- This is part of pre-work for sidecar KEP: [link]
- See also uber issue: [link]

In sidecar container KEP we plan to use the Startup probes state as a way to decide whether the next Init container need to start being initialized. Before this KEP probes results were not used in any of Pod lifecycle decisions. In order to implement this we need to have a probe status at a time we call `findNextInitContainerToRun`. This may need some refactoring on how prober_manager is initialized and used.

Today we calculate changes needed to be performed on Pod including the next init container to run. Then we apply these actions and update the Status of a Pod on API server using `convertStatusToAPIStatus` from `generateAPIPodStatus`. Once we converted the runtime status to API status, we also call `kl.probeManager.UpdatePodStatus(pod.UID, s)` passing the API status object to be updated with the probes results. Thus the probe results are not visible to the `findNextInitContainerToRun` function.

The proposal is to refactor the `prober_manager.go` to operate on `kubecontainer.PodStatus` instead of `v1.PodStatus`. This will require adding the probes status to the `kubecontainer.PodStatus`. We will also move the call into the `prober_manager.go` early in the `syncPod` execution so we know the startup probes result before we call into `findNextInitContainerToRun`.

cc @user

state:
containers get scheduled on --reserved-cpus

Node has 64 vCPUs. CPU manager policy is 'static'

8 vCPUs are marked as resreved (via --reserved-cpus)
The remaining 56 vCPUs are all isolated via kernel command line.
systemd.cpu_affinity is set for all of the --reserved-cpus also (I think this is redundant with isolated CPU command line though)

Workload has two types of pods: those that request full integer CPUs (we'll call these 'dedicated CPU tasks') and those that do not. 'normal tasks'

result:
dedicated CPU tasks get correctly scheduled on the isolated vCPUs
normal tasks do not, and instead, get scheuled to the --reserved-cpus set.

Both dedicated CPU tasks and normal tasks should all get scheduled on the 56 isolated vCPUs.

Based on feedback, if the bug is not obvious, I can try to build a minimized reproduction.

state:
A pod with a still running postStart lifecycle hook that is deleted is not terminated even after terminationGracePeriod

We introduced a postStart hook to one of our pods. Eventually, we noticed these pods hanging in "Terminating" state indefinitely when we try to delete them.
Trying `kubectl logs`yielded
`Error from server (BadRequest): container "reproducer" in pod "reproducer" is waiting to start: ContainerCreating`

That was the first hint that the postStart hook was the problem (since a pod is considered PodInitializing until its postStart hook exits).

We can exec into the container just fine, there we found that indeed our postStart hook was stuck. Killing all processes of the postStart hook made the pod terminate.
Looking at the logs of our PID 1 process (luckily, we also write that to a file...) showed no sign of it receiving a SIGTERM (we have a shutdown hook in that application that would log if it were invoked).

From our observations, we conclude that while the pod is still not done with the postStart hook, K8s does not send a SIGTERM to the container's PID 1 process. To make matters worse, even after the terminationGracePeriod expired, no kill happens, leading to the observed behaviour.

The pod terminates - if not with a SIGTERM to the PID 1 process, then at least with a kill after the terminationGracePeriod expired.

Apply the following pod spec:

(Note that we explicitly set the terminationGracePeriodSeconds to the default 30 for clarity.)
In one terminal, run `watch -d kubectl get pods`.
After applying, the pod will show up, but since the postStart hook will not exit, the pod will stay in ContainerCreating.
Confirm that you cannot see the logs with `kubectl logs reproducer` (error message `Error from server (BadRequest): container "reproducer" in pod "reproducer" is waiting to start: ContainerCreating`)

state:
A pod with a still running postStart lifecycle hook that is deleted is not terminated even after terminationGracePeriod

We introduced a postStart hook to one of our pods. Eventually, we noticed these pods hanging in "Terminating" state indefinitely when we try to delete them.
Trying `kubectl logs`yielded
`Error from server (BadRequest): container "reproducer" in pod "reproducer" is waiting to start: ContainerCreating`

That was the first hint that the postStart hook was the problem (since a pod is considered PodInitializing until its postStart hook exits).

We can exec into the container just fine, there we found that indeed our postStart hook was stuck. Killing all processes of the postStart hook made the pod terminate.
Looking at the logs of our PID 1 process (luckily, we also write that to a file...) showed no sign of it receiving a SIGTERM (we have a shutdown hook in that application that would log if it were invoked).

From our observations, we conclude that while the pod is still not done with the postStart hook, K8s does not send a SIGTERM to the container's PID 1 process. To make matters worse, even after the terminationGracePeriod expired, no kill happens, leading to the observed behaviour.

The pod terminates - if not with a SIGTERM to the PID 1 process, then at least with a kill after the terminationGracePeriod expired.

Apply the following pod spec:

(Note that we explicitly set the terminationGracePeriodSeconds to the default 30 for clarity.)
In one terminal, run `watch -d kubectl get pods`.
After applying, the pod will show up, but since the postStart hook will not exit, the pod will stay in ContainerCreating.
Confirm that you cannot see the logs with `kubectl logs reproducer` (error message `Error from server (BadRequest): container "reproducer" in pod "reproducer" is waiting to start: ContainerCreating`)

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.

state:
Kubelet keeps renewing the lease after the Node object has been deleted

Kubelet, once registered to the apiserver, if the Node object is deleted `kubectl delete node ..` or some external controller per example, never tries to register again.
However, the lease controller is not aware of this and keeps renewing the lease.

In an scenario that a new VM with the same name register and the other kubelet is still running, this may cause a conflict (This is a theory, it has to be verified)

IIUIC, there are two periodic loops with the apiserver:
1. update node status, this will fail with "object not found" , maybe the object is recreated and it will start working again?
2. lease controller, this will keep updating the lease, that is wrong, because the node object doesn't exist, no?

However, the lease controller is not aware of this and keeps renewing the lease.

In an scenario that a new VM with the same name register and the other kubelet is still running, this may cause a conflict (This is a theory, it has to be verified)

IIUIC, there are two periodic loops with the apiserver:
1. update node status, this will fail with "object not found" , maybe the object is recreated and it will start working again?
2. lease controller, this will keep updating the lease, that is wrong, because the node object doesn't exist, no?

state:
Pod status updates take longer to propagate to the API than necessary

#107897 originally identified a number of inefficiencies in how pod status is reported back to the API:

1. Pods are queued in a channel and then processed one by one - this causes HoL blocking and writes every observed status change, but pod status is level driven (split into #116615 for inclusion into #115331)
2. Status is a GET then PATCH, but we now have server side apply and using it would reduce 2 RT to 1 RT and reduce QPS
3. We treat all status updates the same, when in reality certain transitions should be prioritized (unready -> ready, Running -> Succeeded|Failed)
4. Status is single threaded, and we could easily try multiple
5. It's hard to know when our status cache has been brought up to date (so that we can bypass a SSA attempt), we could use ResourceVersion tracking for that (apimachinery proposed allowing it to be parsed)

In general these contribute to #113606 and should be improved.

Faster

See kubelet logs. Several e2e tests stress this flow, but we need a test that shows the improvements.

state:
Mutation of a cached object in kubelet through in place resizing of pods

[link]

mutates the pod object in place (vs creating a copy first). That's illegal and can cause data races or potentially panics (the panic is unlikely here but I can't rule it out).

state:
Minimal kernel version plan: probably 4.18/4.19+

Currently, there is a kernel version check-in system validator that is used by kubeadm. (**// Requires 3.10+, or newer**)
- This issue aims to track which version should minimum kernel version be raised to. The current status and the plan.

[link]

During the weekly sig-node meeting, there was a discussion about adding a kernel-version-sensitive safe sysctl in kubelet. It was noted that 3.16 is considered to be a very low kernel version and it was suggested that we introduce a minimal kernel version for Kubernetes. Alternatively, we should have a warning for low kernel versions(I think that we should add a warning if the kernel version is less than 3.18 or 4.0).
- Cgroups v2 GA opens up the possibility for new features but sets the minimal bar for dependencies again.
- Cgroup v2 suggests `Linux Kernel version is 5.8 or later`. [link]

[link]

Some historical issues related and some CNCF projects like cilium: [link]
- [link]
- [link]

[link]

[link]

[link]
There are specific features used by containerd core code and snapshotters that will require a minimum kernel version on Linux. With the understood caveat of distro kernel versioning, a reasonable starting point for Linux is a minimum 4.x kernel version.

state:
Memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods

If a pod is created and then deleted an entry in processedPods map remains forever (sometimes, it's racy).

The problem comes from the fact that `podWorker` calls volume_manager `WaitForUnmount()` asynchronously. If the last call happens after populator cleaned up resources, an entry is added to processedPods and will never be seen.

An entry in processedPods map must be deleted if pod doesn't exist and pod runtime should removed according to `dswp.podStateProvider`.

To verify that the issue really exists I applaied a simple [patch]([link] printing resources in `processedPods` map. Here is a reproducer:

1. Start brand-new fresh k8s cluster with `hack/local-up-cluster.sh`
2. Check entries in `processedPods`:

3. Create a pod, check its uid:

4. Verify that this uid is accurately reported:

5. Delete the pod, wait for a few mins, check for `processedPods` again:

The entry `a0158a6e-3b23-4a68-a50b-5d44e0fc009a: false` will be kept forever because kubelet doesn't know anything about this pod anymore:

so no more events will ever come to populater for this uid, and the loop in `findAndRemoveDeletedPods()` won't find it because it was already deleted from `dswp.desiredStateOfWorld`.

state:
Graceful Node Shutdown does not update endpoints for terminating pods

When graceful node shutdown is enabled, I expect that services are drained appropriately during pod shutdown (i.e. the same way that `kubectl delete pod` would work). However this doesn't seem to be the case - the pod never enters the `Terminating` state according to `kubectl` and doesn't get removed from the service endpoints until it enters the `Completed` or `Failed` state. This causes connection errors and lost requests in `Cluster`-routed services.

After pod termination starts, the EndpointSlice should be updated to have the pod that is terminating removed or marked terminating, even before the pod is fully shut down. This is what happens when a pod gets removed for any other reason (e.g. `kubectl delete pod`).

You can see the repro at [link] . The repro sets up a 2 node cluster with graceful shutdown enabled and a simple deployment/service.

<details>
<summary>Here is the deployment/service yaml pasted again</summary>

</details>

To reproduce:
* Run the deployment, preferably one pod on each node.
* Run `watch -n 1 'kubectl describe endpointslice my-service-5j2nw'` in a separate terminal (you'll need to figure out the right name unfortunately)
* Use the virtualbox UI to send an ACPI shutdown to one of the nodes.

Within 20 seconds (the preStop hook duration), the EndpointSlice should be updated to have the pod that is terminating removed. This is what happens when a pod gets removed for any other reason (e.g. `kubectl delete pod`).

To ensure that everything else worked, you can reboot the node and see the journal logs (via something like `journalctl -b -1`) of the shutdown sequence triggering the kubelet graceful shutdown logic.

state:
Components in the kubelet are incorrectly pulling state from "desired" instead of the pod worker's "actual"

The kubelet currently confuses "desired" and "actual" state in some subsystems in a way that leads to data races and hinders future features. Pods that have been placed into a config source are "desired" - those then have to be "admitted" (pass hard admission handlers or be failed), and only then can the pod be a candidate to be started by the pod worker. Because pods can overlap by UID in the kubelet (static pods mostly), the pod worker has to hold desired pods until the previous pod with that UID stops. The list of "pods the pod worker has started and are still running" is the "actual" state of the kubelet - what is running right now. Since the pod worker drives the SyncPod method, and the SyncPod method drives runtime components like CRI, volumes, probes, and resources, those components *must* consult the pod worker for state, not the podManager (which holds "desired config").

This was exposed by [link] and must be addressed before we can tackle some larger issues (like the new in-place resizing). A consequence of making this fix will be that admission in the kubelet needs to consult the pod worker rather than the pod manager, and that any subsequent change to in-place resizing must be updated to fit into this model (because the pod worker is now authoritative).

A visual description of the set of problems related to this issue is in [link] (shared with the sig-node google group).

@user @user @user

Probably has to go into 1.28, certainly I consider this a blocker to in-place resizing going beta.

Components downstream of pod worker should consult it for state, not the pod manager.

state:
In place pod resizing should be designed into the kubelet config state loop, not alongside it

#102884 in its alpha state introduces a new challenge to the kubelet state machine - partial and deferred acceptance of spec changes to a pod in the kubelet, while at the same time we are realizing that the kubelet is not properly feeding actual state to components #116970.

Last minute 1.27 fix #116702 works around but doesn't resolve a key side effect of this problem - reverting the pod state incorrectly / temporarily. The pod worker receives new state (in an ordered fashion from admission, and before that podManager) and then invokes SyncPod with the "latest". In-place resizing then mutates podManager directly, and continues its execution with a different syncPod. However, once we fix #116970, this will be impossible - other components have to consult the pod worker for the latest state, not podManager.

Visually this is described at [link] (shared with kubernetes-sig-node google group)

To graduate to beta in-place resizing needs a new capability added to the kubelet state machine - the ability to decide when the spec change requested is "acted on" by the kubelet. There are a couple of ways we could design this, but they need to fit harmoniously into the larger changes we're making to kubelet state vs being working around the kubelet state machine.

To do that we need to make sure we understand the rules that any "level driven update" to pod spec must follow and then implement a mechanism in the kubelet. This issue covers articulating those rules and getting answers as an input to the change we should make to kubelet admission.

To do that we need to make sure we understand the rules that any "level driven update" to pod spec must follow and then implement a mechanism in the kubelet. This issue covers articulating those rules and getting answers as an input to the change we should make to kubelet admission.

Follow up on meeting of 28-03-2022 [Meeting notes]([link] - [Slack thread]([link]

In the meeting was specified that this most likely won't need a KEP and should be started with a Issue

I see that the kernel in cgroups v2 has an option memory.oom.group which would make all the pids of a given container to get killed on OOM:

@user @user

Some workloads that fork the process in the container, when the OOM kicks in, it kills only one process of the cgroup, causing a lot of noise due to process failures but health checks being successfull. We think that for our scenarios, killing all the pids in the containter would be better.

state:
When eventRecordQPS is set to 0, the actual QPS is 5

When setting eventRecordQPS or eventBurst to 0 in KubeletConfiguration the documentation states that no limit is enforced. What happens instead is that eventRecordQPS has the same meaning as "event-qps" kubelet flag. The value is used directly: [link]

The kubernetes client-go API interprets the value of 0 as DefaultQPS which is 5.
The same thing applies to eventBurst as well.

There should be no limit when the values are set to 0.

Set eventRecordQPS/eventBurst to 0 in KubeletConfiguration.

state:
kubelet will be stuck all the time when device plugin process is in T status

I am doing something about fault test in 1.25.3 k8s version. When I set device plugin process as T status(`kill -19 PID`) and created new pod next, I found kubelet would be stuck all the time and can't do any work.
SyncLoopIteration goroutine stack is as follows:

After analyzing the code, maybe we should add context deadline in [[link] or SyncLoopIteration goroutine will be stuck. Is there some special scenarios that cause us not to add this context deadline?

SyncLoopIteration goroutine should not be stuck and my device plugin will be restarted because of failed liveness probe

set device plugin process as T status(`kill -19 PID`) and create new pod next

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.

state:
A completed status pod which request 1 nvidia.com/gpu resource updated to UnexpectedAdmissionError when restart kubelet service

I have a k8s cluster (version v1.23.6) with a GPU node which has 4 GPUs.

Firstly, I submitted a job which request 1 nvidia.com/gpu, and after a while the job successfully finished with a Completed pod status.

Secondly, I submitted a deployment which request 4 nvidia.com/gpu, it keeps ruuning on the GPU node.

Thirdly, I restart the kubelet service on the GPU node, then the job pod updated pod status from Completed to UnexpectedAddmissionError.

Describing the job pod:

The job has completed successfully and release the gpu resource, kubelet should not try to reallocate a GPU resource to a Completed status pod when the kubelet service is restarted.

I expect that the job pod should keep Completed status when kubelet service is restarted.

(1) submitted a job which request 1 nvidia.com/gpu resource, waiting for the job completed,pod status is Completed.
(2) submtted a deployment which request all nvidia.com/gpu resource.
(3) restart kubelet service on the gpu node, and you can see that the job pod updated pod status to UnexpectedAdmissionError.

Pod Garbage collector fails to clean up PODs from nodes that are not running anymore

This happened after upgrading to Kubernetes 1.26 from 1.24

The succession of events we have observed:
- Our workloads use HorizontalPodAutoscaler to scale up due to traffic increase
- Cluster Autoscaler provisions new nodes to accommodate the new replicas
- Traffic goes down
- HPA downsize replicas
- Cluster Autoscaler notices nodes under the threshold of usage and PODs can be accommodated into other nodes
- Nodes are drained and downscaled
- Kubernetes still reports PODs in a "Running" or "Terminating" state in the node that no longer exists
- Kubernetes control plane reports "Orphan pods" on its audit logs

Kubernetes Garbage collector to clean up these PODs after the node is gone

(duplicated port key "containerPort + protocol")

(Duplicated environment variable. Set twice by mistake)

(Duplicated port error)

state:
Support a list of AppProtocols

The Kubernetes Service API allow us to specify an Application Protocol for each Service port. This is used as a hint for implementations to offer richer behavior for protocols that they understand.

According to the [docs]([link] one of the valid values can be `Implementation-defined prefixed names such as mycompany.com/my-custom-protocol`.

There are cases where different implementations installed in the same cluster and different behaviors may be needed for the same ports.

Starting a discussion to gather thoughts, ideas and use-cases about the need for multiple appProtocols support for the same port.

state:
Pod graceful deletion hangs if the kubelet already rejected that pod at admission time

We observed the following series of events:

1) Pod is created with some attributes that later result in the pod being rejected at kubelet admission time
2) The pod is scheduled to a node
3) The pod is gracefully deleted by a controller, i.e. a deletion timestamp is set on the pod
4) The pod is rejected at kubelet admission time
5) The pod never gets deleted and is stuck: despite having the deletion timestamp set. It seems that kubelet does not issue the final force delete for the pod.

This is problematic in many scenarios, but one specific case it was hit was when the pod is backed by a daemonset controller. This issue manifested in way where since the pod never got deleted in step 5 above, the daemonset controller did not create a new pod to run the on the node and thus node was was not running a replica of the daemonset controller pod.

This seems to a be regression in k8s 1.27, I was not able to repro this behavior in 1.26.

It is expected at during the series of events above, after the pod is failed at kubelet admission time, since the pod has a deletion timestamp set, the kubelet should forcefully delete the pod. The pod should not hang in deletion forever.

Create a 1.27 kind cluster:

Stop kubelet

Create a pod bound to the node which will trigger a admission error. The below node selector label does not exist, so we expect that the pod should be rejected in admission.

While kubelet is down issue a graceful deletion to set a deletion timestamp on the pod

Verify deletion timestamp is set (pod is pending)

Start kubelet

Observe pod status, the pod is now in failed phase (as expected).

However, the `kubectl delete pod` hangs, the pod is never force deleted by kubelet.

state:
DRA: delayed allocation: deallocate after use

When a ResourceClaim:
- uses delayed allocation
- does not get created for a specific pod (i.e. not from a template)

then it currently gets allocated and remains allocated until:
- scheduling of a pod fails because the node originally chosen for the allocation isn't suitable, in which case the scheduler triggers deallocation via `claim.status.deallocationRequested`
- the user deletes the claim

What we want instead is that deallocation gets triggered when the last user of such an allocated claim gets removed from `claim.status.reservedFor`. To avoid races, deallocation must be done through `deallocationRequested`.

This can be implemented either as a controller or directly in the API server.

state:
10 second timeout when killing or evicting pod

Killing or evicting a pod that is already terminated will result in a 10 second timeout in killPodNow.

A warning event is logged:

Reason: ExceededGracePeriod, Message: Container runtime did not kill the pod within specified grace period.

The problem appears when using emptyDir volumes with limits. The volume scan might run after the pod has already finished.

killPodNow should exit without timeout and no event should be generated.

Create a pod with emptyDir volume with size limit, write data beyond the size limit and quit immediately. When eviction is triggered if the pod is already finished it will generate an ExceededGracePeriod event.

state:
k8s persistent volume (PV) data gets deleted after pod recreation with all ReclaimPolicy : Retain

1) I created one PV(persistent volume) using .yaml file 10G on aws efs "/data/flink/state"
2) created PVC of 10G and here we are using dynamic provisioning (storage-class) to mount PV.
3) created pod deployment using deploy.yaml file. here we are using FlinkOperator to deploy the application.
4) entered to pod using "kubectl exec -it flow-engine-598f45f7d6-qqv9p -- bash" to access the bash of the pod created.
5) Run the flink application which created the file on above mentioned path i.e "/data/flink/state"
6) now deleted the pod using "kubectl delete pod flow-engine-598f45f7d6-qqv9p
7) now again new pod gets created after deleting the above pod and I accessed the bash of the new pod again
8) And I don't see a file created inside the mount path "/data/flink/state", this file got deleted.

What happened:
after every deletion of the pod, the data will get deleted from that mounted path.

What you expected to happen:
Retain policy: data should be available after every pod recreation unless PV is deleted. And we can able to fetch that data.

1. create a namespace
2. create PV / PVC / and deployment kind pod with local mount path without using any other storage location.
3. Access the pod bash console and write a file inside the mount path of the pod and exit
4. delete the pod and it will automatically recreate the pod.
5. now again access bash of newly recreated pod and check file exist or not.

attached below .yaml file used for creating PVC and storage-class

pvc.yaml
persistentVolumeClaim:
spec:
storageClassName: mkt-efs-sc
accessModes:
- ReadWriteMany
resources:
requests:
storage: 10Gi

storage-class.yaml
storageClass:
provisioner: efs.csi.aws.com
reclaimPolicy: Retain
parameters:
fileSystemId: <efs-id>
provisioningMode: efs-ap
directoryPerms: "777"

state:
kubelet applies defaults to Pods and causes could not process manifest file

When I put a Pod yaml file without `metadata.name` in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`, started the kubelet and hoped it would create the corresponding staticPod for me, I got the following error, which also caused the staticPod to not be created.

I then read the kubelet code and quickly found the problem. When kubelet tries to decode the pod yaml file, it will apply default values and validate the pod. The function to apply the defaults is in `pkg/kubelet/config/common.go L56`.

In this function, the `metadata.name` is set.

This causes an error when `metadata.name` is not set, because it causes the '-' character to be at the front.

I think kubelet should circumvent this error, because `metadata.name` is optional, It is possible for this field not to be set.

When Pod's `metadata.name` is not set, the '-' character at the start should be avoided, as it will cause an error.

Prepare a Pod yaml file without `metadata.name` and set it into `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`.

If the maintainers think this circumvention change is necessary, I'm happy to contribute code to the kubelet!

Does not respect the terminationGracePeriodSeconds of a probe

Kubernetes does not respect the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` of a probe.

I found this while fixing the e2e tests.
[link]

Test result:

The `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` of a container's probe should override the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.

1. Create a pod with long pod-level terminationGracePeriodSeconds and short probe-level terminationGracePeriodSeconds.

2. Check for the container not respecting the probe-level terminationGracePeriodSeconds

state:
PodresourceAPI reports about resources of pods in terminal phase

PodResourcesAPI provide a `List()` endpoint which reports about all the resources that consumed by pods and containers on the node.

The problem is that pods which are in terminal phase (i.e. are in `Failed` or `Succeeded` status) are reported as well. about The internal managers reassign resources assigned to pods in terminal phase, so PodResources should ignore them, because they can still be in used.

PodResources should ignore and not reports about resources which are in used by pods which are in terminal phase.

Provided a new test-case that demonstrates the exact problem and can be used as a reproducer: [link]

The docs that describes PodResourceAPI are not refer explicitly to whether `List()` should ignore terminal pod's resources or not, meaning it might not be a bug at all.

OTOH, internal managers reassign resources assigned to pods in terminal phase so it make sense to not account them.

state:
Kubelet panic when allocates device for pods.

It is suspected to be a concurrent bug of kubelet.

When we delete the last pod that requires GPU on the node and create two or more pods that require GPU at the same time, kubelet may panic on `allocateContainerResources` as following.

I think it's a concurrency issue.

1. Create a pod with GPU request, then kubelet will allocate resource for it. Kubelet try call device plugin to choose preferred device for it. **It will unlock the mutex!.** [link]
2. Then we delete the last pod that requires GPU.
3. Create the second pod with GPU request, kubelet will allocate resource for it also. Kubelet will call `UpdateAllocatedDevices` to recalculate device (delete allocated device if pod deleted). It will update the **allocatedDevices** map of ManagerImpl, because of mutex is unlock by step 1. [link]
4. Kubelet continues with the first pod. If **allocatedDevices** has changed and GPU device is nil, kubelet will panic in the closure allocateRemainingFrom.

Don't panic.

Delete the last pod that requires GPU on the node and create two or more pods that require GPU at the same time.

state:
Kubelet panic when allocates device for pods.

It is suspected to be a concurrent bug of kubelet.

When we delete the last pod that requires GPU on the node and create two or more pods that require GPU at the same time, kubelet may panic on `allocateContainerResources` as following.

I think it's a concurrency issue.

1. Create a pod with GPU request, then kubelet will allocate resource for it. Kubelet try call device plugin to choose preferred device for it. **It will unlock the mutex!.** [link]
2. Then we delete the last pod that requires GPU.
3. Create the second pod with GPU request, kubelet will allocate resource for it also. Kubelet will call `UpdateAllocatedDevices` to recalculate device (delete allocated device if pod deleted). It will update the **allocatedDevices** map of ManagerImpl, because of mutex is unlock by step 1. [link]
4. Kubelet continues with the first pod. If **allocatedDevices** has changed and GPU device is nil, kubelet will panic in the closure allocateRemainingFrom.

Don't panic.

Delete the last pod that requires GPU on the node and create two or more pods that require GPU at the same time.

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.

state:
Incorrect validation of `allowPrivilegeEscalation` with `SYS_ADMIN` capability

Validation logic to disallow `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` in combination with `SYS_ADMIN` capability checks for `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` instead of `SYS_ADMIN` (see [security context validation]([link]

Adding `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` to the security context does not add the `cap_sys_admin` capability to the container, while the `SYS_ADMIN` capability does add it.

⚠️ Tested with containerd, CRI-O seems to "correctly" add the capability when using `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`.

A container that has a `securityContext` set, with both `allowPrivilegedEscalation` set to `false` and configuration to receive `cap_sys_admin` privileges, should be rejected.

Following pod logs the current capabilities of the container and then exits.

example pod, that is rejected:

example pod, that is scheduled with `cap_sys_admin` capability and `allowPrivilegeEscalation`:

Current: cap_sys_admin=ep

This is a small fix for a single incorrect validation, but the problem is that it's possible to create containers that do not receive the expected capabilities without receiving a warning (see [related discussion]([link]

There is a warning, that "...you must omit the `CAP_` portion of the constant..." in the how to [set capabilities for a container]([link] documentation, but none of that is validated.

I will create a PR for this and created a separate issue to propose an enhancement for capability validation in general: [link]

state:
[kubelet-image-gc] minimum-image-ttl-duration not work,when kubelet restart.

when kubelet restart,all images which notused cleaned.
but there is a flag in kubelet,`minimum-image-ttl-duration`,explain：Minimum age for an unused image before it is garbage collected. Examples: '300ms', '10s' or '2h45m'.
i set `minimum-image-ttl-duration` to `20m0s`,it's means if a image not used,it will live 20m and then clean by kubelet（if has disk pressure）.if kubelet not restart, it work,but if restart ther is a bug, `minimum-image-ttl-duration` not work,image will be clean，even if it's no enough time.

`minimum-image-ttl-duration` work, image even if not used,it will live 20m and then clean by kubelet.

1）make node trigger disk pressure.
2）pull some image which not used by pod
3）restart kubelet
4）image cleaned by kubelet after around 10s

i see the source code, and maybe there is a bug.

in [detectImages]([link] func,well detect image and update firstdetect time for every image.

and in [freeSpace]([link] func,well check images livetime by firstDetected.

if kubelet running normal,it work,because there is a [Start]([link] func.

in this line,`_, err := im.detectImages(ctx, ts)`,in first time,ts is zero. so image's firstDetected time is zero,and in freeSpace
`reeTime.Sub(image.firstDetected) < im.policy.MinAge` this check is always false,so image will be cleaned.

maybe we can change to `im.detectImages(time.now())`,can fix this bug.

state:
previous node condition (disk pressure) is wiped when kubelet restarts

I have a k8s cluster(v1.27.2) containing one node. I set `evictionHard: nodefs.available: 90%` and write a large amount of data to kubelet rootdir（used 8GB / total 10GB ） to trigger eviction. `node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressure` taint was added to this node. But when kubelet restarted, previous disk-pressure taint was wiped weirdly. And pending pod is normally scheduled to run on the current node. Then I checked the kubelet logs and found:

kubelet restart:

update node status **NodeHasNoDiskPressure**

eviction manager start to synchronize

Q: Why does kubelet report **NodeHasNoDiskPressure** ?
A: Eviction manager has not yet executed the synchronize method

Normally, a node that was previously marked with taints should retain after reboot otherwise it doesn't make sense. Maybe we need to make sure that taints can't be deleted when kubelet restarts?

previous node taint is not wiped

Restart kubelet repeatedly after the disk pressure eviction is triggered. Observe `node.spec.taints`

Log Attach/Detach controller errors periodically

We have some errors that are logged at level 10 because the ADC reconciler runs very frequently and would cause log spam: [link]

However I think we should at least log the error for a volume the first time, or with a configurable interval to be useful for debugging production issues.

Add a mechanism to throttle error logging per-volume

This would have been useful while debugging [link] but that issue is a race condition and hard to reproduce.

state:
Timeout waiting for systemd to create kubepods-burstable-***.slice

When I **frequently** increase and decrease the **replica count** (with python api)to adjust the number of pods over a period of time:
![image]([link]

The cluster **cost some more** memory but with the same count of services(and pods), and at this point, continuing to adjust replicas will result in a significantly longer time (possibly even more than **600 seconds**, normal is 1.5-3s) required for creating new pods.

As title: Timeout waiting for systemd to create kubepods-burstable-***.slice
![image]([link]

And also: Timed out while waiting for systemd to remove kubepods-burstable-***.slice
![image]([link]

normally start new pod without timeout
![image]([link]

frequent replica adjustments (roughly over 500 times within 15 hours, **up to 40 one by one and reduce to 1 one by one**) for a same service, use python api

I continuously adjust the replica count using a Python program. Under normal circumstances, the startup time of pods is shown in the left graph (where the left side represents the pod count, and the right side represents the startup time of new pods). However, after an extended period of frequent replica adjustments (roughly over 500 times within 15 hours), the duration is shown as depicted in the right graph.
**Even Kubernetes' API timeouts in the end.**
![image]([link]

state:
App container is started before initContainers could complete on node reboot

On node reboot, we see app container is started before initContainers could complete. Essentially both app and initContainers are running in parallel. We are using initContainers to ensure dependent drivers are loaded by other pod before the app container could start. But because app container is starting in parallel, they hit a failure. This was not seen with k8s 1.27 and only happening with 1.28. Also, this happens only on node reboot, not during fresh install of our application (gpu-operator)

Above, we can see even though init container `mofed-validation` is still running, main container `nvidia-driver-ctr` started. Also pod status shows 2/2 main containers ready when initContainer is still running.

Also, another issue we are seeing is for pod `nvidia-operator-validator-ktcxj `, which has 4 init containers, only 1 is run (`driver-validation`) and rest are skipped, while the app container started in parallel again. The start/finish timestamps of these initContainers indicate that clearly below.

initContainers should complete in order before app containers could start on node reboot. Also, all initContainers should run rather than skipped before app-container could start.

Create a pod with multiple initContainers (which wait for about 2-3 mins) and an app container. On node reboot, app-container is started in parallel to initContainer.

On node reboot, we see app container is started before initContainers could complete. Essentially both app and initContainers are running in parallel. We are using initContainers to ensure dependent drivers are loaded by other pod before the app container could start. But because app container is starting in parallel, they hit a failure. This was not seen with k8s 1.27 and only happening with 1.28. Also, this happens only on node reboot, not during fresh install of our application (gpu-operator)

Above, we can see even though init container `mofed-validation` is still running, main container `nvidia-driver-ctr` started. Also pod status shows 2/2 main containers ready when initContainer is still running.

Also, another issue we are seeing is for pod `nvidia-operator-validator-ktcxj `, which has 4 init containers, only 1 is run (`driver-validation`) and rest are skipped, while the app container started in parallel again. The start/finish timestamps of these initContainers indicate that clearly below.

initContainers should complete in order before app containers could start on node reboot. Also, all initContainers should run rather than skipped before app-container could start.

Create a pod with multiple initContainers (which wait for about 2-3 mins) and an app container. On node reboot, app-container is started in parallel to initContainer.

Routing determination: node.

Below was stack trace of crash:

From kubelet logs, Validated around 10000 threads, majority are with this stack trace

Kubelet not to crash and keep memory and thread footprint low

By injecting error in loginD or dbus logic, this should be reproducible.

Traced down the kubelet where [these threads ]([link] getting created in Loop:
Reference to kubelet code: [link]

state:
Device Plugins' Unix socket under host path /var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins/ cannot change with the root directory of kubelet service

After changing the root directory of kubelet service, because the device-plugins canonical directory `/var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins` is constant, it will not change with the root directory of kubelet service.

[link]

When using this function, mounting the changed directory to pod will report an error "failed to initialize topology updater instance: failed to watch: '/host-var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins'; no such file or director" and mounting /var/lib/kubelet to pod will report an error "Error while dialing: dial unix /host-var/lib/kubelet/pod-resources/kubelet.sock: connect: no such file or directory". The pod cannot be used normally.

---
切换Kubelet服务的root目录时，device-plugins的目录没有随着kubelet root目录改变而改变，这将导致使用该功能时，挂载kubelet的root目录后无法获取device-plugins的socket

The directory /var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins changes with kubelet's root directory configuration, as does the pod-resources directory

Use the device-plugins function
See the link for reference documents: [link]

we use the argument `--root-dir` change the kubelet service's root dir

state:
Device Plugins' Unix socket under host path /var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins/ cannot change with the root directory of kubelet service

After changing the root directory of kubelet service, because the device-plugins canonical directory `/var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins` is constant, it will not change with the root directory of kubelet service.

[link]

When using this function, mounting the changed directory to pod will report an error "failed to initialize topology updater instance: failed to watch: '/host-var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins'; no such file or director" and mounting /var/lib/kubelet to pod will report an error "Error while dialing: dial unix /host-var/lib/kubelet/pod-resources/kubelet.sock: connect: no such file or directory". The pod cannot be used normally.

state:
crictl shows the compressed size, and is inconsistent with docker images

Running `crictl images` (latest version) shows the compressed size of each image, which is both misleading and inconsistent with `docker images`, which instead shows the uncompressed size.

See kubernetes-sigs/cri-tools#1264; the inconsistency happens because in the CRI-API there is no reference on which size (blob or uncompressed) should be shown by the runtime.

Using the blob size is misleading as it may trick users into thinking images are using less disk space than they are in reality.

The CRI-API needs to decide which size to handle (blob/compressed, i.e. the size of images as stored in the registry and as transferred over the network; uncompressed, i.e., the actual size once images have been `gunzip`-ped) and enforce that for each runtime.

Assume I download the latest `nginx` image. Running a simple pod and inspecting the contents of the image cache with `crictl` yields:

Downloading the exact image with `docker pull` on the same machine and running `docker images` yields:

`crictl` shows the compressed size, while `docker images` shows the uncompressed (on disk) size.

See discussion on issue kubernetes-sigs/cri-tools#1264 for further details.

state:
crictl shows the compressed size, and is inconsistent with docker images

Running `crictl images` (latest version) shows the compressed size of each image, which is both misleading and inconsistent with `docker images`, which instead shows the uncompressed size.

See kubernetes-sigs/cri-tools#1264; the inconsistency happens because in the CRI-API there is no reference on which size (blob or uncompressed) should be shown by the runtime.

Using the blob size is misleading as it may trick users into thinking images are using less disk space than they are in reality.

The CRI-API needs to decide which size to handle (blob/compressed, i.e. the size of images as stored in the registry and as transferred over the network; uncompressed, i.e., the actual size once images have been `gunzip`-ped) and enforce that for each runtime.

Assume I download the latest `nginx` image. Running a simple pod and inspecting the contents of the image cache with `crictl` yields:

Downloading the exact image with `docker pull` on the same machine and running `docker images` yields:

`crictl` shows the compressed size, while `docker images` shows the uncompressed (on disk) size.

See discussion on issue kubernetes-sigs/cri-tools#1264 for further details.

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.

<details>

state:
NoExecute taint is added with extra 5s delay when a Node's ready condition becomes Unknown

When investigating a delay of Pod eviction on unreachable Node, I found it always took 5s longer than the desired duration.
Looking at the timestamps, I found an odd one: the timestamp when `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable` NoExecute taint was added.

This can be reproducd consistently by terminating kubelet on a Node. The 5s delay of tainting adds 5s delay to the recovery time of Pods which are supposed to be evicted by the taint and recreated on other Nodes sooner. And I can't think of a reason why this taint alone should be added 5s later after the other taint and all other status changes. After investigating the relevant code for how the 5s is introduced, I think it should be an unwanted effect:

`processTaintBaseEviction()` uses the last observed ready condition of the Node instead of the current one to determine whether it should add the Node to the taint queue. When a Node is set to unreachable due to missing heartbeats, the last observed ready condition is still `true` and the current ready condition is `unknown`, we should use the latter for `processTaintBaseEviction()`. Otherwise the taint can only be added when `monitorNodeHealth()` runs another time (5s later) during which the current ready condition becomes the last observed ready condition, like the following logs show:
[link]

I will create a PR to fix it if the above analysis makes sense.

`node.kubernetes.io/unreachable` NoExecute taint shouldn't be added with extra 5s delay, compared with when `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable` NoSchedule taint is added and the Node is detected as unhealthy.

1. Stop kubelet on one Node.
2. Check the timestamps of the taints and condition transition of the Node.

This is required to [GA the feature]([link] but it's also useful in general.

To the best of my knowledge, it's very hard to observe the behavior of memorymanager without peeking into the pod and/or use the podresources interface (kubelet >= 1.24). But even for the latter, no well known components expose metrics consuming this information.

I believe anyway kubelet some expose some basic metrics about memoryumanager behaviour, while deferring more fine grained metrics to external components (NFD, node_exporter, is fine)

state:
Pod lifecycle broken with kubelet's `EventedPLEG` feature

Hi, a really amusing issue that I've uncovered is when we enable the EventedPLEG feature of the Kubelet (1.26.7), Kubelet fails to get container status / delete containers, etc.

The outcome of this is kubelet starts duplicate containers inside the same pod sandbox. This results in pods failing as there are "too many threads!" or "unable to bind to socket as port is in use".

Also raised issue here: [link]

Evented PLEG should behave similarly to non-evented PLEG.

Not sure if this is easy to reproduce on [label] but for us

1. Run 1.26.7
2. enable evented PLEG feature gate
3. observe `crictl ps` output / `systemd-cgls` to see duplicate containers start in same pod.

Running unified cgroup hier + cgroupfs driver

state:
HTTP2_PING_TIMEOUT_SECONDS+HTTP2_READ_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS > 40s will cause all node NotReady

The controller-manager node-lifecycle-controller watches node lease and update `nodeHealthMap` probeTimestamp , and it check node probeTimestamp is before `now - node-monitor-grace-period`. The node-monitor-grace-period default value is 40s.

When the client connection lost, the lease watcher cannot receive new event. With the http2 health check, HTTP2_PING_TIMEOUT_SECONDS default is 30s, HTTP2_READ_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS default is 15s, it will delay 45s to kill http2 connection.

During this period, node-lifecycle-controller will mark all nodes NotReady.

Here are some logs

When the http2 connection lost, the watch should stop as soon as possible. The reflector should relist resource, and node-lifecycle-controller should not mark all node NotReady.

HTTP2_PING_TIMEOUT_SECONDS+HTTP2_READ_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS should be less than 40s.

1. Find the controller-manager node-lifecycle-controller watch client srcIP:srcPort. Drop all tcp package send into srcIP:srcPort.
2. Wait for more than 40 seconds, all node will be marked NotReady
3. All node will be Ready after some seconds.

state:
kubelet: Device plugin fails to connect to new instance of plugin if previous one is terminated

The kubelet fails to connect to the device plugin if a previously running device plugin was running on the node with the same resource name.

Kubelets can get into a situation of running two pods advertising the same device plugin for a brief short period of time. For example, consider the following situation of a vendor hypothetically "upgrading" the device plugin:

1. kubelet runs`first-device-plugin` advertising resource `example.com/resource`
2. device vendor upgrades device-plugin to `second-plugin` and user deploys it
3. kubelet switches to use `second-device-plugin` advertising resource `example.com/resource`
4. user deletes `first-device-plugin`

Prior to v1.25.0, kubelet would handle this situation, and on step 4, disconnect of `first-device-plugin` would ensure that `first-device-plugin` would be disconnected, and maintain connection to `second-device-plugin` (since it was most recently connected).

This regressed as part of [link] where as part of the deletion of the `first-device-plugin` (step 4), kubelet would disconnect from "the most recently" connected plugin, namely `second-device-plugin`, and thus would get into a situation where neither the first or second device plugin would be connected. This would result in kubelet failing to adverting resources for the device. This is because of a bug where kubelet only stores the state of the most recently connected plugin and on disconnect, disconnects the most recently connected plugin.

I expected kubelet to either maintain the same behavior as pre 1.25: when deleting a device plugin pod, to disconnect from the device plugin that was deleted rather then the most recently connected plugin.

state:
"/dev/termination-log must have noexec so unpriviledged user cannot exec from it"

An unprivileged process/user running inside of a pod is able to write to `/dev/termination-log` file.

I thought this was preventable with both pod/container `securityContext` but that didn't turn out to be the case.

I didn't test it till the end but I tried redirecting the output of `/dev/urandom` from within the container to `/dev/termination-log` and filled it with gibberish until it reached the size of 2GB.

I suspect this is a way to compromise/crash node.

Is this an exploitable scenario and what can be done to mount the termination log in a way that doesn't allow unprivileged user/process to write arbitrary stuff to it?

Permissions to be denied when attempting to write `/dev/termination-log` file.

Exec pod container with maximally unprivileged securityContext and write `/dev/termination-log` file with:
`cat /dev/urandom > /dev/termination-log`

state:
"/dev/termination-log must have noexec so unpriviledged user cannot exec from it"

An unprivileged process/user running inside of a pod is able to write to `/dev/termination-log` file.

I thought this was preventable with both pod/container `securityContext` but that didn't turn out to be the case.

I didn't test it till the end but I tried redirecting the output of `/dev/urandom` from within the container to `/dev/termination-log` and filled it with gibberish until it reached the size of 2GB.

I suspect this is a way to compromise/crash node.

Is this an exploitable scenario and what can be done to mount the termination log in a way that doesn't allow unprivileged user/process to write arbitrary stuff to it?

Permissions to be denied when attempting to write `/dev/termination-log` file.

Exec pod container with maximally unprivileged securityContext and write `/dev/termination-log` file with:
`cat /dev/urandom > /dev/termination-log`

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.

Eviction never happens on pods with long-lived postStart lifecycle phase

While a pod's postStart lifecycle phase is running, the pod is not evicted even if its usage exceeds limits.

As soon as the pod exceeds ephemeral disk usage limits, it should be evicted, regardless of active lifecycle phases

The following pod demonstrates the problem:

Thanks to Shiming Zhang (wzshiming on HackerOne) for reporting this issue.

state:
Ephemeral storage limits do not account for data written to /dev/termination-log, pods are not evicted

A pod with an ephemeral storage limit is never evicted due to excessive data written to `/dev/termination-log`.

Data written to `/dev/termination-log` should count against a pod's ephemeral storage limit and result in eviction once too much data is written.

The following pod demonstrates the problem:

This issue was originally reported as part of the Kubernetes HackerOne bug bounty program. The current security posture of the Kubernetes Security Response Committee is to treat issues like this as security hardening bugs, and not as a CVE. Thanks to Chijin Zhou (chijin on HackerOne) for reporting this issue.

state:
align by socket not work when pod using multiple gpu card

I am running an AI application and expect to achieve the highest performance by using the Topology Manager to establish NUMA affinity binding between CPU and GPU.

so i restart kubelet with such options

then I use multiple GPU cards,
if the number of GPU cards are more than one socket, the allocated cpu and gpu are not aligned by socket.

The CPU cores requested by the pod should be from the NUMA node where the GPUs are located.

create pod with more than one nvidia gpu cards, like two gpu cards

1. create pod with 5 nvidia gpu cards
there is one gpu card on every numa and one socket consists of 4 numa node, so i request 5 cards thus gpus have to cross socket.

3. waiting pod running

4. check gpu and cpu core numa topology

5. we can see the allocated gpus are on numa node1,4,5,6,7 while cpus are on numa node1,2,3,4,5, they are not aligned.

state:
A mechanism to fail a Pod that is stuck due to an invalid Image

A mechanism to set a Pod into phase=Failed when the image pull has failed for a number of times (perhaps configurable).
Currently, the Pod just stays in phase=Pending

This is especially problematic for Jobs submitted through a queueing system.

In a queued environment, the time when the job starts running (pods created) might be hours or even days after the Job is created. Then, the user that submitted the job might not realize their mistake until it's too late. Since these Pods block resources in the cluster, it might cause other pending Jobs not to start.

If the Pods stay in phase=Pending, the job controller cannot do anything about them, as it only does "failure handling" once the Pods actually terminate with a phase=Failed.

state:
Liveness probe with an error doesn't trigger container restart

We have a specific case when a health check would error out with `500 INTERNAL SERVER ERROR`. In this particular scenario, the readiness probe will correctly mark pod unready but the liveness probe does not trigger a container restart.

Here are some more details:
1. Kubernetes Server Version: v1.24.16.
2. An application pod is running a single container.
3. Both readiness and liveness probes are `httpGet` and are hitting the same `/healthcheck` endpoint.
4. Healthcheck endpoint is responding with `500 INTERNAL SERVER ERROR`.
5. The readiness probe does mark the container as "unready" as expected.
6. The liveness probe does not trigger a container restart, even after the multiple consecutive failures.

I confirmed that `restartPolicy: Always` and when I exec into the container and run curl, I do get the 500 INTERNAL SERVER ERROR, the same as what I see in the application logs. As per documentation, a failing liveness probe should be triggering a restart but it is not happening.

Here's the log from kubelet:

Also, looking at the code [here]([link] the error does seem to be captured correctly by the probe but restart is not initiated.

Somehow the error is not being handled gracefully I assume. If I change it to an invalid port and cause a timeout the container gets restarted as expected. Also, switching from `httpGet` to `exec` type of healthcheck and running `curl [link] does trigger a restart so I suspect there is some bug with the httpGet probe itself.

This is what I see in the events:

A failing healthcheck in a liveness probe would trigger a container restart.

state:
kubelet starts workloads on a node that is currently in process of being shut down after it is restarted

Currently, when the [Graceful Node Shutdown]([link] is enabled, kubelet will then connect to Dbus and subscribe to the `org.freedesktop.systemd1.Manager` interface (using object path `/org/freedesktop/login1`) to listen for the `PrepareForShutdown` event.

Additionally, aside from listening for an event, kubelet will also place a so-called "inhibitor lock" (see [Inhibitor Locks]([link] for more information) that allows for it to stagger a potential system shutdown or restart up to some configured amount of time, and as such, allowing for workloads to complete their work and terminate gracefully.

Thus, should there be a shutdown or a restart of the underlying node initiated using compliant mechanisms (such as more modern tools that correctly handle the interaction between systemd, systemd-inhibit and Dbus), then kubelet would receive the `PrepareForShutdown` with its boolean attribute set to `true`—this would be a clear indication that the node is due to interrupt its operation, either a shutdown or a restart, and kubelet should remove ability for the node to receive new workloads (scheduling on it will be disabled) and then start gracefully terminating current workloads.

Then, once the last workload is terminated, kubelet will release the "inhibitor lock", allowing for the shutdown or restart to progress uninterrupted. This mechanism works well, given no interruptions to Dbus or kubelet operations.

However, if kubelet had been restarted, let's say as part of an ongoing upgrade or crash, then it would start to schedule workloads again on a currently shutting down node.

state:
Printing CLI parameters for Kubelet is misleading to users.

While working on [link] I ran into an issue where the CLI was reporting that `--fail-swap-on="true"`. But in the code it was actually set to "false". This is because the flag was set in the KubeletConfig.

We have users also noticing that the logs in Kubelet for CLI don't report the actual value as they are actually being read from the KubeletConfig.

We should bring the values of these configurations that they are rather than the CLI fields.

Log at logs for a CLI parameter (swap, eviction, etc) and change those values in the KubeletConfig.

Kubelet logs will display the CLI parameter rather than the KubeletConfig value.

[link]

state:
Printing CLI parameters for Kubelet is misleading to users.

While working on [link] I ran into an issue where the CLI was reporting that `--fail-swap-on="true"`. But in the code it was actually set to "false". This is because the flag was set in the KubeletConfig.

We have users also noticing that the logs in Kubelet for CLI don't report the actual value as they are actually being read from the KubeletConfig.

We should bring the values of these configurations that they are rather than the CLI fields.

Log at logs for a CLI parameter (swap, eviction, etc) and change those values in the KubeletConfig.

Kubelet logs will display the CLI parameter rather than the KubeletConfig value.

state:
PostStart is never executed

If the kubelet is restarted when a pod with a postStart lifecycle hook is started but poststart still not be executed, then the postStart hook will never be executed when the kubelet start.

when kubelet restart, pod's postStart hook can always be run.

I'm not quite clear on how to reproduce this; it might require some luck.
However, maybe we can reproduce it by adding a sleep before executing postStart in the code.Then we can restart kubelet when container has run.

state:
sidecar container readniess result to be used in Pod ready state also for pod.spec.restartPolicy = Never or OnFailure

I created a pod with sidecar container with following manifest:

watch the pod readiness.

in [Sidecar containers and Pod lifecycle]([link] it's mentioned "If a readinessProbe is specified for this init container, its result will be used to determine the ready state of the Pod."

it's true only for pod.spec.restartPolicy = Always, sidecar container readniess result will be used in Pod ready state, neither "Never" or "OnFailure".

I tested with v1.29.0

I expect "If a readinessProbe is specified for this init container, its result will be used to determine the ready state of the Pod." also applicable to pod.spec.restartPolicy = "Never" or "OnFailure".

Set pod.spec.restartPolicy = "Never" or "OnFailure".

state:
Pending image downloads of deleted containers are never interrupted, leading to possible DoS

During a research project on Kubernetes, we discovered a potential bug on any reasonably recent Kubernetes version (we tested in 1.25 to 1.29) that affects all clusters regardless of the container runtime used. By exploiting the fact that the CRI-API does not maintain the container download status, we created a denial of service via resource exhaustion.

----

When an user deploys a pod, the deployed container(s) may rely on image(s) that are not present on the target node, triggering a download by the container runtime. However, if that pod is deleted (either with or without the `--force` flag) before the container runtime completes the download of the image, this download will be carried on anyway. Kubernetes tracks no information at all about the download, and there is no way of interrupting it unless the container runtime is forcibly terminated and recreated.

This (useless, as the images will never be used) sequence of downloads will waste the node’s CPU and network bandwidth and block the download queue, preventing the deployment of other containers with images yet to be downloaded. We experimented on a wide variety of settings, including but not limited to private clouds, public clouds and edge devices, with different container runtimes (containerd and CRI-O) and different Kubernetes providers (kubeadm, microk8s, and GKE).

The impact this bug has on the cluster is twofold. First, by the way the download queue is implemented in the container runtime, queuing up multiple image download requests prevents legitimate users from deploying workloads that require an image download to be run. Since deleting a container from Kubernetes does not affect the container runtime download queue, this queue can grow uncontrolled **even if the requests are canceled before the download starts**.

state:
[umbrella issue]: poor visibility/observability of the kubelet (cpu,memory,device,topology) managers

The kubelet {cpu, memory, device, topology} manager, collectively known as resource managers, give little to none feedback to their consumers. Once the kubelet is configured with the relevant settings (e.g. cpuManagerPolicy=static or topologyManagerPolicy=restricted, say) and once the workload requests exclusive resources provided by the managers, the implicit contract is that if the pod is admitted, then all the resources are provisioned according to the spec. Similarly, if the kubelet cannot allocate the resources as requested (and as configured) the pod will fail admission with a TopologyAffinityError or similar generic error.

The problem is twofold:
- there's no **explicit** feedback about resource allocation. For example, the system explicitly acknowledges a pod got its image pulled succesfully with a event, yet it does not for resource allocation, even though both are arguably prerequisites to have the pod running, and both could be theoretically inferred from the fact the pod started. The point of this example is to highlight the lack of explicit feedback about allocation.
- on error, there's no way to learn what gone wrong except in most generic term (pod failed with TopologyAffinityError). The only option is to look at kubelet logs, but the kubelet verbosity has to be >= 4 anyway.

On success, the system should somehow explcitely acknowledge the resource classes being allocated, for example "CPUs" and that NUMA alignment took place.

On admission failure, the system should give indication of what caused admission failure, like unable to allocate enough memory on the selected NUMA zone, or missing device affine to the selected NUMA zone. But any more information that is presented now is welcome.

In both cases we probably don't want or need to expose the details of the concrete resources, at least not initially.

1.

state:
Parallel pod deletion makes kubectl stuck forever

`kubectl delete pod` may become stuck during execution of the following steps:
* Restart kubelet `systemctl restart kubelet`
* Force remove all containers for static pods `crictl ps --name '(kube-apiserver|kube-scheduler|kube-controller-manager|etcd)' -q | xargs -I CONTAINER sudo crictl rm -f CONTAINER`
* Try to delete some static pod `kubectl delete pod -n kube-system kube-controller-manager-k8s-control-plane-1`

Result: kubectl prints that the pod is deleted, but never exits.

It seems that the problem is caused by parallel deletion of the pod by kubelet.
Please see details in the steps to reproduce.

state:
Persistent Thread and Memory Allocation by Kubelet Post-Workload

`Kubelet` does not release threads and their associated memory allocations after handling high workloads, leading to inefficient resource usage and potential node performance degradation.

Expected kubelet to free up threads and memory resources once the workload decreases, returning to baseline resource usage levels.

- Deploy a set of pods with containers that have frequent readiness probes, simulating a high workload on kubelet.

- Monitor kubelet process resource usage (threads and memory) before, during, and after the workload using system monitoring tools.

- Observe resource usage after reducing the workload to verify if resources are released.

This issue may lead to resource exhaustion and affect the overall performance of the Kubernetes node, especially in dynamic workload environments.

state:
DRA: kubelet: checkpoint checksum changes when API gets extended

When adding the `StructuredData` field to `resourcev1alpha2.ResourceHandle`, old checkpoint files became invalid because the checksum that gets calculated by hashing the `spew` output in `pkg/util/hash` no longer matches. This caused kubelet to fail to start with:

Here's what the checksum in a unit test gets calculcated for:

Note the new `StructuredData:(*v1alpha2.StructuredResourceHandle)<nil>`.

Not sure what the right behavior is. Perhaps kubelet should have ignored the invalid checkpoint?

Revert the pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/state/state_checkpoint_test.go update in [link]

The state.DRAManagerCheckpoint contains a version field, which is set to v1.I think that's where things fall apart: that version must exactly match the type that gets serialized, which is not the case here. The type changes over time, but the version is fixed.

Let's reconsider what should get checkpointed and how we can make that stable. Also, is checkpointing really worth it? What bad things happen if we remove it?

state:
Eviction manager: When stats calls failed, we evict the pod that we couldn't get stats for.

As I was investigating the eviction tests, I discovered an interesting problem. We are seeing a wide range of flakes where the one pod that should not be evicted gets evicted in the eviction test.

Eviction tests work by assigning one pod that it should never be evicted and then it ranks these pods and evicts the other pods. If there is a stats API failure, we evict the pod that we couldn't get stats for.

This seems to be by design (cc @user)

We should maybe consider a more deterministic approach if stats fails.

Try running the eviction tests on the PR.

Code that causes this is here:

[link]

state:
Pod Crashloop backoff requeue issues

When stepping through the pod crashloop backoff implementation, I noticed a few issues:

1. Backoff errors are unsuccessfully suppressed:
- This code is non-functional, since there will always be a non-error result present (`ConfigPodSandbox`) with a nil error: [link]
2. The propogated backoff error means that the pod worker always immediately requeues the pod: [link]
- If the backoff error were suppressed, then the default 1m sync frequency would be used, which would cause very long initial backoffs.

The result of these issues are:
1. Log spam: `E0301 01:06:01.286649 1869 pod_workers.go:1294] "Error syncing pod, skipping" err="failed to \"StartContainer\" for \"alpine\" with CrashLoopBackOff: \"back-off 5m0s restarting failed container=alpine pod=restarting-pod_default(ca0d5836-1435-497e-9a41-547fbcc10484)\"" pod="default/restarting-pod" podUID=ca0d5836-1435-497e-9a41-547fbcc10484` get's logged in a frequent loop
2. Kubelet does unnecessary work to reexamine pods and containers in backoff
3. (minor) the error retry period is 10s, which adds up to 10s to the backoff time

I think the ideal fix is to propagate the backoff retry time up from SyncPod [1] to the pod worker [2], so that the pod can be requeued with the exact (jittered) right amount of retry time. One option is to use a custom error type to encapsulate the backoff time, which I started working on here: [link]

Of course, there is very little test coverage across these code paths too.

state:
The image of a running container was deleted by the image garbage collection

The image of the container was deleted while pod was running.
When I noticed it, it was already almost two weeks after the pod was created, and by prometheus metrics, I could see at the time that the pod was created the kubelet performed image garbage collection on the node and images were deleted.

It might be worth mentioning that nothing other than the kubelet could have deleted the image from the node.

This situation happen a while ago, and I couldn't deal with it for too long while it happened, So unfortunately I don't have data to share. But by looking in the code the following scenario seems to make sense:
1. At the start of the garbage collection process the image was already in the node (for a while), but not in used yet.
2. The garbage collection get the current images and pods on that node from the runtime, because this image is not in use by any pod, it is considered unused. Ref: [link]
3. Before the image is actually deleted, A pod using this image is scheduling at this node. since the image is already on the node and the `imagePullPolicy` is `IfNotPresent` there is no need for pulling and the container is start to running. There is no knowledge about that the image is about to be deleted. Ref: [link]
4. The garbage collection is still running, and it eventually comes to delete this image. There is no knowledge about that the image is in use now.

In short, I think that in the time between pods are detected from runtime to find the unused image to the time those images are actually deleted (the time between step 2 to step 4), new pods could be scheduling on that node, and make use of the images that will be deleted by the garbage collection immediately afterwards.

state:
DRA: beta: CEL validation

At the moment, `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/namedresources/cel/compile.go` uses 1.0 as version for everything in its CEL environment to grant the alpha API CEL expressions access to things defined in the 1.30 release. We need to change that to the real version before promotion to beta.

New expression must not use CEL expressions which become invalid on a downgrade, so only features already available in the previous release are valid.

state:
DRA: kubelet: avoid API permission error log entries

When kubelet starts and begins watching NodeResourceSlice objects with an informer, it initially logs errors like:

This seems to be caused by the informer being started at a time when the kubelet REST client doesn't have the final credentials yet. The errors are harmless and can be ignored because eventually the List call succeeds.

Ideas for solving this:
- change when the registration handler is called or
- wait in the `pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/plugin/noderesources.go` code until List succeeds without logging errors, then start the informer

Error logs are confusing.

DRA: scheduler: refactor foreachPodResourceClaim

`foreachPodResourceClaim` in `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources.go` could be changed so that it gathers all information about a claim, including structured claim and class parameters. Instead of two slices of the same size (`claims` and `informationsForClaim`) we should only have one.

- `isSchedulableAfterClaimChange` can then trigger only for claims with structured parameters and ignore the others
- Some checks currently only done in `PreFilter` can already be done in `PreEnqueue`.

Together this reduces the overall work.
