state:
GRPC healthprobe cannot handle TLS

Since version 1.27 kubernetes supports the gprc healthserver for readyness and liveness probes.
I now have several services that use grpc with self-signed tls certificates. The certificates are stored as secrets in the cluster. It took me quite a while to understand why my liveness probes always fail. So I rebuilt my service so that the endpoints are offered with TLS and the health server without. That works.

The grpc-health-probe also supports TLS connections. However, according to the documentation, parameters must be set for this. Here is the link to Repo: [Health Checking TLS Servers]([link]

A GRPC server with TLS and the corresponding code for the health probe should be sufficient. Here is a small example:

I think it would be easiest if you could tell the probe whether it is a TLS connection and, if in doubt, refer to a secret in the cluster where the CA certificate or similar is located.

It took me quite a while to understand why my liveness probes always fail. So I rebuilt my service so that the endpoints are offered with TLS and the health server without. That works.

The grpc-health-probe also supports TLS connections. However, according to the documentation, parameters must be set for this. Here is the link to Repo: [Health Checking TLS Servers]([link]

A GRPC server with TLS and the corresponding code for the health probe should be sufficient. Here is a small example:

I think it would be easiest if you could tell the probe whether it is a TLS connection and, if in doubt, refer to a secret in the cluster where the CA certificate or similar is located.

Routing determination: node.

state:
Warnings on missing pull secrets can be confusing

A previous enhancement has added a warning event when a pull secret is missing: [link]

If the image has pulled successfully because either another pull secret did the job, or the image doesn't need auth, the warning is distracting.

As an example, this pod is running perfectly fine and has no problems, and yet when described, has had 11k warning events emitted over the last 9 days.

We have been including multiple pull secrets in our pulls because it's more flexible to point to a few that may exist than to have to very exactly map each pod to a pull secret. This change means we will get warnings even when everything is working exactly as we wanted it to.

No warnings if an image is pulled successfully.

Create a pod or service account that references a missing pull secret that is not required to pull the image.

My suggestion would be to only emit that warning if the image cannot be pulled (for example, reaches ImagePullBackOff), or to include the detail about the missing secret in the existing image pull failure events.

state:
NUMA-aware memory manager and Topology Manager policy of "restricted" results in TopologyAffinityError when it shouldn't

Running K8s 1.29.2, with the kubelet NUMA-aware memory manager policy set to "Static" and the Topology Manager policy set to "restricted".

1. The /var/lib/kubelet/memory_manager_state file shows:

2. Created a pod kube-mgrr-1, then checked pod status and memory_manager_state file content

3. Created a new pod which exceeds memory of NUMA node 0 and check if the pod is pinned to both NUMA nodes.

4. Delete kube-mgrr-1 pod

5. Add kube-mgrr-1 back . Pod status is TopologyAffinityError

Note: if the topology manager policy is set to "best-effort" the request to respawn the Pod succeeds.

When re-creating the pod that was killed, it should be able to start up again since there is enough memory available on a single node to satisfy the memory and CPU requests.

Set the memory manager policy to "Static" and topology manager policy to "restricted". On a two-NUMA-node worker node create a smallish Pod in the Guaranteed QoS class that easily fits on one NUMA node worth of memory. Create a second Pod in the Guaranteed QoS class with a big enough memory request that it cannot fit on one NUMA node. Delete the first Pod. After the memory freed up by the Pod deletion shows as available, attempt to recreate the first Pod.

[FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] containers with a CPU limit below 10m have a resize status of InProgress indefinetly

There is an implicit minimum of `10m` for CPU limits, so the actual resource limit is always clamped at a minimum of 10m. If the desired CPU limit is below 10m, the comparison of desired == actual fails, and the resize status is set to in-progress.

This is very similar to the case of minimum shares addressed in [link]

state:
In terminating pod, status of containers is not updated

When a pod with several containers is terminating, until all of those containers successfully terminate, the number of ready containers is not updated. For example, if you have a pod with two containers and one of them immediately exits and one of them has a prestop hook that sleeps for several minutes, the pod will show up as 2/2 containers ready even though one container immediately exits.

See kubelet logs here: [link]

I expect that the pod status should reflect the number of containers that is actually ready, even if the pod is terminating.

Create a pod with two containers, one of which has a prestop hook that sleeps:

Delete the pod, and notice that it will stay at 2/2 ready until both containers die even when the runtime acknowledges that one container has been successfully shut down early on

state:
[FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Revisit ResizeStatus and state transitions

There are several problems with the current approach to pod ResizeStatus, including:

1. Race condition setting the status: the kubelet can overwrite the Proposed status set by the API server ([link]
2. Can technically have 2 parallel resize statuses: a {Proposed/Deferred/Infeasible} resize when desired resources != allocated resources, and an InProgress resize when allocated resources != actual resources. Currently the former just overrides the latter.
3. Separate mechanism for surfacing details related to error states (Deferred, Infeasible, stuck InProgress)
4. No status to capture desired memory limit < actual memory usage, which can lead to a resize stuck in InProgress (maybe this should move to the deferred state?)

Before graduating to Beta, we should revisit the design of ResizeStatus, and take a holistic look at the user experience.

state:
[FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Enable memory limit decrease

When shrinking the pod-level memory limits (sum of container limits iff all containers have limits), the Kubelet checks the current pod memory usage, and doesn't apply the new limits if the new limits < current usage. However, the Kubelet doesn't place the same restriction on containers, and we don't require container runtimes to make the same check.

In practice, this means that for a single container pod, decreasing the memory limit below usage will result in the resize being indefinitely in progress, but for a multiple container pod, if some containers have sufficient free memory, you can shrink the memory limits below usage for a container in the pod, resulting in that container being OOM-killed.

What is the desired behavior here?

[link] provides more background information and several options for how this should be handled.

state:
Failed to get rootfs info if the host machine uses bcachefs raid array

If you create a host machine with bcachefs file system with multiple drives:

The filesystem device is in every linux tool defined as `/dev/nvme0n1p2:/dev/nvme1n1p2`.

As you might know, docker displays this file system label if you add any unnamed volumes to your container. And this brings us to the k8s issue. If you create a cluster e.g. with kind or minikube, it starts a kubelet service in the container. Kubelet tries to read all mounts, and fails to parse the bcachefs filesystem:

What you _can_ do is to just take the first partition from the list and use that. But here we have kubelet just crashing, rendering systems such as kind or minikube not working.

Kubelet should just not care the filesystem name format. The system should start even when using bcachefs.

Spin up a virtual machine with two disks. It's probably easiest to run on NixOS:

[link]

Create the root volume with

Continue the installation as instructed.

state:
Failed to get rootfs info if the host machine uses bcachefs raid array

If you create a host machine with bcachefs file system with multiple drives:

The filesystem device is in every linux tool defined as `/dev/nvme0n1p2:/dev/nvme1n1p2`.

As you might know, docker displays this file system label if you add any unnamed volumes to your container. And this brings us to the k8s issue. If you create a cluster e.g. with kind or minikube, it starts a kubelet service in the container. Kubelet tries to read all mounts, and fails to parse the bcachefs filesystem:

What you _can_ do is to just take the first partition from the list and use that. But here we have kubelet just crashing, rendering systems such as kind or minikube not working.

Kubelet should just not care the filesystem name format. The system should start even when using bcachefs.

Spin up a virtual machine with two disks. It's probably easiest to run on NixOS:

[link]

Continue the installation as instructed.

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.

state:
devicemanager stuck in Allocate RPC and causing all new coming pods pending on admitting

After created pod with device request, its state always be `Pending`, even though it was scheduled.
And at the same time, new coming pod (without device request) on the same node is on `Pending` state too.

After a bit investigation with goroutines, devicemanager was stucking in `Allocate` RPC, and wait device plugin's response:
![image]([link]

Accroding to this stack, pod admitting is stucked obviously.

Device plugins' bug or out-of-service, should not lead kubelet pod admit procedure blocking.

Reproduct it with [link] Add some sleep time in `Allocate` call:
![image]([link]

![image]([link]

pod with dummy device and new coming pod without dummy device are in `Pending` state:
![image]([link]

After running out sleep time, all pod return to `Running` state:
![image]([link]

state:
kubelet could reject pods with NodeAffinity error due to incomplete informer cache on the node object

In our end (AKS), we observed that there is a case that kubelet could reject pods with NodeAffinty status if the node watch call got closed due to unknown reason during kubelet start up.

An illustrated procedure is (using `Tx` to indicate time):

- T1: kubelet starts, spawns the processes for registering node (create node) and node informer for syncing the node object in parallel
- T2: the node informer successfully listed empty nodes list from kube-apiserver , proceeding to watch call
[link]
- T3: the watch call stopped due to unknown issue, for instance network closed. In this case, the watch call would exit with error like:
very short watch: k8s.io/client-go/informers/factory.go:160: Unexpected watch close - watch lasted less than a second and no items received

In this case, the node informer will back-off and retry with new list-watch steps:
[link]
- T4: kubelet successfully created the node object in kube-apiserver side. Kube-scheduler kicks in and assigns pods to the node
- T5: because in T3 the list call was succeeded with empty results, the node informer had been marked as synced:

[link]
[link]
In this case, kubelet starts syncing pods and attempts to run. If these pods are set with affinity settings, the kubelet node admission check will fail the pods with "NodeAffinity" status because the node informer cache is empty. Kubelet uses a minimal node object without expected node labels for performing admission check:
[link]
- T6: kubelet node informer retry kicks in, this time it successfully synced the node object from remote. Now retried pods scheduling on this node would succeed as the node labels are expected

In our reproduction, we captured the following logs:

In the normal case, the retry back off (between T6 and T5) should be short and kubelet should not leave many pods failed.

state:
[FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] avoid checking the configuration of resource managers to learn their expected behavior

The VPA logic needs to know if resource managers (cpumanager, memory manager) can allocate exclusively resources.
To do so, it peeks in their configuration and second-guesses their expected behavior.
This is unfortunate and due to the lack of resource manager API which can report the same information

As result of this approach, there's an actual bug in the current VPA logic: this check is wrong [link] because the name of the policy for cpumanager is `static` (lowercase "s") while for memory manager is `Static` (uppercase "s")

VPA should be able to learn about resource manager behavior in a safe and supported way

configure memory manager with `Static` policy and enable VPA. the `canResizePod` logic will behave incorrectly

behavior introduced in 2d8939c4aef8f060d413bb27272ba38cd7171fbe

state:
[FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] avoid checking the configuration of resource managers to learn their expected behavior

The VPA logic needs to know if resource managers (cpumanager, memory manager) can allocate exclusively resources.
To do so, it peeks in their configuration and second-guesses their expected behavior.
This is unfortunate and due to the lack of resource manager API which can report the same information

As result of this approach, there's an actual bug in the current VPA logic: this check is wrong [link] because the name of the policy for cpumanager is `static` (lowercase "s") while for memory manager is `Static` (uppercase "s")

VPA should be able to learn about resource manager behavior in a safe and supported way

configure memory manager with `Static` policy and enable VPA. the `canResizePod` logic will behave incorrectly

state:
Container remains ready causing Pod and EndpointSlice to Report False Ready State for the entire terminationGracePeriod

containerStatuses.ready is not set to false immediately when a pod it deleted. This is results in pod reporting ready status when the pod is deleted after terminationGracePeriodSeconds have passed.

After the pod termination starts, the containerStatuses should set ready: false for all the containers in the pod and hence pod status should report as ready: false.

Run the above pod and issue a delete call when the containers become ready

$ kubectl delete pod b382559131

Monitor the readiness status:

$ while true; do date && kubectl get pod b382559131 -o json | jq .status.containerStatuses.[].ready && sleep 1; done
Sat Dec 21 11:05:16 PM PST 2024
true
true
Sat Dec 21 11:05:17 PM PST 2024
true
true

< snip >

Sat Dec 21 11:06:21 PM PST 2024
true
true
Sat Dec 21 11:06:22 PM PST 2024
Error from server (NotFound): pods "b382559131" not found
Sat Dec 21 11:06:24 PM PST 2024
Error from server (NotFound): pods "b382559131" not found

The pod has a termination grace period of 60s. The delete was issued at 11:05:21 and we see that the ready status was true until the pod was deleted at 11:06:22 (60s later).

The pod reports ready status until the last container exits.

state:
Update secret and then upgrade the pod, Sometimes pod will get the old value of secret

Mount the secret to the specified directory in the pod. The startup script of pod will read the value of secret. Our program will update the secret and then upgrade the pod. Sometimes the pod read the old value of secret, after container restart it will read the new value of secret. We use WatchChangeDetectionStrategy, Looks like there's a problem with the kubelet cache update.

The newly created pod immediately detects the secret cache update in kubelet.

The probability of the problem is very low, we only encountered it twice in total. I suspect that limiting the CPU resources of the apiserver process and triggering a large number of pods(pods in same node and use same secret) to rebuild may increase the probability of this problem. I am trying to reproduce this problem in this way.

I'm having problems probably due to pkg/kubelet/util/manager/watch_based_manager.go method _AddReference_ and _DeleteReference_. I think all the secrets used by new pods should be created with a new list-watch listener instead of reusing the ones already created. From the perspective of method implementation, if multiple pods use the same secret and are on the same node, this situation may occur.

state:
[EventedPLEG] EventedPLEG should detect resize completion rapidly

EventedPLEG should detect completion of pod resizing in the runtime as rapidly as GenericPLEG.

Since v1.32 (#128518), GenericPLEG polls container resources in the runtime at resizing a pod so that it detects resize completion rapidly. This poll is actuated when GenericPLEG relists pods regularly:
[link]

EventedPLEG depends on GenericPLEG for this polling:
[link]

When EventedPLEG is enabled, GenericPLEG relists pods every five minutes:
[link]

Then, it takes at most five minutes till pod resize appears to be completed in the API.

Pod resize should complete as quickly as if EventedPLEG is not enabled.

Considering maturity of features, I don’t think this issue blocks promotion of InPlacePodVerticalScaling. This issue should be solved for promoting EventedPLEG.

Since v1.32 (#128518), GenericPLEG polls container resources in the runtime at resizing a pod so that it detects resize completion rapidly. This poll is actuated when GenericPLEG relists pods regularly:
[link]

EventedPLEG depends on GenericPLEG for this polling:
[link]

When EventedPLEG is enabled, GenericPLEG relists pods every five minutes:
[link]

Then, it takes at most five minutes till pod resize appears to be completed in the API.

Pod resize should complete as quickly as if EventedPLEG is not enabled.

Considering maturity of features, I don’t think this issue blocks promotion of InPlacePodVerticalScaling. This issue should be solved for promoting EventedPLEG.

Pods Pending when loaded via file, omit resources in the spec and LimitRange is present

We deploy control-plane components as Pod manifests for Kubelet to load. Here is an example of our APIServer Pod manifest: [link]

As you can see it *does not* specify any resource requests/limits.

All our Namespaces have LimitRange like this:

Starting with v1.32 - these Pods no longer start, they stay `Pending` and the error is:

If we add resource requests+limits to the Pod definition, Pods successfully start. If we remove LimitRange from the Namespace, the Pods successfully start.

We suspect this issue is related to [link] and [link] .

We are going to specify resources in all our static Pod definitions, its the right thing to do for us, but this seems like incorrect behavior that was worth a Github Issue.

Pods that do not specify resource requests / limits are able to start in a Namespace with a LimitRange.

Create a static Pod definition that is loaded by Kubelet, omit specifying resources.
Create a LimitRange that specifies cpu and memory.
Running v1.32 Pod should stay `Pending`.

state:
Migrate Kubelet codebase to contextual logging

### **What would you like to to?**

Support contextual logging in Kubelet.

To implement [link]

### **How to do it?**

General instructions can be found here: [link]

The approach I'd like to propose for `Kubelet` is to do it directory by directory, making as little changes as possible to other components. If the first level directory requires a lot of changes, consider migrating its subdirectories in a separate PRs, e.g. instead of migrating `pkg/kubelet/cm` at once, consider migrating `pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager`, `pkg/kubelet/cm/containermap`, etc.

Use `context.TODO()` to create context that should be passed as an argument in future to avoid massive changes in other components. Add a comment explaining that this is a temporary solution and when it needs to be replaced by the direct context usage.

Look at the existing `context.TODO()` and `context.Background()` calls in the directory. Replace them by the ctx usage if possible. Replace `context.Background()` with `context.TODO()` if ctx is not yet accessible there.

After all source files in the directory are migrated, add the directory path to the `./hack/logcheck.conf` and run `hack/update-golangci-lint-config.sh` to generate `hack/golangci*.yaml` configs. This will prevent usage of non-contextual logging for the directory.

Last step of this migration is to migrate `pkg/kubelet/*.go`, add `pkg/kubelet` to the `./hack/logcheck.conf`, remove all its subdirectories from there and regenerate `golangci` configs.

### **Which components are already migrated and which still need to be migrated?**

state:
kubelet /stats/summary includes terminated init container in memory.usageBytes

For a pod with an init container that copies some files, the `memory.usageBytes` value reported by `kubelet`'s `/stats/summary` endpoint includes the memory consumption of the init container forever, even though the init container has terminated already.

The value of `memory.usageBytes` differs significantly from what `kubectl top pod` reports for the same pod.

Here is a screenshot where the kubelet reports around 100 MB while `kubectl top` and `k9s` both report 0 MB. (My assumption is that 0 MB is correct for this container and 100 MB is wrong.)

(For the record, kubelet also reports 0 MB when the same pod definition is used, just with the init container removed.)

![Image]([link]

* I expect `kubelet`'s `/stats/summary` endpoint (and in particular the `memory.usageBytes` value) to only include non-terminated containers of the pod.
* I expect the pod memory usage from `kubectl top pod` and the value of kubelet's `/stats/summary`, `memory.usageBytes` to be the same, or at least close to each other.

I created a full **reproducer** with instructions here: [link]

I already did a fair bit of analysis by building Kubernetes locally and adding additional logging to what kubelet is doing.

I am pretty sure the root cause is the heuristic by which kubelet picks through the result of the [`getCadvisorContainerInfo(p.cadvisor)`]([link] call to determine whether a container is terminated. For some reason, this heuristic fails to identify the terminated init-container as terminated, and it includes its memory usage into the pods memory usage. From my understanding this is wrong, because a terminated container should not count towards a pod's memory usage.

Here is what happens in more detail:

state:
Pod Allocate failed due to requested number of devices unavailable for nvidia.com/gpu. Requested:1, Available: 0, which is unexpected

Recently, we encountered an intermittent issue that occurs approximately once a week. The error event is as follows:

After this error occurs, pods scheduled to the node persistently report the UnexpectedAdmissionError, and restarting the kubelet resolves the issue.

**Context:**
- We use GPU scheduling with jobs that request GPU resources (multi-GPU or single-GPU),each pod includes an init container and an app container.
- In abnormal scenarios, when a pod fails to start (status: Failed), it is forcibly deleted (`kubectl delete pod --force`).

**Analysis:**
After adding debug log, we observed that the `m.allocatedDevices` (a data structure tracking device allocations) contained stale data, causing devices to remain "occupied" indefinitely.

We analyzed the code and found that `m.allocatedDevices` is reset during pod allocation. However, the reset logic is skipped under a specific condition:

When activePods matches `m.podDevices.pods()` (the list of pods tracked by the device manager), the code does not reset `m.allocatedDevices`.

By adding debug logs, we confirmed that when the kubelet repeatedly reports UnexpectedAdmissionError, the condition `len(podsToBeRemoved) <= 0` (no pods marked for removal) prevents the update of `m.allocatedDevices`. This leaves stale data in `m.allocatedDevices`, leading to incorrect resource allocation.

[link]

After analyzing up to this point, I still haven't identified the root cause of why the kubelet enters this state. Any insights would be greatly appreciated. Thanks in advance!

[FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Handle Downward API resource updates

The [Downward API]([link] can expose resource values to containers, but if those values are updated without restart the downward API values can be stale.

What is the correct behavior here? For other mutable downward API values (e.g. labels), it is expected that envvars can be stale, and volumes are kept up-to-date.

If we handle updates in the downward API volumes, should those continue tracking the desired resources from the pod spec, or should those report the allocated resources?

state:
DRA helper: report dropped fields

When a DRA driver asks to publish ResourceSlices, the ResourceSlice controller creates or updates existing slices. If the DRA driver is asking to publish slices that the cluster doesn't support (for example, need the partitionable devices feature and that feature is turned off), the unknown or unsupported fields get dropped.

A DRA driver might want to be notified when this happens.

Normally, the admin should avoid that by configuring the driver appropriately *before* disabling a feature.
But as a second line of defense, perhaps the DRA driver can switch to a simpler mode of operation instead of publishing incomplete ResourceSlices.

state:
Add Container Event Notification for CRI's Update*Resources Interface to Support In-Place Pod Resizing

The current evented PLEG implementation in CRI generates container events (create/start/stop/delete) to trigger `syncPod`, but it fails to accommodate the in-place pod resizing feature. During in-place pod resizing, after completing container resource updates via `UpdateContainerResources/UpdatePodSandboxResources`, we need to re-trigger `syncPod` to update the container status.

In the generic PLEG implementation, this is achieved by forcing a synthetic container event during the next PLEG relist after doPodResizeAction, which triggers `syncPod`. However, for evented PLEG (where events originate directly from the container runtime via CRI), there is no native event generated when resource updates occur. Currently, In PR #131024, I implemented a temporary workaround by simulating container runtime-generated events to achieve this behavior. While this approach unblocks testing, it remains a short-term fix.

To fully align with evented PLEG's design, we need container runtimes to emit a dedicated "Update" event when their `UpdateContainerResources` or `UpdatePodSandboxResources` CRI interfaces are invoked. This event should notify the Kubelet to trigger syncPod, ensuring consistent behavior between generic and evented PLEG implementations.

During in-place pod resizing, after completing container resource updates via `UpdateContainerResources/UpdatePodSandboxResources`, we need to re-trigger `syncPod` to update the container status.

In the generic PLEG implementation, this is achieved by forcing a synthetic container event during the next PLEG relist after doPodResizeAction, which triggers `syncPod`. However, for evented PLEG (where events originate directly from the container runtime via CRI), there is no native event generated when resource updates occur. Currently, In PR #131024, I implemented a temporary workaround by simulating container runtime-generated events to achieve this behavior. While this approach unblocks testing, it remains a short-term fix.

To fully align with evented PLEG's design, we need container runtimes to emit a dedicated "Update" event when their `UpdateContainerResources` or `UpdatePodSandboxResources` CRI interfaces are invoked. This event should notify the Kubelet to trigger syncPod, ensuring consistent behavior between generic and evented PLEG implementations.

state:
Kubelet failed to start on reboot with memory manager's `Static` policy

Memory manager's `Static` policy will cause kubelet fail to start on reboot, when total memory of each numa node changes after each reboot, while they still sum up to a fixed number, just as [link] describes.

Though Kubernetes v1.32 [improves memory manager reliability and consistency]([link] with [link] by @user, the issue is still not fixed because it still checks whether numa node's total memory is unchanged:

[link]

Thus following error happened in kubelet on reboot:
<details>

</details>

1. Memory state json before reboot:
<details>

</details>

2. Memory state json after reboot:
<details>

</details>

We can see total memory of node 0, 1 is unchanged, but node 2, 3 changed while they sum up to a same count.

Improve the implementation of `areMemoryStatesEqual`, to allow for numa node total memory change as long as the total summed up memory is consistent (and the current memory state can serve allocated pods?).

1. Prepare a multi numa-node machine where memory of each numa node varies on reboot.
2. Start kubernetes cluster with kubelet memory manager policy to be `Static`.
3. Reboot to see the failure of kubelet.

[link] says issue described there would be classified as a feature request instead of bug. But I think this is a bug given that Kubernetes v1.32 is [improving memory manager reliability and consistency]([link]

The kubelet does not guarantee pod ordering when admitting pods after a restart or reboot.

In certain edge cases, this behavior could cause the memory manager to reject some pods, and in more extreme cases, it may cause kubelet to fail upon restart.

Previously, the beta implementation lacked certain checks and logic to prevent these issues.

To stabilize the memory manager for general availability (GA) readiness, small but critical refinements have been made to the algorithm, improving its robustness and handling of edge cases.

[link] says issue described there would be classified as a feature request instead of bug. But I think this is a bug given that Kubernetes v1.32 is [improving memory manager reliability and consistency]([link]

The kubelet does not guarantee pod ordering when admitting pods after a restart or reboot.

In certain edge cases, this behavior could cause the memory manager to reject some pods, and in more extreme cases, it may cause kubelet to fail upon restart.

Previously, the beta implementation lacked certain checks and logic to prevent these issues.

To stabilize the memory manager for general availability (GA) readiness, small but critical refinements have been made to the algorithm, improving its robustness and handling of edge cases.

state:
allowPrivilegeEscalation:false insufficient for privilege escalation prevention

The issue relates to how allowPrivilegeEscalation: false doesn't prevent all forms of privilege escalation through dangerous capabilities.

When a container's security context sets allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, the current validation only blocks CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability. However, other dangerous capabilities that can also lead to privilege escalation are still allowed.

Technical Details:
1. Current Validation:
- Blocks: CAP_SYS_ADMIN when allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
- Allows: CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_MODULE, CAP_SYS_PTRACE, etc.

2. Example:

3. Dangerous Capabilities Still Allowed:
- CAP_NET_ADMIN: Network stack manipulation, potential for network namespace escape
- CAP_SYS_MODULE: Loading kernel modules
- CAP_SYS_PTRACE: Process debugging and memory access
- CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH: Bypass file permission checks
- CAP_SYS_RAWIO: Direct I/O access
- CAP_AUDIT_CONTROL: Audit system manipulation

Impact:
- False sense of security when using allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
- Privilege escalation still possible through allowed capabilities

Proposed Fix:
Extend the validation to block all dangerous capabilities when allowPrivilegeEscalation is set to false.

I’d love to hear your thoughts! Have you run into situations where `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` didn’t cut it?
Thanks

Kubelet Swap metrics are missing

Kubelet's swap related metrics were introduced in [link] However, these swap-related metrics are missing from `/metrics/resource` endpoint. Only node-level swap usage metrics are visible. The pod-level and container-level swap usage are available from `/stats/summary` endpoint, but no metrics are visible from `/metrics/resource`.

Container-level swap usage `container_swap_usage_bytes` and pod-level swap usage `pod_swap_usage_bytes` metrics should be available from `/metrics/resource` endpoint.

Create a node with swap enabled ([link]

Get the swap metrics `kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node-name>/proxy/metrics/resource"

The node is using ~~cadvisor~~ CRI for resource metrics.

Also happened for kind: [link]

state:
docker credential JSON: validate non UTF-8 characters

Using base64 encoding, it’s possible to include arbitrary data (including non-UTF-8 strings) that can pass Kubernetes validation. While this may be a minor issue within Kubernetes itself and likely not exploitable directly, it could pose a risk to external systems that consume these secrets. If such systems assume UTF-8 encoding, they might be vulnerable to unexpected behavior or exploitation.

The input should be rejected with an "invalid UTF-8" error.

A test case for [link]

kube-scheduler does not schedule these two pods on the same node, following the behavior for pods using hostNetwork ports via a main container.

state:
API can be streamlined: assume same key for some `EnvVarSource`

[link]

All `EnvVarSource` must specify `name` in the parent, but the `ConfigMapKeyRef` and `SecretKeyRef` fields both require a `key` to be specified. [link] introduces another case.

It seems like we could assume the env var's name if the key is not specified. One less line of YAML in many cases.

It would require a feature gate which means a (small) KEP.

Impl is in pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go

state:
Evented PLEG: kubelet panics under host pressure

While testing evented PLEG locally, I encountered an issue where the kubelet panics when pods are created rapidly. The panic produces the following logs:

This is not a typical issue. The root cause appears to be a synchronization problem between goroutine lifecycles and channel lifecycles, resulting in attempts to send data to a closed channel. One possible solution might involve introducing a cancellable context or notifying producers when the channel is closed to prevent sending messages to a closed channel.

kubelet does not panic.

On a node with limited resources (4-core CPU, 8GB RAM), with the EventedPLEG feature gate enabled, rapidly create a large number of pods (exceeding 600).

state:
kubelet_pod_start_duration_seconds Metric Incorrectly Reports Double Pod Count

The kubelet_pod_start_duration_seconds metric appears to be double counting pod creations. During testing in an empty cluster, creating 1 pod resulted in the metric reporting values for 2 pods. After creating a second pod, the metric reported 4 pods.

The metric `kubelet_pod_start_duration_seconds_count` should reflect the actual number of pods created.

Create a Kubernetes cluster, deploy any pod, and check the metrics.

The metric `kubelet_pod_start_duration_seconds_count` should reflect the actual number of pods created.

Create a Kubernetes cluster, deploy any pod, and check the metrics.

Routing determination: node.

state:
Clean up circular dependencies around the kubelet's admitHandlers and the container runtime

Basically, this TODO:

[link]

The reason that we have `AddPodAdmitHandlers` as a separate method for the allocation manager as opposed to just passing in the admit handers into the constructor is because of some circular dependencies:

### shutdown manager and probe manager
- Construction of the [container runtime]([link] depends on the [allocation manager]([link]
- One of the [allocation manager's handlers]([link] depends on the shutdown manager.
- The shutdown manager depends on the [probe manager]([link]
- The probe manager depends on the [container runtime]([link]

potential resolution: it doesn't look like the shutdown manager uses the probe manager for anything, so that dependency in the shutdown manager can be removed, thus removing the dependency cycle.

### shutdown manager and volume manager
- Construction of the container runtime depends on the allocation manager.
- One of the allocation manager's handlers depends on the [shutdown manager].
- The shutdown manager depends on the [volume manager]([link]
- The volume manager depends on the [container runtime]([link]

potential resolution: it doesn't look like the volume manager uses the container runtime for anything, so that dependency in the volume manager can likewise be removed, removing the dependency cycle.

### eviction manager and image manager
- Construction of the [image manager]([link] depends on the container runtime.
- Construction of the container runtime depends on the allocation manager.
- One of the [allocation manager's handlers] depends on the [eviction manager]([link]
- The eviction manager depends on the image manager.

potential resolution: ???

This isn't a huge issue, but in general this a symptom of the kubelet code being filled with bloated and circular dependencies. It makes the code hard to work with. There are probably more that I haven't listed here, but didn't fully dive into it.

state:
DRA resource claim controller: fails to clean up deleted ResourceClaims on startup

* kube-controller-manager is stopped.
* A allocated claim with one pod in ReservedFor is marked as deleted (but not removed yet because of the finalizer).
* That pod gets deleted, terminates and gets removed.
* kube-controller-manager is restarted.

The ResourceClaim controllers logs:

It does not do anything, so the claim remains pending.

This was triggered while working on upgrade/downgrade scenarios.

The ResourceClaim controller should remove the pod from ReservedFor, the allocation, and the finalizer, thus unblocking the removal of the ResourceClaim.

Not easy, needs WIP test.

This is a regression introduced by [link]

The logic here is inverted:
[link]

The correct expression is `deleted := newObj == nil`.

This causes the enqueuing of the claim for processing to get skipped in

[link]

Normally, this gets mitigated by pod removal which also has the desired effect, but in this particular case that removal is never observed - the pod is already gone when the kube-controller-manager starts.

state:
ImageMaximumGCAge's requirement to be less than ImageMinimumGCAge is incorrect

A little background just in case: `ImageMinimumGCAge` options controls after how much time **after the image was first seen** it can be deleted by GC in case of disk pressure:

[link]

`ImageMaximumGCAge` in turn controls how much time **image was unused** before it can be removed:

[link]

There's currently a requirement for `ImageMaximumGCAge` to be less than `ImageMinimumGCAge`:

[link]

I believe this requirement is incorrect, as these two min/max parameters are not closely related as they're counted from different moments. The more specific example when one would want to set max < min is the following situation happening in our production workloads.

We have a multi-container pod with multiple large images. Our hosts are experiencing disk pressure often, so GC tries to clean up the images every time. If the deployment strategy is `RECREATE`, the old pod is removed first when deploying a new version. The individual container's images between sequential deployments usually intersect a lot, so there's no reason to remove and pull these images again until the new pod is created. However, if GC is run between the old pod is removed and the new one is created, it collects the images based on `MinAge` (because it's counted since the first time image appeared, i.e. a week ago and the start of the previous deployment). It makes sense to set a high `MinAge` (more than our usual deployment interval) and a small `MaxAge` (a bit higher than we expect for all images to be pulled). Small `MaxAge` would lead to the leftover images to be removed after the new pod is created, and large `MinAge` (or even to disable this option altogether, which is currently impossible as well) would ensure the GC is not removing images before the new pod is created.

imageMaximumGCAge download /remove loop with CreateContainerConfigError state

Hi,

After setting `imageMaximumGCAge: "168h"` in our clusters we noticed high traffic from one development cluster. This is caused by same images being re-downloaded every 5 minutes.

These images are used in pods currently in `CreateContainerConfigError` state. Would be nice not to have those, but developers tend to leave their configs broken for a while from time to time...

Apparently images are downloaded even if the there is a config error, so they should not be GCd.

Set low `imageMaximumGCAge` and create pod with config error. Download loop should happen after `imageMaximumGCAge` is hit.

After setting `imageMaximumGCAge: "168h"` in our clusters we noticed high traffic from one development cluster. This is caused by same images being re-downloaded every 5 minutes.

These images are used in pods currently in `CreateContainerConfigError` state. Would be nice not to have those, but developers tend to leave their configs broken for a while from time to time...

Apparently images are downloaded even if the there is a config error, so they should not be GCd.

Set low `imageMaximumGCAge` and create pod with config error. Download loop should happen after `imageMaximumGCAge` is hit.

state:
[Pod Level Resources] Pod-level resource validation fails when container-level is set for other resource

When a Kubernetes Pod defines resources.requests at the Pod level, but only specifies a subset of the supported resources requested by its containers (e.g., only cpu at the Pod level, while a container requests memory), Kubernetes' validation implicitly assigns a request of "0" for the unstated resource (e.g., memory) at the Pod level. This "0" value then triggers a validation error because it's less than the actual aggregated request from the containers, even though the user might expect the Pod to implicitly aggregate the container's memory request.

When a user defines resource requests at the container level, Kubernetes already aggregates these requests internally to determine the total resource needs of the Pod. If the Pod.spec.resources.requests field is present, but only specifies a subset of resources (e.g., cpu but not memory), the intuitive expectation is that Kubernetes would implicitly aggregate the memory request from the containers, rather than defaulting the Pod's memory request to 0.

[link] needs to be fixed to compare container aggregates with pod-level values only if pod-level value for that resource is set.

state: main container never starts with restartPolicy: Never and sidecar container has a startupProbe and fails the first attempt There is a bug in `kubelet` `startupProbe` if sidecar container is configured. [link] The worker's decision to continue (return true) or stop (return false) is based only on the pod's restart policy, not the containers (sidecar have restartPolicy:Always) This can lead to a racing condition if the sidecar container fails at the first time and prober incorrectly exits: If sidecar container restarted with no problem at second attempt, startupProbe will never run again. This leads kubelet to think the initContainer never successfully initialized. There is another bug in [link] the probe can possibly get recreated here. However if there are more than one containers has startup probes, and the first container has a running probe, it will skip other containers (because of an early`return`). As a result, reproduction requires at least 2 startup probes. With the example in the "How to reproduce", the `main-container` is stuck in Initializing state.

state: main container never starts with restartPolicy: Never and sidecar container has a startupProbe and fails the first attempt There is a bug in `kubelet` `startupProbe` if sidecar container is configured. [link] The worker's decision to continue (return true) or stop (return false) is based only on the pod's restart policy, not the containers (sidecar have restartPolicy:Always) This can lead to a racing condition if the sidecar container fails at the first time and prober incorrectly exits: If sidecar container restarted with no problem at second attempt, startupProbe will never run again. This leads kubelet to think the initContainer never successfully initialized. There is another bug in [link] the probe can possibly get recreated here. However if there are more than one containers has startup probes, and the first container has a running probe, it will skip other containers (because of an early`return`). As a result, reproduction requires at least 2 startup probes. With the example in the "How to reproduce", the `main-container` is stuck in Initializing state.

state:
[KEP-4680] DRA: Health status is not applied to pods that have already terminated

The DRA health status feature introduced by KEP-4680 does not currently work for pods that have already reached a terminal state (Failed or Succeeded).
E2E testing has revealed a race condition in the Kubelet's current implementation. The sequence is as follows:

1. A pod using a DRA resource runs and its container terminates.
2. The Kubelet immediately calls NodeUnprepareResources to begin garbage collection.
3. The DRA manager (pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go) deletes the ClaimInfo from its cache, severing the link between the pod and the allocated device.
4. A health update from the DRA plugin arrives after this cleanup.
5. The Kubelet's health manager receives the update but can no longer find which pod was using the device, so the update is discarded and the PodStatus is never updated.

This prevents the "post-mortem" troubleshooting use case for batch jobs, which was an intended goal of the KEP.

The `pod.status.allocatedResourcesStatus` field on the terminated pod object should be updated to reflect the health of the device at the time of failure, even if the health report arrives after the pod has stopped running.

This was discovered via an e2e test, which can be reproduced with the following logic:

1. Create a pod with `RestartPolicy: Never` and a command that runs for a short time before exiting, (e.g. sleep 10 && exit 1). Ensure it uses a DRA resource.
2. Wait for the pod to enter the Running phase to confirm the resource was successfully prepared.
3. Wait for the pod to enter the Failed phase.
4. After the pod is Failed, send an Unhealthy status update for its device from the DRA plugin.
5. Observe the pod's status. The allocatedResourcesStatus field is never populated with the unhealthy status.

This issue is being filed to track a known limitation for [KEP-4680: Add Resource Health Status to the Pod Status]([link]

state:
[KEP-4680] DRA: Make device health check timeout configurable

The timeout for marking a DRA device's health as "Unknown" is currently hardcoded to 30 seconds. This should be made configurable.

This is an update/enhancement for the new DRA Device Health feature being introduced by KEP-4680.

As discussed in the review for PR #130606 ([link] a single hardcoded timeout is not ideal for all types of hardware. Different devices (e.g., GPUs, FPGAs, TPUs, storage) may have very different health-reporting characteristics and require different timeout values.

state:
Kubelet shutdown manager not properly initialized due to race condition in systemd-logind configuration reloading

Observed error log
`
kubelet.go:1667] "Failed to start node shutdown manager" err="node shutdown manager was unable to update logind InhibitDelayMaxSec to 30s (ShutdownGracePeriod), current value of InhibitDelayMaxSec (5s) is less than requested ShutdownGracePeriod"
`

And the shutdown inhibitor is not registered to the system so shutdown manager would not be in effect.

The bug seems to be a race condition between systemd-logind config reloading and getting the updated `InhibitDelayMaxSec`. The root cause is the reload command is signaled to systemd-logind with no waiting until the reload is complete.

I am thinking a low cost fix, rather than properly implementing something to get the reload completion signal, is to just backoff wait up to 5 retries to get the new `InhibitDelayUSec` value

Kubelet shutdown manager should work properly

Wrote a program trying to reproduce it

, which had pretty low reproduction rate (`Tested 80500 times, reproduced the bug 1 times/Tested 257500 times, reproduced the bug 4 times`) but on real cases, it should significantly higher because the kubelet is started during OS boot period and a lot of churns on systemd so the logind reload takes more time to take effect.

state:
Kubelet may duplicate `SystemOOM` events via `oom_watcher_linux`

The current logic in [oom_watcher_linux]([link] will duplicate `SystemOOM` events if the ring buffer (`/dev/kmsg`) has not been flushed between restarts of kubelet.

`SystemOOM` events arrive from `cadvisor` over a channel of `OomInstance` objects. `cadvisor` discovers these events by reading the kernel ring buffer via the [kmsgparser]([link] package. The default behaviour of this package is to read from the **beginning** of the ring buffer each time the `OomInstance` object is created. It is likely this behaviour is not expected.

Generating duplicate events may be confusing for operators of clusters if they're auditing SystemOOM events in their cluster. In the current state the number of SystemOOM events reported by kubelet may not reflect the correct count that occurred on the underlying OS. Ideally, the kubelet reports one event for each `SystemOOM` that is encountered and doesn't duplicate events.

Given the following example, a single `SystemOOM` event that occurred on an Ubuntu node running GKE 1.32.

The kubelet picks up this event as intended.

To create duplicate events, we can simply restart the kubelet. There are now 2 events.

Restart kubelet a 3rd time, yields another event.

.. _repeat as desired_ ..

kubelet logs also confirm this is the same event, based on the `OomInstance.TimeOfDeath` field

I logged PR [link] as there are a few consumers of the `oomparser` cadvisor package. These use-cases may be unintentionally double counting OOM events. The change in that PR exposes another constructor that seeks to the end of `/dev/kmsg`, ensuring only new messages arrive since the creation of the instance.

If the current behaviour is not intended and the cdavisor PR is merged, I could log a follow-up PR here to flip to the `NewFromNew()` constructor once the updated deps are pulled in.

The current logic in [oom_watcher_linux]([link] will duplicate `SystemOOM` events if the ring buffer (`/dev/kmsg`) has not been flushed between restarts of kubelet.

`SystemOOM` events arrive from `cadvisor` over a channel of `OomInstance` objects. `cadvisor` discovers these events by reading the kernel ring buffer via the [kmsgparser]([link] package. The default behaviour of this package is to read from the **beginning** of the ring buffer each time the `OomInstance` object is created. It is likely this behaviour is not expected.

Generating duplicate events may be confusing for operators of clusters if they're auditing SystemOOM events in their cluster. In the current state the number of SystemOOM events reported by kubelet may not reflect the correct count that occurred on the underlying OS. Ideally, the kubelet reports one event for each `SystemOOM` that is encountered and doesn't duplicate events.

Given the following example, a single `SystemOOM` event that occurred on an Ubuntu node running GKE 1.32.

The kubelet picks up this event as intended.

To create duplicate events, we can simply restart the kubelet. There are now 2 events.

Restart kubelet a 3rd time, yields another event.

.. _repeat as desired_ ..

kubelet logs also confirm this is the same event, based on the `OomInstance.TimeOfDeath` field

I logged PR [link] as there are a few consumers of the `oomparser` cadvisor package. These use-cases may be unintentionally double counting OOM events. The change in that PR exposes another constructor that seeks to the end of `/dev/kmsg`, ensuring only new messages arrive since the creation of the instance.

If the current behaviour is not intended and the cdavisor PR is merged, I could log a follow-up PR here to flip to the `NewFromNew()` constructor once the updated deps are pulled in.

state:
The pod is in the UnexpectedAdmissionError state.

We found that after the kubelet process restarts, some pods dependent on device plugins may enter the UnexpectedAdmissionError state.
The reason is that when the kubelet restarts, it retrieves the pod list from the apiserver and begins processing the pods. At this point, the device plugin has not yet had the chance to register, which can cause the pods to enter an UnexpectedAdmissionError state. As a result, the containers are killed, and the workload then pulls up a new replica.
Assuming the service has only two replicas, the aforementioned reasons may lead to the pod being rebuilt, during which the service will be interrupted.

Containers should not exit due to kubelet restarts.

Configure the pod to depend on the device plugin and restart kubelet.

state:
Pod crashloop backoff isn't entered until after the first restart

While working on a crashloop backoff fix, I noticed that containers are often restarted immediately when they first crash, rather than being delayed by the appropriate backoff time. Essentially, containers have to crash twice before a backoff is applied.

When a pod first runs, [doBackOff]([link] is called but exits early because the container status is not “exited”. The container then starts and crashes, with the restart count at 0.

In the next sync loop, `doBackOff` is called again and returns false because no entry exists from the previous crash (because of the early exit). The backoff tracker adds an entry due to the call to `backOff.Next()` before returning. The container is restarted with a restart count of 1 and crashes a second time.

In the third loop, `doBackOff` properly reports the backoff duration and the pod is enqueued.

state:
DRA Extended Resource: support nodes where device plugin was uninstalled

[deployDevicePlugin]([link] leaks the extended resource example.com/resource in node's status.Allocatable/Capacity. This causes conflicts for multiple tests using the extended resource in the same cluster.

deployDevicePlugin does not leak the example.com/resource in node's status.Allocatable/Capacity, after the test deploying the device plugin completes, the example.com/resource should be cleaned up from node's status.Allocatalbe/Capacity.

test/dra/dra.go has tests calling deployDevicePlugin, run the test would be able to reproduce the problem.

state:
Race condition in kubelet's PodCertsManager might lead to memory leaks

Introduced in [link] and only observable after enabling the `PodCertificateRequest` feature gate.

When [link] gets called, it queues PCRs for a given pod to be handled by a `podcertificate.Manager` instance.

However, if the queue keys for these PCRs get async-processed before [link] is called, the `podcertificate.Manager` will never again attempt to clear its internal state for these PCRs as kept in its `Manager.credStore` map.

Kubelet's state gets cleaned for a given pod when the pod is removed.

Write a unit test that runs [link] expose the `podcertificate.Manager{}.credStore` variable, and observe what happens to the `credStore` variable when a cached PCR's state is supposed to get removed. Run a couple hundred times to make sure the race condition appears.

Discussed at [link]

typo in the error message for enableSystemLogQuery feature gate validation

There is a typo in the error message generated when the NodeLogQuery feature gate is required for enableSystemLogQuery in pkg/kubelet/apis/config/validation/validation.go. The code currently appends the following error message:

allErrors = append(allErrors, fmt.Errorf("invalid configuration: NodeLogQuery feature gate is required for enableSystemLogHandler"))

However, it should state "enableSystemLogQuery" instead of "enableSystemLogHandler" to accurately reflect the configuration option being validated.

The error message should state: "invalid configuration: NodeLogQuery feature gate is required for enableSystemLogQuery" to match the configuration option being checked.

Trigger Kubelet configuration validation with enableSystemLogQuery set to true but without enabling the NodeLogQuery feature gate.

In the kubelet configuration:
- disable NodeLogQuery feature gate; i.e. "NodeLogQuery": false
- enable the enableSystemLogQuery flag; ie. enableSystemLogQuery: true

Observe the error message output.

state:
typo in the error message for enableSystemLogQuery feature gate validation

There is a typo in the error message generated when the NodeLogQuery feature gate is required for enableSystemLogQuery in pkg/kubelet/apis/config/validation/validation.go. The code currently appends the following error message:

allErrors = append(allErrors, fmt.Errorf("invalid configuration: NodeLogQuery feature gate is required for enableSystemLogHandler"))

However, it should state "enableSystemLogQuery" instead of "enableSystemLogHandler" to accurately reflect the configuration option being validated.

The error message should state: "invalid configuration: NodeLogQuery feature gate is required for enableSystemLogQuery" to match the configuration option being checked.

Trigger Kubelet configuration validation with enableSystemLogQuery set to true but without enabling the NodeLogQuery feature gate.

In the kubelet configuration:
- disable NodeLogQuery feature gate; i.e. "NodeLogQuery": false
- enable the enableSystemLogQuery flag; ie. enableSystemLogQuery: true

Observe the error message output.

state:
Pods rejected by kubelet admission control enter 'ContainerStatusUnknown' state after kubelet restart

In scenarios where kubelet [rejects]([link] a pod via its own admission control (`canAdmitPod`), for instance-

- When the NodeResourcesFit filter is disabled in kube-scheduler, or when a pod is directly created with a spec.nodeName (ensuring the scheduler does not validate pod resource requests against a node's capacity) AND the pod's requests exceed the node's available capacity. In this case, kubelet will reject the pod, eg. with the reason 'OutOfCpu'.

- When pods are stuck pending due to taints on a node, and the taint is removed, there appears to be a race between kube-scheduler placing the pod on the node and kubelet detecting the updated taints on the node (which makes sense, they are both presumably backed by independent watches). In this case, kubelet will reject the pod with the 'TaintToleration' reason. This is a lot harder to reproduce though, because it's racey.

This leaves the pod with a status that has an overall failed phase but no containerStatuses.

After a kubelet restart (Which can be done for a few reasons, eg. handling in-place node resize, or a node reboot.), these pods transition into a ContainerStatusUnknown state.

where the overall status now has additional conditions for last probe time, container statuses showing container status unknown, etc.

A similar issue can also be reproduced when using init containers

I'm not sure if this is by design, but I would expect such rejected pods to remain in an OutOfCpu/TaintsToleration failure state. No containers were ever started as the pod was rejected in admission control. The error _sounds_ like something went missing from the container runtime, but that did not happen, of course.

state:
Kubelet rejects pod with "NodeAffinity failed" due to stale informer data

This issue is similar to [link] and [link]

We have a controller that adds labels to a node after it starts up. It looks like there are cases where the scheduler is able to see the new node labels and schedule a pod, but the kubelet somehow doesn't see the new labels - it has stale data in its informer cache. Whatever the reason for the stale data, the result is that the kubelet rejects the pod with "NodeAffinity failed".

Kubelet to be able to detect the new node labels and not reject the pod.

The only reason that we need to keep the node affinity / node selector check in the kubelet is in case someone sets `nodeName` directly on the pod, so that it does not go through the scheduler, so we can't just remove enforcement on the node level.

The short-term fix would be for the kubelet to synchronously fetch the node object when (and only when) it sees these "NodeAffinity failed" errors and try again. To ensure we do not introduce additional heavy traffic when there many pods being scheduled at once, we will have to keep a new cache, separate from the informer cache. The logic would be like:
- Read the node object from the informer
- If we get a NodeAffinity failed error, read the node object from our new cache
- If we still get a NodeAffinity failed error, fetch the node object synchronously from the api server
The cache should be updated whenever we see a node object that is newer than the one we are currently storing - this can come from either the informer or from the synchronous fetch.

Long term, maybe we can re-consider the flow for `nodeName`, or leverage something like [kubelet synchronous admission]([link] to keep the scheduler and kubelet coordinated. There are also some more general discussions about what to do when informer data is stale, maybe the outcomes there can help here.

state:
Kubelet crashes on EKS Windows Node when compiler optimizations enabled

Hi all,

I am seeing Kubelet crashing on some Windows nodes when trying to deploy pods with EBS volumes attached. the crash seems to only happen when kubelet is built with _compiler optimizations_ flags turned on. If I disable compiler optimization flag ` -gcflags="-N -l"`, I can no longer reproduce the crash.

Kubelet should not crash, regardless of compiler optimization settings.

1. Create a windows node with `m7i.large` instanceType and `WindowsServer2022FullContainer` amiFamily
2. Create a Windows storage class
3. Create a PVC
4. Deploy a Windows pod with persistent volume:

Currently I am suspecting that the crash is related to this specific line which appears in the crash dump:
[link]

***
1. `log()` function calls `fmt.Sprintf()` to format the `spec` parameter
2. `spec` is a `*volume.Spec` containing a PersistentVolume object
3. `PersistentVolume.String()` method is called (generated protobuf code)
4. This calls `PersistentVolumeStatus.String()` which includes:
go
LastPhaseTransitionTime: + strings.Replace(fmt.Sprintf("%v", this.LastPhaseTransitionTime), "Time", "v1.Time", 1) + ,,

5. LastPhaseTransitionTime is a *metav1.Time (pointer to metav1.Time)
6. When fmt.Sprintf("%v", this.LastPhaseTransitionTime)
is called on a nil pointer, Go attempts to call the String() method
7. metav1.Time embeds time.Time, and time.Time.String() has a value receiver: func (t Time) String()

8. To call this method, Go tries to dereference the nil *metav1.Time pointer, causing a panic

**Windows-specific behavior:**
- fmt.Sprintf normally recovers from panics during string formatting
- However, on Windows with compiler optimizations enabled, sometimes this panic recovery fails
- The panic escalates to runtime.sigpanic and eventually runtime.throw
- **Workaround:** Changing the log statement to print spec.Name instead of the full spec
object avoids the crash

**Evidence supporting this theory:**
1.

I am seeing Kubelet crashing on some Windows nodes when trying to deploy pods with EBS volumes attached. the crash seems to only happen when kubelet is built with _compiler optimizations_ flags turned on. If I disable compiler optimization flag ` -gcflags="-N -l"`, I can no longer reproduce the crash.

Kubelet should not crash, regardless of compiler optimization settings.

1. Create a windows node with `m7i.large` instanceType and `WindowsServer2022FullContainer` amiFamily
2. Create a Windows storage class
3. Create a PVC
4. Deploy a Windows pod with persistent volume:

Currently I am suspecting that the crash is related to this specific line which appears in the crash dump:
[link]

***
1. `log()` function calls `fmt.Sprintf()` to format the `spec` parameter
2. `spec` is a `*volume.Spec` containing a PersistentVolume object
3. `PersistentVolume.String()` method is called (generated protobuf code)
4. This calls `PersistentVolumeStatus.String()` which includes:
go
LastPhaseTransitionTime: + strings.Replace(fmt.Sprintf("%v", this.LastPhaseTransitionTime), "Time", "v1.Time", 1) + ,,

5. LastPhaseTransitionTime is a *metav1.Time (pointer to metav1.Time)
6. When fmt.Sprintf("%v", this.LastPhaseTransitionTime)
is called on a nil pointer, Go attempts to call the String() method
7. metav1.Time embeds time.Time, and time.Time.String() has a value receiver: func (t Time) String()

8. To call this method, Go tries to dereference the nil *metav1.Time pointer, causing a panic

**Windows-specific behavior:**
- fmt.Sprintf normally recovers from panics during string formatting
- However, on Windows with compiler optimizations enabled, sometimes this panic recovery fails
- The panic escalates to runtime.sigpanic and eventually runtime.throw
- **Workaround:** Changing the log statement to print spec.Name instead of the full spec
object avoids the crash

Add Verbose Logging to net/http for Egress Auditing and Rename probe/http/http.go

This proposal includes two related changes to improve egress traffic visibility from core Kubernetes components and to refine logging controls:

Add Verbose Logging to staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/net/http.go: Introduce new klog V-level logs to provide visibility into outbound HTTP requests and how they are handled by proxy settings.

A V(5) log will be added to record requests that are proxied (i.e., not matching the NO_PROXY environment variable). This helps identify traffic that would be blocked in a restricted environment.

A V(6) log will be added to record requests that are not proxied (i.e., explicitly allowed via NO_PROXY). This helps verify that allowlist rules are functioning as expected.

Rename pkg/probe/http/http.go to pkg/probe/http/http_prober.go: Rename this file to prevent a logging conflict with the file mentioned above, which is the actual target for our enhanced logging.

Downstream distributions of Kubernetes, such as GKE, are implementing security features to strictly control and block all egress traffic originating from the kube-apiserver. A core part of this mechanism involves using HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY environment variables to route traffic through a controlled gateway or a "blackhole" proxy, while using a NO_PROXY variable to allowlist essential cluster endpoints.

To safely roll out such a feature, it is critical to have a data-driven way to discover and audit all outbound requests made by the kube-apiserver and other components. This allows operators to build a comprehensive NO_PROXY allowlist and ensure no critical functions are broken. The proposed verbose logging in net/http.go provides this essential visibility.

The second change—renaming pkg/probe/http/http.go—is necessary to avoid unintended log spam.

state: Incorrect PodMemory usage after container termination PodMemory metric continued to be available for few minutes after pod was removed from the node. PodMemory metric should have been removed from the old pod instance as soon as new pod was destroyed or new pod was created. From initial understanding, kubelet/cAdvisor housekeepingInterval seems to be the static interval at which housekeeping should occur. If allowDynamicHousekeeping is enabled, cAdvisor determines the actual housekeeping interval based on houseKeepingInterval and maxHousekeepingInterval as shown in [manager/container.go#L481C1-L505C2]([link] with some jitter. Need to understand the behaviour of [statsCacheDuration]([link] and maxHousekeepingInterval when kubelet is restarted. Does kubelet dump the cache data to disk before the package upgrade? Moreover, since these maintenance are happening for kubelet upgrades, does time to upgrade and bootstrap kubelet could lead to additional delay in housekeeping. One more weird observation I could find is, node uuid has changed twice, once while upgrading at 11 AM(which is relevant for this issue) and then again at 2 PM(which is unrelated).

PodMemory metric should have been removed from the old pod instance as soon as new pod was destroyed or new pod was created. From initial understanding, kubelet/cAdvisor housekeepingInterval seems to be the static interval at which housekeeping should occur. If allowDynamicHousekeeping is enabled, cAdvisor determines the actual housekeeping interval based on houseKeepingInterval and maxHousekeepingInterval as shown in [manager/container.go#L481C1-L505C2]([link] with some jitter. Need to understand the behaviour of [statsCacheDuration]([link] and maxHousekeepingInterval when kubelet is restarted. Does kubelet dump the cache data to disk before the package upgrade? Moreover, since these maintenance are happening for kubelet upgrades, does time to upgrade and bootstrap kubelet could lead to additional delay in housekeeping. One more weird observation I could find is, node uuid has changed twice, once while upgrading at 11 AM(which is relevant for this issue) and then again at 2 PM(which is unrelated).

state:
DRA consumable capacity failed to allocate the same device once device consumes counterSet

The device that consumed counterSet is skipped if the counter is not left enough even it was selected and allowMultipleAllocations is set.

The reason is that the checkAvailableCounters is called and return false as it is selected once before the capacity will be checked.

[link]

The device which is once consumed capacity from the counterSet should be able to allocated if there is enough capacity left for another request. Meaning that the alloc.checkAvailableCounters should be skipped - do not check, do not consume.

counterSet0: 4
device1 (allowMultipleAllocations): consume 3 from counterSet0
device2 (allowMultipleAllocations): consume 4 from counterSet0

req0: request capacity 1
req1: request capacity 1

req0 can get device 1 but req1 is failed to get the same device

state:
No longer testing CgroupV1 with fedora-coreos images

Fedora CoreOS is default booting up as CgroupV2 even though it is instructed to use CgropuV1 in yaml: `SYSTEMD_CGROUP_ENABLE_LEGACY_FORCE=1`

- when running the ignition file, the template does not provision a cgroupv1 node; not sure why
- initial investigation from: [link]

Expecting the `"Summary API [NodeConformance] when querying /stats/summary under pressure [Feature:KubeletPSI] [Serial] should report Memory pressure in PSI metrics"` to be skipped since it is intended for cgroupv2 and we are supposedly running a cgroupv1 node.
The test is running because the fedora coreos image defaults to cgroupv2.

Recreate the node with the same image:
example:

and running this command will confirm it is a cgroupv2 node: `ls /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.controllers`

@user has more insights as well!

state:
Clean up features for SIG Node e2e tests

We use features to indicate the environment that is "not standard" for e2e tests - i.e. requires extra configuration beyond feature gates.

This is uber issue to review sig-node features and clean them up:

1. If the Feature is used to indicate just a "category" of tests - remove it
2. If the Feature is used when FeatureGate must be used - replace with the FeatureGate
3. If the Feature truly indicate a special environment, make sure it is well documented and corresponding test lanes are marked appropriately

Once we clear things up we may decide to pass the `Feature` as an argument for the test lane (similar to [link] idea) and have more automated validation that the test requiring the Feature are only run in the test lane implementing this special environment

state:
Incorrect pod phase transition after node reboot with init containers

A Pod with multiple init containers does not transition to the correct phase after a Node restart. I came across this issue while investigating the flaky test in [link] For more information, see [link]

The Pod phase is determined based on the ContainerStatus state of regular init containers, restartable init containers, and regular containers. For example, if there are any regular or restartable init containers that haven’t started yet, the Pod phase is considered Pending.

When a Node reboots, all containers in the Pod are restarted. In this case, the previous ContainerStatus state is preserved until the container actually restarts. As a result, if multiple init containers exist, the Pod phase incorrectly transitions to Running right after the first init container completes.

Here’s a rough timeline of what happens after a Node reboot:

1. Node reboots
1. Since all containers are stopped, if restartPolicy=Always, the Pod is considered Running because containers are being restarted
[link]
1. While a regular init container is running, the Pod phase becomes Pending
[link]
1. Once the regular init container exits, we fall back to step 2 and the Pod phase becomes Running again1. This flip-flop continues for each regular/restartable init container (Pending while running, Running once exited)

Ideally, the Pod should remain in Pending until the regular containers have started (i.e. `podHasInitialized=true`). But we’ll need to carefully check that fixing this doesn’t break other scenarios outside of Node reboots.

You can reproduce this issue by starting a Pod with multiple init containers similar to this Node E2E test case. And then deleting the PodSandbox to simulate a Node reboot.

[link]

state:
High-throughput container logs cause kubelet log rotation to hang, leading to unbounded 0.log growth (v1.27+ timestamp-based rotation)

In Kubernetes clusters running v1.27+, the new timestamp-based container log rotation mechanism (0.log.YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS) fails to rotate logs for high-throughput containers (e.g., >50 MB/s). The 0.log file grows indefinitely (observed >12 GiB), even though containerLogMaxSize is set (e.g., 100Mi).

Kubelet’s log shows repeated "Adding new entry to the queue for processing" every containerLogMonitorInterval seconds, but no "rotateLog" or "rotateLog finished" logs for the affected container — indicating the rotation task never gets executed.

log config :
containerLogMaxSize: 100Mi
containerLogMaxFiles: 5
containerLogMonitorInterval: 1s
containerLogMaxWorkers: 10

The kubelet should properly rotate container logs even under high-throughput logging workloads — specifically, the log rotation mechanism should not hang or fail to trigger when a container generates logs at a high rate. The 0.log file should be rotated once it exceeds containerLogMaxSize, preventing unbounded disk usage.

Kubelet’s log shows repeated "Adding new entry to the queue for processing" every containerLogMonitorInterval seconds, but no "rotateLog" or "rotateLog finished" logs for the affected container — indicating the rotation task never gets executed.

state:
preStop sleep continues after PID 1 exits

I've configured the podSpec of a Job to include a preStop sleep lifecycle hook. If the Pod is asked to terminate before it completes, the preStop sleep begins and runs for its full duration - even if the Pod completes its processing and PID 1 exits before the preStop sleep is complete. The Pod remains in "Terminating" and the Job remains in "Running" state until the preStop sleep finishes, which delays the completion of the Job.

I expect the preStop sleep to end when PID 1 in the Pod exits. The Job should be marked as complete at that time and the Pod should finish terminating. This is the behavior when a preStop exec is used to run the sleep command in the container's shell.

Define a Job with a preStop sleep lifecycle hook:

Apply the manifest and then delete the resulting Pod. Observe that the Pod is now in "Terminating" state. The preStop sleep will have begun.

After 60 seconds the Pod should complete but instead it remains in Terminating state and the Job shows 0 completions. Only after 2 minutes has elapsed (from the time the `delete` command was issued) does the Pod finish terminating and the Job shows a completion.

This kind of configuration is useful to ensure that batch jobs run to completion even if they are asked to terminate for whatever reason (maintenance, preemption, autoscaler consolidation, etc.). The fact that the Job takes longer to complete when the Pod is asked to terminate is problematic when timely completion of the Job is desired. Imagine that the Job takes an hour instead of a minute and so the prestop sleep is set to 3600. Then imagine that the Pod is asked to terminate at minute 59. The duration of the Job will now be 119 minutes instead of 60.

Using a preStop exec to run /bin/sleep produces the expected behavior where the Pod finishes terminating and the Job shows as complete when PID 1 in the container exits.

state:
preStop sleep continues after PID 1 exits

I've configured the podSpec of a Job to include a preStop sleep lifecycle hook. If the Pod is asked to terminate before it completes, the preStop sleep begins and runs for its full duration - even if the Pod completes its processing and PID 1 exits before the preStop sleep is complete. The Pod remains in "Terminating" and the Job remains in "Running" state until the preStop sleep finishes, which delays the completion of the Job.

I expect the preStop sleep to end when PID 1 in the Pod exits. The Job should be marked as complete at that time and the Pod should finish terminating. This is the behavior when a preStop exec is used to run the sleep command in the container's shell.

Define a Job with a preStop sleep lifecycle hook:

Apply the manifest and then delete the resulting Pod. Observe that the Pod is now in "Terminating" state. The preStop sleep will have begun.

After 60 seconds the Pod should complete but instead it remains in Terminating state and the Job shows 0 completions. Only after 2 minutes has elapsed (from the time the `delete` command was issued) does the Pod finish terminating and the Job shows a completion.

This kind of configuration is useful to ensure that batch jobs run to completion even if they are asked to terminate for whatever reason (maintenance, preemption, autoscaler consolidation, etc.). The fact that the Job takes longer to complete when the Pod is asked to terminate is problematic when timely completion of the Job is desired. Imagine that the Job takes an hour instead of a minute and so the prestop sleep is set to 3600. Then imagine that the Pod is asked to terminate at minute 59. The duration of the Job will now be 119 minutes instead of 60.

Using a preStop exec to run /bin/sleep produces the expected behavior where the Pod finishes terminating and the Job shows as complete when PID 1 in the container exits.

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.
