state:
Static Memory Manager doesn't verify OS reported available huge pages during pod admission

Hi there,

We have configured the static memory manager to enable numa aware scheduling of our Guaranteed QoS pods. We run various workloads on an m6id.32xlarge 2 numa node system, which accepts both Guaranteed and non Guaranteed QoS pods. These pods run Java based applications which in turn are configured to use huge pages.

We have noticed an issue that once the pod was scheduled, the JVM was not able to start as it was not able to reserve enough memory (8GB). The pod was configured with the following resource limits:

Upon inspection of the node, we noticed that one of the numa nodes are very short on available huge pages:

which happens to be where this pod was assigned to.

When we looked at what the memory controller thought as free memory is, we found that its much more than what the OS is reporting as free:

I am no expert in this space but with a quick inspection of the memory controller code it looks like it assumes all pods on the node are running in Guarnateed QoS, it calculates what the free HP utilisation should be based on those but it doesn't take into account any best effort/burstable pods which can also use up huge pages, resulting in the startup failure we have seen.

At least the memory controller should look at what the OS is reporting as free memory and reject the pod admission/suggest an alternative numa node if the memory requirements at the time can't be satisfied with the amount of free memory available on the numa node. Also it could consider evicting best effort/burstable pods to free up more memory on a given numa node.

Given the following kubelet args:

on a 2 numa node system, schedule 2 pods onto said node, one with Burstable and another one with Guaranteed QoS. Both apps should reserve the pod's limits worth of huge pages on start Expect:

state:
PodReadyToStartContainers condition gets flipped to true after image pull.

According to documentation [link]

The PodReadyToStartContainers condition is set to True by the kubelet after the successful completion of sandbox creation and network configuration for the Pod by the runtime plugin. The kubelet can start pulling container images and create containers after PodReadyToStartContainers condition has been set to True.

What I am observing is that kubelet is flipping this condition to true after application container image is pulled.
Also noticed kubelet patched pod with pod ip after image pull.

PodReadyToStartContainers to flip to true as as soon as network ip is assigned and containerd sets up the sand box. To set up the sandbox, AFAIK containerd only needs pause container. It flips condition to ready here [link]

Created docker image 3.5Gb large.

pod yaml

Pull this image and watch for pod events and podcontainerready status.

state:
No share ID in DRA kubelet plugin's API

kubelet plugin API does not support ShareID information. The ShareID is an additional identifier to the device name which may be generated by DRAConsumableCapacity feature ( that is introduced in [link]

The DRA driver which refers to this API for preparing resource needs to pass ShareID to CDI spec's device ID. Otherwise, the same node will fail to create a container according to the duplicate ID.

Pods can be successfully created when sharing the same device with DRAConsumableCapacity.

Enable DRAConsumableCapacity feature, Enable DRA driver with allowMultipleAllocations device, Create two pods allocating the same device.

Without the change to k/k, a driver can have a workaround which wrap the plugin API appending with shareID and use it as a PreparedDevice.

From

to

implemented code: [link]

However, it looks cleaner when we do that in the provided API.
The change needs at driver is only extending the CDI id with share id if not nil: [link]

state:
A potential goroutine leak in pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/operationexecutor/operation_executor_test.go

If the `time.After` case is selected before the `case <-ch:`
[link]
which leads to the ch <- nil below get blocked, results in a goroutine leak.
[link]

If the `time.After` case is selected before the `case <-ch:`, the ch <- nil doesn't get blocked either.

1.Set time.After(5 * time.Second) to time.After(time.Millisecond * 100)
2.Add time.Sleep(time.Millisecond * 200) before the `ch <- nil`
[link]
The two steps make the time.After happen before the `case <-ch:`.
3.Using goleak to detect the goroutine leak in the test function
[link]

The error report is as follows,

How to fix the bug:
[link]
Change the unbufferd channel to a buffered channel. So that the `ch <- nil` can't get blocked in any case.
`make(chan interface{}, 1)`

Almost everywhere we check whether a pod has pod level resources (PLRs) we don't differentiate between nil and empty PLRs. For example:

[link]

However, in `ComputePodQOS` we don't make this distinction:

[link]

This could lead to some weird situations where you have a best-effort pod running with resources specified. For example:

I'm not sure exactly what the implications of this are, but since it breaks some fundamental assumptions, it's probably not good.

What was the reason for ignoring empty pod level resources?

We'll need to be careful about backwards compatibility when fixing this.

state:
Concurrent map write error when creating a pod with empty volumes

I enabled the `LocalStorageCapacityIsolationFSQuotaMonitoring` feature gate.
Creating and deleting pods with an emptyDir simultaneously causes a fatal error in the kubelet, as shown below.

It seems that `supportsQuotasLock` is not set before deleting element in `supportsQuotasMap`, and the latest version of kubelet hasn't fixed this issue either.

no panic of kubelet

Frequently creating and deleting pods with multiple emptyDir volumes causes the issue.
Run the script below, and it will reproduce the panic within a few hours.

[fsquota.tar.gz]([link]

Concurrent map write error when creating a pod with empty volumes

I enabled the `LocalStorageCapacityIsolationFSQuotaMonitoring` feature gate.
Creating and deleting pods with an emptyDir simultaneously causes a fatal error in the kubelet, as shown below.

It seems that `supportsQuotasLock` is not set before deleting element in `supportsQuotasMap`, and the latest version of kubelet hasn't fixed this issue either.

no panic of kubelet

Frequently creating and deleting pods with multiple emptyDir volumes causes the issue.
Run the script below, and it will reproduce the panic within a few hours.

[fsquota.tar.gz]([link]

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.

state:
[InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Deferred resizes can prevent other pods from being scheduled / resized

When the kubelet is making a decision about whether a new resize can be allocated, or the scheduler is scheduling a new pod, it uses max(spec, allocated, actual) of pods to determine how much resources they are using.

This means that if a resize comes in that is too large, and ends up deferred, from the node's perspective we are already "committed" to those resources. That means a pending resize can prevent new smaller pods from being scheduled to this node, or other smaller resizes from succeeding, even though there may be space that is available.

Additionally, when `describe`ing the node, a deferred resize causes the node to appear overcommitted:

The behavior is confusing, but I'm on the fence about whether it is incorrect. If we change the behavior, it could lead to smaller resizes generally being favored while larger resizes starve.

With the resize allocation decision with the kubelet, I'm not sure if there is a good alternative without introducing a race condition. But if we consider moving the allocation decision to the scheduler, would it then be sufficient to just look at max(allocated, actual) when making fit decisions?

This issue was brought to me by @user from VPA, opening an issue to capture thoughts and discussions.

state:
failing device-plugin health checks causing kubelet SIGABRT by systemd watchdog during initialization.

We have Kubelet, version 1.34, running in a systemd service, configured to expect watchdog updates atleast every 20 seconds.

If the updateRuntimeUp function does not run to completion within this deadline, it causes the `device-plugin` health check to fail, causing watchdog updates to not be sent to systemd, which causes kubelet to crash-loop.

In our case, the updateRuntimeUp function was blocked on [link]

The device-plugin health check is failing because device manager service is initialized, but the device-plugin start is blocked by the delayed updateRuntimeUp.

device-plugin health check should not be expected to pass until kubelet is fully initialized?

run kubelet with the recommended watchdog timeout of ~15 seconds, and cause updateRuntimeUp to be blocked on first start.

state:
Kubelet admission check includes rejected pods in resource accounting, causing subsequent pods to be incorrectly rejected

The kubelet has a race condition in pod admission logic where rejected pods pollute the resource accounting for subsequent pod admissions.

From Openshift CI logs:
- Pod 1 (pod-out-of-cpu) requested 1000000000000000 millicores (intentionally absurd for testing)
- Rejected at 03:12:06.086 with used: 759 millicores
- Pod 2 (resize-test-kngwb) requested 20 millicores
- Rejected at 03:12:06.220 (134ms later) with used: 1000000000000759 millicores
- This is exactly: 1000000000000000 + 759

The rejected Pod 1's CPU request was incorrectly included in the "used" calculation for Pod 2.

From kubelet logs (worker-2):

CI Run: [link]

Failed Test:
[sig-node] Pod InPlace Resize Container [FeatureGate:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] [Beta]

Rejected pods should not affect resource accounting for subsequent pod admission checks

We have observed this intermittently in Openshift CI.

state:
Creating a Service without Name creates an invalid IPAddress

When creating k8s Service without name it tries to create an invalid IPAddress.

This is because the Service apiserver registry tries to allocate the ClusterIP, if not set, before the object name has been validated.

We could/should validate that the IPAddress object we are going to be create is correct, and fail fast avoiding the penalty of failing an API request, something like

We should also add an integration test and corresponding unit test.

When you have multiple runtime OCI runtime handlers configured, the list returned by the CRI runtime may not always be in same order, because they might be interesting over a map internally. If the returned order changes, then this causes unnecessary update to the node object even though actual list of runtime handlers is same as earlier (but with different order)

Unless the actual runtime handlers change, there should not be an update to node CR.

Have large list of runtime handlers like this, and you would see the order would change everytime you query it,

Note that, containerd ensures the [ordering of the runtime handlers]([link] so this bug doesn't really affect containerd. But CRI-O on the other hand, [iterates over a map]([link] causing this issue.

Initially I considered fixing it in CRI-O, but then IMO it won't be a bad idea to have this defensive code in the kubelet as well, so it doesn't rely on CRI runtimes to do the right thing, especially if CRI API doesn't explicitly mandate that the list of handlers need to be sorted. So this will safeguard kubelet against any future CRI runtimes as well who may not send the sorted list.

state:
kubelet TopologyManager Stalls on Large NUMA Systems (e.g. Nvidia GB200 Compute Tray with 34 NUMA nodes)

When scheduling a pod (e.g. KubeVirt virt-launcher pod) that requests a PCI device on a very large NUMA system, kubelet’s TopologyManager never finishes computing topology hints and the pod is effectively stuck in admission:

- The pod is scheduled to the node.
- kubelet never reaches the device Allocate call for the requested resource.
- From a higher-level consumer (KubeVirt in our case), the virt-launcher pod stays in Pending and the VM remains in Starting with Ready = False.
- kubelet is responsive, but many goroutines are stuck in topology hint generation.

In our environment this manifests as:

- KubeVirt VM with a hostDevice (GPU, InfiniBand or NVMe) never transitions to Running, even though the node has the capacity and the device is free.
- Disabling TopologyManager or constraining the NUMA fan-out immediately lets the VM start

kubelet should compute topology hints in bounded time, even on systems with many NUMA nodes (in a case GB200 with 34 NUMA nodes where only 2 NUMA nodes have CPUs, the rest are for HBM/NVLink), and call device-plugin Allocate so that pods/VMs using PCI host devices can start.

## High-level repro:
1. Use a host with a large NUMA topology
Example: Nvidia GB200-class system with 34 NUMA nodes visible to the OS.

2. Run Kubernetes with kubelet configured roughly as follows:

3. Deploy a device plugin that:
- Advertises a PCI resource (e.g. GPU, InfiniBand or NVMe) as a kubelet device resource.
- Exposes the device with topology information referencing many NUMA nodes (up to 34 in our case).

4. Create a Pod
Requests one unit of that device resource.
Uses Guaranteed QoS (requests == limits for CPU/memory) so that TopologyManager participates fully.

5. Observe
- The pod is scheduled to the node.
- kubelet never calls Allocate on the device plugin for that resource.
- The pod stays in Pending indefinitely.

state:
kubelet TopologyManager Stalls on Large NUMA Systems (e.g. Nvidia GB200 Compute Tray with 34 NUMA nodes)

When scheduling a pod (e.g. KubeVirt virt-launcher pod) that requests a PCI device on a very large NUMA system, kubelet’s TopologyManager never finishes computing topology hints and the pod is effectively stuck in admission:

- The pod is scheduled to the node.
- kubelet never reaches the device Allocate call for the requested resource.
- From a higher-level consumer (KubeVirt in our case), the virt-launcher pod stays in Pending and the VM remains in Starting with Ready = False.
- kubelet is responsive, but many goroutines are stuck in topology hint generation.

In our environment this manifests as:

- KubeVirt VM with a hostDevice (GPU, InfiniBand or NVMe) never transitions to Running, even though the node has the capacity and the device is free.
- Disabling TopologyManager or constraining the NUMA fan-out immediately lets the VM start

kubelet should compute topology hints in bounded time, even on systems with many NUMA nodes (in a case GB200 with 34 NUMA nodes where only 2 NUMA nodes have CPUs, the rest are for HBM/NVLink), and call device-plugin Allocate so that pods/VMs using PCI host devices can start.

## High-level repro:
1. Use a host with a large NUMA topology
Example: Nvidia GB200-class system with 34 NUMA nodes visible to the OS.

2. Run Kubernetes with kubelet configured roughly as follows:

3. Deploy a device plugin that:
- Advertises a PCI resource (e.g. GPU, InfiniBand or NVMe) as a kubelet device resource.
- Exposes the device with topology information referencing many NUMA nodes (up to 34 in our case).

4. Create a Pod
Requests one unit of that device resource.
Uses Guaranteed QoS (requests == limits for CPU/memory) so that TopologyManager participates fully.

5. Observe
- The pod is scheduled to the node.
- kubelet never calls Allocate on the device plugin for that resource.
- The pod stays in Pending indefinitely.

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: a bug.

In this [OpenShift CI run]([link] the upstream `[sig-node] Lifecycle sleep action zero value when create a pod with lifecycle hook using sleep action with a duration of zero seconds prestop hook using sleep action with zero duration` test failed because SyncTerminatedPod timed out. The kubelet logs shows:

The systemd journal reveals that the slice was actually removed successfully ~30 seconds before the kubelet timeout:

This shows that systemd completed the slice removal at 21:18:39, but kubelet still timed out at 21:19:08 (exactly ~30 seconds later). The timeout occurred because the kubelet goroutine that initiated the removal never received the D-Bus completion signal.

Pod deletion should complete promptly after containers terminate, without a 30-second timeout.

### How can we reproduce it? (as minimally and precisely as possible)

1. Create a cluster with cgroupsPerQOS enabled (default)
2. Run a workload that creates and deletes many pods rapidly
3. Observe that some pods take 30+ seconds to fully terminate

The race is more likely to occur when:
- Multiple pods are being terminated simultaneously
- The orphaned pod cgroup cleanup housekeeping runs during pod termination

#### Root Cause

There is a race condition between two code paths that call `pcm.Destroy()` on the same pod cgroup:

1. **`SyncTerminatedPod`** - [pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go]([link]

2. **`cleanupOrphanedPodCgroups`** - [pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go]([link]

Both paths can run concurrently for the same pod cgroup. The `Destroy()` method calls systemd's `StopUnit` via D-Bus using `go-systemd`.

#### Why the 30-second timeout occurs

When `StopUnitContext` is called, the `go-systemd` library:

1. Sends a D-Bus method call to systemd's `StopUnit`
2. Systemd returns a **job path** (e.g., `/org/freedesktop/systemd1/job/12345`)
3.

ImageVolume: Empty image.reference in Pod templates passes API validation but fails at runtime

When creating a Deployment or StatefulSet with an ImageVolume that has an empty `image.reference` field, the API validation passes, but Pod creation fails at runtime. This creates a confusing user experience where workloads appear to be created successfully but never produce running Pods

**Direct Pod creation correctly rejects empty reference:**

**But Deployment/StatefulSet incorrectly accepts it:**

The error only appears in Events when the ReplicaSet controller tries to create Pods:

API validation should reject empty `image.reference` in Pod templates (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, etc.), not just in direct Pod creation.

state:
Support cpu.idle (SCHED_IDLE) for BestEffort QoS to improve isolation and node utilization

Kubelet should start successfully even if `cpu.idle` is enabled for the BestEffort cgroup. Kubelet should either detect that `cpu.idle` is enabled and skip setting `cpu.shares` or `cpu.weight`, or handle the write error gracefully.

1. On a node with a Kernel supporting `cpu.idle` interface (Linux).

2. Manually (or via an external agent) set `cpu.idle` to `1` for the BestEffort slice:

3. Restart Kubelet.
4. Observe the startup failure.

5. Manual verification of the conflict:

- **Context:** We use `cpu.idle` (SCHED_IDLE) for BestEffort tasks to utilize the enhanced scheduling isolation provided by Linux Kernel 5.4+ (Patch: `sched/fair: Improve the scheduling of SCHED_IDLE tasks`). This is often a superior alternative to low `cpu.shares` for maximizing node utilization without interfering with high-priority workloads.

- **Kernel Behavior:** When `cpu.idle` is configured to `1`, the kernel forces `cpu.shares` to `1` and `cpu.weight` to `1` and forbids modification, leading to the Invalid argument error when Kubelet tries to write min shares(or weight)

- **Workaround:** Setting `cpu.idle` back to `0` allows Kubelet to start.

**Proposed Solution:**

1. **Short-term fix (Resilience)**: Modify the Kubelet `qos_container_manager` logic. Before attempting to set `cpu.shares` for the BestEffort cgroup, check if cpu.idle is configured (if the interface exists).

If `cpu.idle == 1`: Skip setting `cpu.shares` and `cpu.weight` (accept the kernel's forced value).

If `cpu.idle == 0` or file does not exist: Proceed with setting `cpu.shares` to `2`and `cpu.weight` to `1`.

2. **Long-term feature**: Add native support in Kubelet configuration to support `cpu.idle` (SCHED_IDLE) for BestEffort pods, allowing users to opt-in to this scheduling policy directly via Kubelet rather than relying on external agents.

**Benefits:**

state:
[kubelet] Unnecessary continuous reconciliation loop for DRA Pods due to non-kubelet-owned fields comparison

For Pods using Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), the kubelet status manager continuously logs "Pod status is inconsistent with cached status" and triggers a reconciliation loop (needsReconcile -> syncPod, every ~10s). This loop is unnecessary because no actual status changes are applied, but it adds avoidable load on kubelet, API server, and etcd.
kubelet log -v=4

The kubelet should ignore non-kubelet-owned fields (ResourceClaimStatuses, ExtendedResourceClaimStatus) during status comparison, and not trigger unnecessary reconciliation loops for DRA Pods.

1. Deploy a Kubernetes cluster with DRA enabled.
2. Create a Pod that uses DRA resources (with ResourceClaim).
3. Observe the kubelet logs and API server/etcd load.
4. Find the continuous "status inconsistent" logs and repeated reconciliation operations.

This issue is caused by the `isPodStatusByKubeletEqual` function comparing the entire Pod status, including fields that are not managed by kubelet (populated by control plane components). A fix is provided in PR #136238.

state:
kubelet saving inconsistent cpu-manager state to checkpoint file

During allocation of CPU resources in CPU manager's static policy and during removal of a container, two modifications to state happen:
* CPU set of the container is changed;
* default CPU set is updated.

CPU manager uses state checkpoint for keeping allocated resources state and after each operation that changes this state, data is saved to checkpoint file.

If the kubelet is interrupted and killed between changing container's CPU set and default CPU set, the state that is saved in checkpoint file is inconsistent.

This can cause:
* **CPU leak** if exclusive CPUs are already removed from default CPU set, but not yet assigned to a container CPU set;
* **CPU leak**, when container and its CPU set is removed from allocated resources, but the CPUs are not returned to default CPU set.

I expect consistent state of cpu sets to be saved to cpu-manager's checkpoint file to properly restore resources after kubelet's restart.

During creation or removal of container using exclusive CPUs:
1) Detect first save operation on filesystem (cpu assignment for container is changed)
2) Restart kubelet before 2nd save operation (or block second save operation and restart kubelet)

I found the issue during review of the cpu-manager's code.
I didn't reproduce it on the cluster.

kubelet saving inconsistent cpu-manager state to checkpoint file

During allocation of CPU resources in CPU manager's static policy and during removal of a container, two modifications to state happen:
* CPU set of the container is changed;
* default CPU set is updated.

CPU manager uses state checkpoint for keeping allocated resources state and after each operation that changes this state, data is saved to checkpoint file.

If the kubelet is interrupted and killed between changing container's CPU set and default CPU set, the state that is saved in checkpoint file is inconsistent.

This can cause:
* **CPU leak** if exclusive CPUs are already removed from default CPU set, but not yet assigned to a container CPU set;
* **CPU leak**, when container and its CPU set is removed from allocated resources, but the CPUs are not returned to default CPU set.

I expect consistent state of cpu sets to be saved to cpu-manager's checkpoint file to properly restore resources after kubelet's restart.

During creation or removal of container using exclusive CPUs:
1) Detect first save operation on filesystem (cpu assignment for container is changed)
2) Restart kubelet before 2nd save operation (or block second save operation and restart kubelet)

I found the issue during review of the cpu-manager's code.
I didn't reproduce it on the cluster.

state:
Some crashed or OOMKilled containers fail to restart in v1.35

After upgrading Kubernetes from v1.34.2 to v1.35.0, we observed a scenario where a pod with multiple containers does not restart a crashed application container, leaving the pod in an Error state indefinitely.

This behavior was not observed on v1.34.2. Reverting the kubelet back to v1.34.2 causes the issue to disappear.

**Observed Behavior:**
The main container terminates but never restarts:

The sidecar container continues to run normally:

Pod conditions show:

No useful logs or errors appear in `kubectl describe pod` output, events, or `kubelet` logs.

**Notes:**
- This issue seems to only affect pods with more than one container
- We are unsure whether it's just pods with an `initContainer` or does it also apply to `container` sidecars
- Manually killing the process in the sidecar container or deleting the pod helps getting it back to working state
- `RestartAllContainersOnContainerExits` is not enabled

**Possibly related?**
- [link]

Containers should reliably restart every time they crash.

The best way we found to reproduce this is by running a pod with 2 containers: an initContainer with `restartPolicy: Always` and an application container that we manually crash with `kill 1` command.
It might not work right first time, but we managed to reproduce this multiple times getting pods stuck in Error state that they never recover from automatically.

state:
image pull credential verification doesn't work

I wanted to use a recently introduced feature called "image pull credential verification". It has been described at:

1. [link]
2. [link]
3. [link]

I execute scenario with following conditions:

1. registry always requires authentication for the image in question
2. two sample pods are created which use the same image
3. pod definition requests to be scheduled to a specific node and it is always started there
4. the node does not have the image locally initially

The scenario:

1. pod A is started in namespace A without specifying service account or image secrets
2. default service account in ns A has a secret attached for the registry in question
3. kubelet pulls the image successfully
4. pod B is started in namespace B, the default service account has no secrets attached
5. pod B is successfully started but it should fail, this is the problem of this issue

sample-device-plugin:1.7 image referenced in test manifest is missing from test/utils/image/manifest.go

The DaemonSet manifest at `test/e2e/testing-manifests/sample-device-plugin/sample-device-plugin.yaml` references the image `registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/sample-device-plugin:1.7`, but this image is not registered in `test/utils/image/manifest.go`. This is inconsistent with how other e2e test images are tracked and can cause problems for downstream projects that need to pre-provision or mirror images for air-gapped or custom test environments.

`sample-device-plugin:1.7` should be added to `test/utils/image/manifest.go` with a new ImageID constant (e.g. `SampleDevicePlugin`) and a corresponding entry in `initImageConfigs`.

Test config issue, not really reproducible outside of test environments that require images to be pre-staged... mostly just look at the image manifest and see that this required image is not present in it.

[PodLevelResources] CPU Request in PodSpec Status.Resources becomes invalid

Hey! Today I noticed what seems to be strange behavior in a Kind cluster (1.35) when using the Pod level resources feature. When I create the following Pod:

in the next kubelet loop, the Pod's `status.resources` stanza is updated to:

The CPU request (from `status.resources`) automatically changes from 50m to 28m. Even for other desired cpu requests the field under `status.resources` shows lower value after the next kubelet loop.

I asked why this was happening on [Slack]([link] and I got a pretty detailed write-up explaining it (shoutout to @user - thanks again!).

Overall, it seems that when the CPU shares are converted to a weight and saved into cpu.weight, another part of the code later converts the weight back to CPU millicores (the read path). The returned value does not match the millicores I originally set, and this value ends up overwriting `status.resources.requests.cpu`.

Furthermore, I created [this]([link] small Go program to replicate the issue. For a 50m request, it returns 28.

The Pod's `status.resources` stanza should remain the same, i.e:

wait until the next kubelet loop, and the Pod's `status.resources` stanza will be updated to:

state:
MemoryQoS does not set memory.high for BestEffort pods on cgroup v2

With `MemoryQoS` enabled on a cgroup v2 node, BestEffort pods do not get a finite memory.high value. Instead, memory.high remains unset and reads as max.

This appears inconsistent with the [MemoryQoS KEP]([link] which says that for BestEffort pods: _requests.memory = 0 limits.memory should be substituted with node allocatable memory in the memory.high formula:_
`memory.high = floor[ (memoryThrottlingFactor * node allocatable memory) / pageSize ] * pageSize`

In the current kubelet implementation, kubelet skips setting memory.high entirely when both memory requests, limits are 0.

For a BestEffort pod on cgroup v2 with MemoryQoS enabled, memory.high is set to the value calculated as the formula defined in the KEP

Prerequisites
- Linux node with cgroup v2 enabled
- kubelet with MemoryQoS=true

Pod manifests

After the pod is running, inspect the pod/container cgroup files on the node.

state:
performance: prune non-preferred branches early in Topology Manager to avoid combinatorial explosion

`Topology Manager`'s `iterateAllProviderTopologyHints` expands the full Cartesian product of all topology hint providers' hint sets. When a provider returns a large number of hints (e.g. Device Manager (GPU device plugin) calling `bitmask.IterateBitMasks` for all NUMA node power sets), this causes exponential time and memory blowup, making the kubelet unresponsive during pod admission. On an 8-NUMA-node system, a single provider can generate 255 (2^8-1) hints, leading to ~4.2 billion merges with 4 providers.

Measured on Apple M4 Pro (arm64):

**Before optimization:**

A single `Admit()` call took 258 seconds and allocated 407 GB of memory.

`Admit()` completes in bounded time. The hint merging algorithm should not degrade to exponential complexity when providers return large hint sets.

To reproduce, first modify the function:

func (m HintMerger) mergePreferred() *TopologyHint {
}

Force it to return nil directly.

Then run the benchmark:

go test ./pkg/kubelet/cm/topologymanager \
-run BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists \
-bench BenchmarkHintMergerPreferredExists \
-benchmem -count=1

The benchmark will run for ~4 minutes and consume several hundred GB of memory, reproducing the performance issue.

state:
Eviction signal is not hugepages aware

On nodes with hugepages configured, the kubelet's memory.available eviction signal overstates real available regular memory by the total hugepage reservation. This causes eviction to fire later than the configured threshold intends, causing OOM kills.

The root cause is that AvailableBytes is computed as root_cgroup.memory.limit - root_cgroup.memory.workingSet, where:
- memory.limit is set to MemTotal from /proc/meminfo (includes hugepage-reserved RAM)
- memory.workingSet comes from the memory cgroup controller (does not track hugetlb allocations — those use a separate controller)

This creates "phantom" available bytes equal to the hugepage reservation. The kernel's own MemAvailable in /proc/meminfo does not have this problem because hugepage-reserved pages are removed from the buddy allocator's free pool at boot and never appear in MemFree.

memory.available should reflect memory available for regular (non-hugepage) allocations.

Configure a node with hugepages.
Query the kubelet summary API: kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/stats/summary".
Observe node.memory.availableBytes — it exceeds what is physically available as regular memory by exactly the hugepage reservation.

The issue can be fixed by subtracting the node's total hugepage capacity from AvailableBytes in the summary stats provider (pkg/kubelet/server/stats/summary.go) before the stats are consumed by the eviction manager. This is a minimal, targeted adjustment at the point where NodeStats.Memory is constructed. It aligns the kubelet's computation with the kernel's own MemAvailable accounting.

state:
kubelet: SyncPod kills liveness-failed containers sequentially, blocking replacement starts

When multiple containers in a pod fail liveness probes, kubelet's `SyncPod()` kills them sequentially in Step 3 — each `killContainer()` call blocks for up to `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` before moving to the next container. Step 8 (start replacements) only runs after the entire Step 3 kill loop finishes.

A container killed early in the loop cannot get its replacement until all sibling kills in the same cycle complete.

Reproduced with 4 containers, `terminationGracePeriodSeconds=30`, and a `preStop` hook that sleeps 25s. All 4 containers shared one liveness file; removing it caused all 4 to fail simultaneously.

Container restart timestamps from `kubectl logs` and `kubectl logs --previous`:

app-b was killed at 07:09:46 but could not restart until 07:10:54 because kubelet was still sequentially killing app-c and app-d in the same Step 3 loop. With longer `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (e.g., 300s for connection draining), the first-killed container in a 4-container cycle would wait **15 minutes** instead of 5.

Additional observations:
- The kill order within a cycle is non-deterministic (`ContainersToKill` is a Go map)
- How many containers end up in each cycle is timing-dependent: `computePodActions()` snapshots the liveness cache; only containers that have already crossed `failureThreshold` at that instant are included

A container's replacement should start as soon as its own kill completes, without waiting for sibling container kills to finish.

The whole-pod kill path (`killContainersWithSyncResult` at `kuberuntime_container.go:886-921`) already kills containers in parallel using goroutines + `sync.WaitGroup`. The per-container liveness restart path should either:
1. Parallelize kills using the same pattern, or
2. Start each replacement immediately after its specific kill completes

Steps:
1. `kubectl apply -f repro.yaml` — wait for 4/4 Running
2.

Step 8 (start replacements) only runs after the entire Step 3 kill loop finishes.

A container killed early in the loop cannot get its replacement until all sibling kills in the same cycle complete.

Reproduced with 4 containers, `terminationGracePeriodSeconds=30`, and a `preStop` hook that sleeps 25s. All 4 containers shared one liveness file; removing it caused all 4 to fail simultaneously.

app-b was killed at 07:09:46 but could not restart until 07:10:54 because kubelet was still sequentially killing app-c and app-d in the same Step 3 loop. - The kill order within a cycle is non-deterministic (`ContainersToKill` is a Go map)
- How many containers end up in each cycle is timing-dependent: `computePodActions()` snapshots the liveness cache; only containers that have already crossed `failureThreshold` at that instant are included

Preloaded image pull spec poisoned by a pulled image

This seems to be a corner case in the "Ensure secret pulled images" [feature]([link]

1. pre-load an image from repo X behind kubelet's back
2. deploy pod A, which references the image from repo X, **without** specifying a pull secret and with `imagePullPolicy: Never`; delete pod A
3. deploy pod B, referencing the same (in terms of identical content digest) image but from a different repo Y, **using** a pull secret and default `imagePullPolicy`; delete pod B
4. deploy the same pod A again -> get `Container image "X..." is not present with pull policy of Never`

Step (4) should continue working if step (1) did.

state:
kubelet: QoS-level memory.min / memory.low is not cleared after MemoryQoS feature gate is disabled (regression from #138430)

After #138430 re-gated the call to `setMemoryQoS` behind `utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(kubefeatures.MemoryQoS)`, disabling the `MemoryQoS` alpha feature gate no longer clears stale `memory.min` / `memory.low` values from QoS-level cgroups (`kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice`, `kubepods.slice/kubepods-guaranteed.slice`, etc.) on cgroup v2 unified systems.

Before #138430, `setMemoryQoS` was invoked unconditionally from `UpdateCgroups` on cgroup v2 unified mode. Its zero-out branch at [`pkg/kubelet/cm/qos_container_manager_linux.go#L303-L308`]([link] resets `memory.min` / `memory.low` to 0 whenever `memoryReservationPolicy != TieredReservation`, which covers the "feature disabled or policy = None" case. With the gate check added at [L358]([link] that zero-out branch is unreachable whenever the gate is off.

This is the QoS-level analogue of the pod-level regression that #137674 / #137726 already address. #137726 added `ReconcilePodMemoryMin` on `podContainerManagerImpl` but does not touch QoS-level cgroups, so the stale values at the QoS level remain indefinitely on any node that previously ran with the alpha gate enabled and was later rolled back.

When MemoryQoS is disabled (feature gate off, or `memoryReservationPolicy = None`), QoS-level `memory.min` / `memory.low` should be reset to 0 on the next `UpdateCgroups` cycle. This matches the explicit assumption in #137674 that "QoS-level cgroups are correctly reset via the periodic `setMemoryQoS()` loop."

1. Cgroup v2 unified node.
2. Start kubelet with `--feature-gates=MemoryQoS=true` and `memoryReservationPolicy: HardReservation`.
3. Create a few Burstable pods so that QoS-level values are populated. Verify:
`cat /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/memory.low` → non-zero.
4.

state:
Kubelet restart triggers UnexpectedAdmissionError for pods using device plugins in both initContainers and containers

Restarting the kubelet causes pods to fail with an UnexpectedAdmissionError when both initContainers and containers use device plugins.

Restart kubelet should not cause running pods to restart

1. Create a pod whose containers and initContainers both use device plugins.
2. Restart kubelet.

pods have initContainers and containers both requesting the same device plugin resources. After kubelet restart, the pod is killed with:

`Allocate failed due to no healthy devices present; cannot allocate unhealthy devices <resource>`

After kubelet restart, the device manager tries to re-allocate for the completed initContainer and fails.

cherry-picked [link] — it does not fix this scenario. This matches the issue reported in [link] and [link]

Kubelet restart triggers UnexpectedAdmissionError for pods using device plugins in both initContainers and containers

Restarting the kubelet causes pods to fail with an UnexpectedAdmissionError when both initContainers and containers use device plugins.

Restart kubelet should not cause running pods to restart

1. Create a pod whose containers and initContainers both use device plugins.
2. Restart kubelet.

pods have initContainers and containers both requesting the same device plugin resources. After kubelet restart, the pod is killed with:

`Allocate failed due to no healthy devices present; cannot allocate unhealthy devices <resource>`

After kubelet restart, the device manager tries to re-allocate for the completed initContainer and fails.

cherry-picked [link] — it does not fix this scenario. This matches the issue reported in [link] and [link]

Routing determination: node.

state:
Kubelet regression in 1.32, 1.31 and possibly 1.33 and 1.34 where pods get stuck in RunContainerError on OS with cgroupv1

We observed a Kubelet regression in 1.32 and 1.31 (and similar symptoms in 1.33 and 1.34) where pods get stuck in `RunContainerError` on Rocky Linux 8.6 OS which uses cgroup v1. While upgrading Kubernetes from 1.30 to 1.31 and 1.32, we observe the issue once we put the node out of maintenance mode.

The issue is observed with Containerd 1.7 and 1.6 as well.

We initially opened this issue [link] however at the time we didn't know what caused the regression and what versions were affected. We performed a git bisect (using GKE internal builds) and identified the regression was introduced in PR [#131018]([link] This commit was merged into 1.34 and backported all the way to 1.31. Kubelet works perfectly in the commits immediately preceding this PR.

Following this commit, we observe a massive spike in masked paths. Given our 96-core machines, the `thermal_throttle` paths alone add 96 new entries to the maskedPaths array for every container:

We suspect that this high volume of masked paths is causing kernel-level starvation or resource exhaustion on our cgroup v1 / Rocky 8.6 nodes when scheduling a large number of multi-container pods.

So far we compiled, we compiled a custom Kubelet that breaks the loop after adding the first `thermal_throttle` path. Under load testing, the system remained completely stable with this patch:

The following kernel settings currently resolve the issue so it is not tracking kernel memory:
* Set the `cgroup.memory=nokmem` config during the OS upgrade.
* Reboot the node as part of the OS upgrade process.
* Upgrade K8s to 1.31

Not tracking kernel memory to mitigate this issue is a big NO for us.

state:
Excessive events generated for Image Volumes (every image, once per minute)

I added 10 image volumes to a pod. Each of those image volumes generates an event on every pod sync. e.g.:

The actual problem this is causing me is a CI failure due to excessive events, but I think this is objectively too many events.

I'm not familiar with this code, but it seems [`getImageVolumes`]([link] which is called from SyncPod re-uses [`EnsureImageExists`]([link] which is also called by `startContainer`. `EnsureImageExists` logs unconditionally, which is where the noise comes from. I suspect this unconditional logging is appropriate in `startContainer`, but perhaps not in `getImageVolumes` when called from the reconcile loop?

Events are not generated for steady state.

Create a pod with an image volume.

state:
CPU manager AddContainer does not write cgroup cpuset, reconciler never corrects mismatches

CPU manager's `AddContainer` sets `lastUpdateState` to the desired cpuset without calling `updateContainerCPUSet` to write the cgroup. The reconciler compares `desired` vs `lastUpdateState` — since they always match, it never detects or corrects cpuset mismatches caused by the container runtime.

Additionally, the cpuset is not applied before the container starts. The container inherits the pod-level cgroup cpuset and only gets the correct dedicated cpuset when the reconciler runs (up to 10 seconds later, if the bug above didn't prevent it entirely).

The container should have its dedicated cpuset written to the cgroup before it starts, and the reconciler should detect and correct any subsequent mismatches.

1. Create a Guaranteed QoS pod with `cpuManagerPolicy: static` and integer CPU requests
2. Check the container's cgroup `cpuset.cpus.effective` immediately after the container starts
3. Compare with `cpu_manager_state` — they may not match
4. Wait 10+ seconds — the reconciler still does not correct the mismatch because `lastUpdateState` was set without writing

Observed on Dell R760xa with KubeVirt VMs using `dedicatedCpuPlacement` + `guestMappingPassthrough`. The compute container's cgroup showed all odd CPUs (NUMA 1) while `cpu_manager_state` showed CPUs 4,6,68,70 (NUMA 0). The mismatch persisted indefinitely.

KubeVirt's virt-launcher reads `cpuset.cpus.effective` once at startup to build guest NUMA topology. With the wrong cpuset, it generated QEMU memory bindings for NUMA 1, but `cpuset.mems` only allowed NUMA 0, causing `set_mempolicy: Invalid argument`.

The bug is in `pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/cpu_manager.go` in the `AddContainer` function.

state:
In-place container memory resize does not work when pod is in status OOMKilled

I have a pod which is in status `OOMKilled`. I want to give the container more memory by doing an in-place container resource resize. Despite the pod having enough memory after the resize, it stays in an OOM crash loop and does not recover.

I would have expected that after the resize, the pod recovers and it starts up correctly.

I'm attaching a standalone application which allows reproducing the bug, please follow the `README` in [memhog.zip]([link]

- I stumbled upon this issue when trying to use in-place updates with the VPA controller. This bug made it fail but the problem is not specific to VPA which is why I'm reporting it here.
- The problem only occurs if the pod is in the status `OOMKilled` when the resize command is run.
- The new memory is set correctly in the cgroup of the **container**. You can see that in the logs of the pod.
- The new memory is **NOT** set correctly in the cgroup of the **pod**. Please check the `README` of the attached example where I show how I checked the cgroup memory on pod level.
- I have the same problem when using AWS EKS (v1.35), where I initially encountered it. The behaviour is the same as on K3d.

state:
In-place container memory resize does not work when pod is in status OOMKilled

I have a pod which is in status `OOMKilled`. I want to give the container more memory by doing an in-place container resource resize. Despite the pod having enough memory after the resize, it stays in an OOM crash loop and does not recover.

I would have expected that after the resize, the pod recovers and it starts up correctly.

I'm attaching a standalone application which allows reproducing the bug, please follow the `README` in [memhog.zip]([link]

- I stumbled upon this issue when trying to use in-place updates with the VPA controller. This bug made it fail but the problem is not specific to VPA which is why I'm reporting it here.
- The problem only occurs if the pod is in the status `OOMKilled` when the resize command is run.
- The new memory is set correctly in the cgroup of the **container**. You can see that in the logs of the pod.
- The new memory is **NOT** set correctly in the cgroup of the **pod**. Please check the `README` of the attached example where I show how I checked the cgroup memory on pod level.
- I have the same problem when using AWS EKS (v1.35), where I initially encountered it. The behaviour is the same as on K3d.

state:
HTTP/TCP probes with unresolved named port return Unknown and hide root cause ("port not found")

For HTTP/TCP liveness/readiness/startup probes, port can be `intstr.IntOrString`.

In [ResolveContainerPort]([link] does:
- try `findPortByName` for `intstr.String`
- if not found, fallback to `strconv.Atoi(param.StrVal)`

When probe uses a named port and name is wrong/missing (for example `controller`), kubelet emits:

Then prober returns `probe.Unknown` in [runProbe]([link]

Why this is problematic:
- Real reason (`port <name> not found`) is hidden by `strconv.Atoi` parse error.
- Behavior is inconsistent with numeric-port probes:
- `int` port with unreachable endpoint -> regular probe failure path.
- bad named port -> repeated `Unknown` events, not failure semantics.
- API validation for port names ([IsValidPortName]([link] requires at least one letter, so pure numeric strings are not valid named ports anyway; `Atoi` fallback in string branch is effectively misleading.

If probe port is `intstr.String` and named port is not found:
- return explicit error like `port "<name>" not found` (no `Atoi` parse noise),
- and consider handling this case as probe `Failure` instead of `Unknown` to match practical liveness behavior.

Suggested direction:
1. Remove `Atoi` fallback from string branch in `ResolveContainerPort`.
2. Optionally add typed `ErrPortNotFound` and map it to `Failure` in prober.

state:
CPUManager shrinks multi-NUMA TopologyManager affinity when distributing exclusive CPUs across NUMA

We observed that CPUManager receives a multi-NUMA affinity selected by TopologyManager, but the final exclusive CPU allocation is still shrunk to fewer NUMA nodes.

The node topology is:

- 256 logical CPUs
- 4 NUMA nodes
- 8 GPUs distributed across all 4 NUMA nodes
- NICs also distributed across all 4 NUMA nodes

Kubelet configuration:

The pod requests:

TopologyManager selects an all-NUMA affinity because the pod requests 8 GPUs distributed across all 4 NUMA nodes:

CPUManager receives this affinity:

However, the final CPU allocation only uses 3 NUMA nodes:

So CPUManager appears to treat the TopologyManager affinity as an allowed NUMA set, then reselects the minimum number of NUMA nodes needed to satisfy the CPU request.

On this node, 176 CPUs can fit into 3 NUMA nodes, so the final CPUSet is distributed roughly as:

This is not aligned with the GPU/NIC topology selected by TopologyManager.

When TopologyManager selects a multi-NUMA affinity and passes it to CPUManager, CPUManager should preserve that topology intent when allocating exclusive CPUs.

In this case, since the 8 GPUs and NICs span all 4 NUMA nodes, we expected the exclusive CPU allocation to also cover all 4 NUMA nodes, roughly:

At minimum, there should be an opt-in CPUManager static policy option to distribute exclusive CPUs across all NUMA nodes in the TopologyManager affinity, instead of shrinking the allocation back to the
minimum number of NUMA nodes required by the CPU request.

1. Use a node with this topology:

2. Configure kubelet with static CPUManager and NUMA distribution:

3. Create a Guaranteed pod requesting 8 GPUs and 176 exclusive CPUs:

4. Check kubelet logs for TopologyManager and CPUManager allocation:

5. Observe that TopologyManager selects the all-NUMA affinity, but CPUManager allocates the final CPUSet from only 3 NUMA nodes.

apiserver: return 4xx instead of 500 when pod runtimeClassName is empty

The Kubernetes API Server returns HTTP 500 Internal Server Error when creating a Pod whose `spec.runtimeClassName` is set to an empty string.

The following request sets `spec.runtimeClassName` to `""`:

Actual response:

The request is invalid or incomplete, but the API Server returns an internal server error.

The API Server should return a client-side error, such as HTTP 400 Bad Request or HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity, instead of HTTP 500 Internal Server Error.

Since `spec.runtimeClassName` is invalid when it is an empty string, the error should be reported as a validation error rather than an internal server error.

1. Start a Kubernetes cluster with an affected version.
2. Start a local API proxy:

3. Send the following request:

4. Observe that the API Server returns HTTP 500:

This issue was found during RESTful API fuzzing of the Kubernetes API Server.

The request is invalid because `runtimeClassName` is empty and the Pod body is incomplete. However, this should not be surfaced as HTTP 500. It appears that an empty `runtimeClassName` is propagated to runtime class lookup logic and reported as an internal error.

This behavior is reproducible in my tests on Kubernetes v1.33.1 and v1.36.0.

state:
apiserver: return non-500 response for node proxy request when node has no preferred addresses

When sending a node proxy request to a Node object that does not contain any usable address in `status.addresses`, the API Server returns HTTP 500.

The error message indicates that no preferred node address can be selected:

bash
kubectl proxy --port=8001
bash
curl -X POST '[link] \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
--data-raw '{
"apiVersion": "v1",
"kind": "Node",
"metadata": {
"name": "fixed"
}
}'
bash
curl -X POST '[link]
bash
{
"kind": "Status",
"apiVersion": "v1",
"metadata": {},
"status": "Failure",
"message": "no preferred addresses found; known addresses: []",
"code": 500
}
bash
curl -X DELETE '[link]

state:
kubelet CleanSubPaths can leave pods stuck Terminating when subPath target stat returns ENOENT but mountinfo still has the mount

A pod using a CSI volume with `volumeMount.subPath` got stuck in `Terminating`.

The workload container had already exited, but kubelet repeatedly failed during volume cleanup before calling CSI `NodeUnpublishVolume`.

Example kubelet logs:

If a subPath target path returns ENOENT but the mount is still present in mountinfo, kubelet should not skip cleanup and then fail on the parent directory with directory not empty.

Kubelet should either detect the stale/deleted mountpoint from mountinfo and attempt to unmount it, or re-check/re-walk remaining subPath entries before failing the parent directory removal.

We do not yet have a manifest-only reproducer. The key failure state is:

state:
DRA ResourceSlice validation panics on zero validRange.step

DRA `ResourceSlice` validation can panic with `runtime error: integer divide by zero` when `DRAConsumableCapacity` is enabled and a capacity request policy contains `validRange.step: 0`.

The panic happens in `pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation.go` because `validateRequestPolicyRangeStep` computes a modulo with `step.Value()` without first rejecting a zero step value:

When `step` is the zero quantity, `stepVal == 0`, so `added % stepVal` panics.

Validation should reject zero or non-positive `validRange.step` values with a normal field validation error. It should not panic.

Expected behavior:

- `validRange.step: 0` returns a validation error such as `step must be greater than 0`.
- ResourceSlice create/update validation remains fail-closed and does not panic.

This is reproducible with a local focused Go test. The minimal shape is a `ResourceSlice` device with `AllowMultipleAllocations: true`, capacity, and a request policy whose `validRange.step` is zero while `DRAConsumableCapacity` is enabled.

Example test outline:

Observed local output from the focused test:

I also verified the REST strategy path reaches validation after `PrepareForCreate` when the feature gate is enabled, and that when `DRAConsumableCapacity` is disabled the relevant fields are dropped before validation.

The issue is validation robustness for DRA consumable capacity request policies.

The fix should reject zero/non-positive steps before calling `validateRequestPolicyRangeStep`. It may also be worth adding regression coverage for create/update validation paths in `pkg/registry/resource/resourceslice`.

Suggested fix shape:

state:
DRA ResourceSlice validation panics on zero validRange.step

DRA `ResourceSlice` validation can panic with `runtime error: integer divide by zero` when `DRAConsumableCapacity` is enabled and a capacity request policy contains `validRange.step: 0`.

The panic happens in `pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation.go` because `validateRequestPolicyRangeStep` computes a modulo with `step.Value()` without first rejecting a zero step value:

When `step` is the zero quantity, `stepVal == 0`, so `added % stepVal` panics.

Validation should reject zero or non-positive `validRange.step` values with a normal field validation error. It should not panic.

Expected behavior:

- `validRange.step: 0` returns a validation error such as `step must be greater than 0`.
- ResourceSlice create/update validation remains fail-closed and does not panic.

This is reproducible with a local focused Go test. The minimal shape is a `ResourceSlice` device with `AllowMultipleAllocations: true`, capacity, and a request policy whose `validRange.step` is zero while `DRAConsumableCapacity` is enabled.

Example test outline:

Observed local output from the focused test:

I also verified the REST strategy path reaches validation after `PrepareForCreate` when the feature gate is enabled, and that when `DRAConsumableCapacity` is disabled the relevant fields are dropped before validation.

The issue is validation robustness for DRA consumable capacity request policies.

The fix should reject zero/non-positive steps before calling `validateRequestPolicyRangeStep`. It may also be worth adding regression coverage for create/update validation paths in `pkg/registry/resource/resourceslice`.

Suggested fix shape:

Routing determination: node.

state:
[SIG NODE Discussion] Metrics and dashboards for monitoring SIG-Node CI test failures and bug triage health

### Context
In the recent SIG-Node CI subgroup meetings (6/10/2026), we discussed the need to better track our CI stability and test degradation over time.

Currently, we are manually tracking the status of our Testgrid dashboards in a [Spreadsheet Tracker]([link] before every meeting. We document the current status (Passing/Flaky/Failing) of the jobs and link them to tracking GitHub issues, but doing this manually makes it hard to see historic data and trends.

### Goals
We would like to gather community input on what metrics, tooling, and dashboards we should use to automate this monitoring. For starters, we can try to answer questions like:
* How long has a specific test or job been failing?
* Is a recurring failure caused by the same error or a new regression?
* How long do SIG-Node CI bugs remain open?
* How many `important-soon` bugs do we currently have, and what is their average resolution time?
Please recommend any more you think of, open to all suggestions!!

### Existing Efforts & Ideas
* We dug up an [existing dashboard started by dims]([link] but we need to determine how persistent this data is, how it's generated, and how we can best utilize or adapt it.
* Could we leverage existing Kubernetes `test-infra` tooling (like BigQuery metrics/[Kettle]([link] `k8s-triage` in the [aggregated failures dashboard]([link] to automate the data we currently put in our manual spreadsheet?

### Call to Action
We are opening this issue to invite ideas from the CI/CD community.
1. What metrics do you think are most important for us to track?
2. Are there existing dashboards or tools in the Kubernetes ecosystem we should be leveraging?
3. Any volunteers interested in helping build out or maintain this reporting?

Please drop your thoughts and suggestions below!

[SIG NODE Discussion] Metrics and dashboards for monitoring SIG-Node CI test failures and bug triage health

### Context
In the recent SIG-Node CI subgroup meetings (6/10/2026), we discussed the need to better track our CI stability and test degradation over time.

Currently, we are manually tracking the status of our Testgrid dashboards in a [Spreadsheet Tracker]([link] before every meeting. We document the current status (Passing/Flaky/Failing) of the jobs and link them to tracking GitHub issues, but doing this manually makes it hard to see historic data and trends.

### Goals
We would like to gather community input on what metrics, tooling, and dashboards we should use to automate this monitoring. For starters, we can try to answer questions like:
* How long has a specific test or job been failing?
* Is a recurring failure caused by the same error or a new regression?
* How long do SIG-Node CI bugs remain open?
* How many `important-soon` bugs do we currently have, and what is their average resolution time?
Please recommend any more you think of, open to all suggestions!!

### Existing Efforts & Ideas
* We dug up an [existing dashboard started by dims]([link] but we need to determine how persistent this data is, how it's generated, and how we can best utilize or adapt it.
* Could we leverage existing Kubernetes `test-infra` tooling (like BigQuery metrics/[Kettle]([link] `k8s-triage` in the [aggregated failures dashboard]([link] to automate the data we currently put in our manual spreadsheet?

### Call to Action
We are opening this issue to invite ideas from the CI/CD community.
1. What metrics do you think are most important for us to track?
2. Are there existing dashboards or tools in the Kubernetes ecosystem we should be leveraging?
3. Any volunteers interested in helping build out or maintain this reporting?

Please drop your thoughts and suggestions below!

cc: @user

Routing determination: node. Bug assessment: not a bug.

state:
Supporting concurrent processing of PLEG events is needed

In kubelet, [GenericPLEG.Relist]([link] periodically retrieves Pods/Containers from the container runtime and compares them with the information in memory to update the cache. When there are a large number of changes to containers on a single node (our production scenario already supports up to 300, although the default is currently 110 Pods), this process can take a significant amount of time, even exceeding 3 minutes. Therefore, we believe that parallel processing should be supported in this area.

In [GenericPLEG.Relist]([link] updates to the cache can be processed concurrently.

This problem is not always reproduced. However, when a large number of pods or containers exist on a node, this problem may be triggered.

state:
DRA: allocator clears DeviceAllocationConfiguration.Requests too aggressively, widening a per-request config to the whole claim

The DRA structured allocator post-processes allocated configs to drop a `DeviceAllocationConfiguration.Requests` list to `nil` when the config "applies to all requests" (the *empty means all* semantic). It decides this with a length comparison:

`len(config.Requests) == len(claim.Spec.Devices.Requests)` is **not** equivalent to "this config covers every request in the claim", because `config.Requests` entries may be sub-request references of the form `"<request>/<subRequest>"` the allocator matches them that way a few lines earlier:

A config that references **N sub-requests of a single parent request** has `len(config.Requests) == N`. If the claim has **N top-level requests**, the lengths match even though the config covers only one of them so its `Requests` is cleared and the config is silently re-scoped to **every** request in the claim.

The same defect is present in all three production implementations:
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go` (the cleanup loop)
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/incubating/allocator_incubating.go`
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go`

A config that references only sub-requests of one request should remain scoped to that request. `Requests` should be cleared to `nil` (the "applies to all" form) only when the config actually covers **all** top-level requests in the claim.

Add this case to the shared table in `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/allocatortesting/allocator_testing.go` (`TestAllocator`) and run `go test ./structured/internal/experimental/ -run 'TestAllocator/repro-config-subrequests-not-all'` (fails identically for `incubating` and `stable`):

state:
kubelet memory growth: `startPodSync` `context` memory leak on every `SyncPod`

On a single-node cluster of `1.36.0-do.1` with 8-day uptime, `kubelet` process memory grows holding almost a million cancelable contexts:

`startPodSync` creates a context and stores `status.cancelFn`:

[link]

This can overwrite the previous cancelFn without cancelling it, leaking the context.

There doesn't appear to be anything that calls the `cancelFn` in the normal `SyncPod` success case.

Per [context docs]([link]

Failing to call the CancelFunc leaks the child and its children until the parent is canceled.

Stable memory usage

state:
[kubelet] Make AllocationManager the source of truth for pod allocations

This was the intention, but there are some outstanding issues today:

- Not all components that should handle allocated pods do.
- Proposal: Expose pod getter functions on AllocationManager to get the allocated pod. Audit callers of PodManager to identify components that should be migrated to calling AllocationManager instead. Open to discussing alternative architectures.
- `getAllocatedPods` first calls `getActivePods` and then filters the list. We should make the allocation the source of truth. This requires ensuring that the Allocation is promptly removed for terminated pods.

See also [link]

state:
[kubelet] Calling UpdatePod on an untracked but terminated pod should mark it as terminated, not terminating

The first call to `UpdatePod` for a failed (rejected) pod sets `terminatingAt` but doesn't set `termitatedAt` because we need to run `SyncTerminatingPod` to clean up:

[link]

However, the first time we enter the pod worker loop, I'm pretty sure we end up saying the pod can never start, and exit the worker loop:

[link]

[link]

[link]

[link]

Unless I'm missing something, this looks like a bug with how we handle clean up in this case. But, if that cleanup isn't actually necessary, then maybe we can just set the `terminatedAt` timestamp immediately for the failed pod, which would cause it to be considered inactive.

Note: There is a test case that is suppose to cover this, but since the test uses a fake cache implementation that doesn't match the defaulting logic of the real cache, it skips over the code that generates the terminating sync status.

[link]

The final mapped value is:

The kubelet persisted user namespace state for this pod confirms the same terminal range:

state:
DRA-backed extended resources do not report ResourceHealthStatus in PodStatus

When a Pod uses an extended resource backed by Dynamic Resource Allocation, kubelet prepares the generated special ResourceClaim and injects the CDI devices, but it does not populate `pod.status.containerStatuses[].allocatedResourcesStatus` for those resources.
﻿
For DRA-backed extended resources, the container request is in `container.Resources.Requests`, not in `container.Resources.Claims`, so the health status update path never considers `pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus.RequestMappings`.
﻿
As a result, DRA-backed extended resources can be prepared and passed into the container, but their health is not reflected in PodStatus.

When `ResourceHealthStatus` is enabled and a DRA plugin reports health for a device allocated via a DRA-backed extended resource, kubelet should publish that health in `pod.status.containerStatuses[].allocatedResourcesStatus`.
﻿
The reported status should correspond to the generated special ResourceClaim and request from `pod.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus.requestMappings`.

﻿
The reported status should correspond to the generated special ResourceClaim and request from `pod.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus.requestMappings`.

state:
Kubelet UID-qualified exec/run routes ignore mismatched pod UID during pod resolution

While investigating kubelet streaming endpoints, I noticed that the UID-qualified `exec` and `run` routes do not appear to enforce the supplied pod UID during pod resolution.

Routes:

parse and forward the UID, but the underlying lookup prefers the pod full name whenever it is available.

As a result, a request using a stale or mismatched UID can still resolve successfully to the currently running pod with the same namespace/name.

I initially treated this as a potential security concern and performed a deeper investigation of the authorization path.

After tracing the complete request flow multiple times, I could not identify any authorization bypass or privilege escalation. Authorization is already enforced before these handlers, so the observed behavior appears to be a correctness/consistency issue rather than a security issue.

I have reproduced and re-verified this behavior twice using the existing runtime tests and local code tracing.

When a UID-qualified kubelet route is used and a non-empty pod UID is supplied, the request should require both:

- pod full name
- pod UID

to match the current pod.

For example:

should be rejected instead of resolving to the recreated pod.

This would also make the behavior consistent with the existing `attach` and `port-forward` implementations, which explicitly reject UID mismatches.

The existing runtime test already documents the lookup precedence.

Run:

The test demonstrates that:

returns the pod identified by its full name even when the supplied UID belongs to a different pod.

Relevant request flow:

I reproduced this behavior twice during investigation and obtained the same result both times.

Additional investigation:

- Traced the complete kubelet exec/run request path.
- Compared behavior with `attach` and `port-forward`.
- Verified that authorization occurs before the streaming handlers.

state:
kubelet /configz leaks --manifest-url-header credentials (Authorization / API keys)

kubelet exposes its resolved `KubeletConfiguration` at the `/configz` endpoint. When kubelet is run with `--manifest-url` and `--manifest-url-header` carrying credentials (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …` or `X-API-Key: …`), those header values **are returned in cleartext** by `GET /configz`, with no masking.

The codebase already knows these values are secret: the internal type tags the field `datapolicy:"token"`:

…and the **logging** path masks it before printing (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:288-291`):

But the **`/configz`** path does not. `setConfigz` (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:558-569`) converts the *original, un-masked* internal config to the external `v1beta1.KubeletConfiguration` and registers it:

`configz` then serializes registered objects with plain `json.Marshal` (`staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/configz/configz.go:129-145`), so the header values ship out verbatim. The v1beta1 field is a plain `map[string][]string` with no custom marshaler and no `datapolicy` tag, so nothing redacts it.

`/configz` is installed on kubelet's authenticated server (`pkg/kubelet/server/server.go:648`) and runs through the auth chain (`pkg/kubelet/server/auth.go:108-109`): with `KubeletFineGrainedAuthz` it maps to `nodes/configz`; otherwise it falls under `nodes/proxy`.

`/configz` should mask `StaticPodURLHeader` exactly as the logging path does (`server.go:288-291`) — on a deep copy before registration via `setConfigz`/`initConfigz` (`server.go:558-579, 775-776`), or omit the field from external JSON. The existing `datapolicy:"token"` tag and the logging mask express the intent; `/configz` silently bypasses both. Redaction must not depend on operators avoiding sensitive headers, since the field is the documented place to put upstream auth.

Copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root).

kubelet logs --manifest-url-header credentials (Authorization / API keys) to runtime logs

When kubelet is configured with `--manifest-url` and credential-bearing `--manifest-url-header` values (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …` or `X-API-Key: …`), those header values are written to kubelet runtime logs at startup, in cleartext.

At static-pod source init, `makePodSourceConfig` copies the config map into a plain `http.Header` and logs it directly:

The codebase already knows this field is secret and masks it elsewhere:

…and the *config-dump* path redacts it before logging the full `KubeletConfiguration` (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:287-290` masks the map to `<masked>`). But `makePodSourceConfig` logs the **runtime `http.Header` copy**, not the config map — so neither the `datapolicy:"token"` tag nor the logging-mask applies, and the header values ship out verbatim. (`datapolicy` only fires on a strongly-typed field argument; here the value has been flattened into an `http.Header` passed as a generic `"header"` argument.)

`makePodSourceConfig` should not log the header values. The `datapolicy:"token"` tag and the `server.go:287-290` config-mask both express the intent that `StaticPodURLHeader` is secret; this code path bypasses both by logging a runtime copy. The sink should mask/drop the `header` field (e.g. log only that headers are present, or redact like the config-dump path does). Redaction must not depend on operators avoiding sensitive headers, since the field is the documented place to put upstream auth.

Copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). It drops a same-package Go test under `pkg/kubelet` that calls the real `makePodSourceConfig` with a custom `logr` sink capturing klog output, sets `Authorization: Bearer static-pod-url-secret`, and asserts the secret appears in the captured logs. Cleans up after itself; no cluster or running kubelet needed.

state:
Excessive "Label not found" V(4) logs for optional container annotations flood kubelet logs and cause rapid disk space consumption

When kubelet runs with `--v=4` (a common debug level), the log is continuously flooded with lines like:

In a kubemark cluster, this was observed to run continuously and consume disk space rapidly, with approximately 220 pods (2 containers per pod) running on each node.

Logging "Label not found" for optional annotations at V(4) might be too verbose, since these labels are typically absent for many containers. It would be better to raise the log level so it doesn't appear during typical debug verbosity, or perhaps consider removing the line entirely.

1. Run kubelet with --v=4.
2. Schedule a high density of pods on the node (e.g., ~200 pods), whose containers have no preStop handler, no ports, and whose pod has no deletionGracePeriodSeconds (i.e. almost every pod).
3. Observe the three "Label not found" lines being emitted continuously during pod syncs, consuming disk space rapidly.

Commit [ab839c93]([link]

In `pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/labels.go`, the "Label not found" logs are emitted by `getInt64PointerFromLabel` and `getJSONObjectFromLabel` whenever a label is absent.

These labels are only written conditionally in `newContainerAnnotations`:

`podDeletionGracePeriodLabel` — only if `pod.DeletionGracePeriodSeconds != nil`
`containerPreStopHandlerLabel` — only if `container.Lifecycle.PreStop != nil`
`containerPortsLabel` — only if `len(container.Ports) > 0`
Since these conditions are not met for most containers, the labels are expected to be missing. However, `getContainerInfoFromAnnotations` is called on every status lookup, triggering the log on the normal path.

state:
kubelet HTTP probe logs probe `httpHeaders` (Authorization / Cookie / API keys) at -v=4

When kubelet runs an HTTP liveness/readiness/startup probe, it logs probe parameters at verbosity `-v=4` — and the logged fields include the raw `HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders` values taken directly from the PodSpec:

`headers := p.HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders` is the user-supplied header list with **no redaction**, emitted into the `"headers"` structured field.

The kubelet prober should not log raw probe `httpHeaders`. The `"headers"` field should be dropped or redacted (e.g. log only header names, or omit the value) in the `HTTP-Probe` line at `prober.go:173` — matching how other secret-bearing probe fields are handled. As written, attacker/operator-supplied credential headers are emitted verbatim into verbose logs.

copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). state:
Evaluate node stability risks and support hybrid workload Memory QoS in KEP 2570

### Problem: KEP-2570 `memory.min` Introduces Node Stability Risks & Bin-Packing Regressions

The current Memory QoS (KEP-2570) implementation brings vital cgroups v2 protections, but enforcing `memory.min` as the default, one-size-fits-all solution for Guaranteed pods creates severe operational risks for mixed workloads.

Mapping memory requests to the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) is structurally necessary to satisfy node-local agents (NRI plugins, telemetry daemons) without injecting synchronous HTTP calls to the `kube-apiserver` during pod startup. However, the chosen cgroup primitive (`memory.min` for Guaranteed) fundamentally breaks node elasticity.

#### 1. The `memory.min` Bin-Packing Problem

The KEP assumes all Guaranteed pods require strict, kernel-level memory locking. In reality, users often set requests equal to limits solely to prevent Kubelet eviction (e.g., for ML inference or periodic batch jobs). These workloads might allocate a large heap but sit idle for long periods. When mapped to `memory.min`, the kernel is legally forbidden from reclaiming their idle page cache. Locking unused memory behind a hard wall destroys the node's ability to safely maximize resource utilization and share capacity with neighboring pods.

#### 2. Behavioral Shifts and Starvation

Because the Kubelet applies this logic universally by default via `TieredReservation`, existing cluster behavior will change drastically. When Guaranteed pods hoard idle cache behind a node-wide `memory.min` wall, the node exhausts shareable memory much faster. During memory pressure, instead of gracefully and proportionally reclaiming page cache, the kernel hits a hard wall and is forced to immediately OOM-kill BestEffort and Burstable pods.

#### 3. Node-Level Enforcement Breaks Mixed Workloads

Relying exclusively on node-level configurations forces a single profile onto all workloads.

### Problem: KEP-2570 `memory.min` Introduces Node Stability Risks & Bin-Packing Regressions

The current Memory QoS (KEP-2570) implementation brings vital cgroups v2 protections, but enforcing `memory.min` as the default, one-size-fits-all solution for Guaranteed pods creates severe operational risks for mixed workloads.

Mapping memory requests to the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) is structurally necessary to satisfy node-local agents (NRI plugins, telemetry daemons) without injecting synchronous HTTP calls to the `kube-apiserver` during pod startup. However, the chosen cgroup primitive (`memory.min` for Guaranteed) fundamentally breaks node elasticity.

#### 1. The `memory.min` Bin-Packing Problem

The KEP assumes all Guaranteed pods require strict, kernel-level memory locking. In reality, users often set requests equal to limits solely to prevent Kubelet eviction (e.g., for ML inference or periodic batch jobs). These workloads might allocate a large heap but sit idle for long periods. When mapped to `memory.min`, the kernel is legally forbidden from reclaiming their idle page cache. Locking unused memory behind a hard wall destroys the node's ability to safely maximize resource utilization and share capacity with neighboring pods.

#### 2. Behavioral Shifts and Starvation

Because the Kubelet applies this logic universally by default via `TieredReservation`, existing cluster behavior will change drastically. When Guaranteed pods hoard idle cache behind a node-wide `memory.min` wall, the node exhausts shareable memory much faster. During memory pressure, instead of gracefully and proportionally reclaiming page cache, the kernel hits a hard wall and is forced to immediately OOM-kill BestEffort and Burstable pods.

#### 3. Node-Level Enforcement Breaks Mixed Workloads

Relying exclusively on node-level configurations forces a single profile onto all workloads.

Routing determination: node.
